text:
While Peruvian citizens protested the U.S. Secretary of State's visit, the country has—from another perspective—become the latest battleground in the Western Hemisphere where the U.S. seeks to suppress China's presence, following Panama and Venezuela.

Before visiting Peru, Rubio criticized the influx of capital into Latin America from outside the hemisphere—specifically from China—claiming such investments entail "opaque contracts, unsustainable debt, labor exploitation, and environmental damage," and urging Latin American nations to be wary of external forces.

Last December, the Trump administration released a new National Security Strategy designating the Western Hemisphere as a top strategic priority; the document was viewed internationally as a "new Monroe Doctrine." Since then, the U.S. has launched a series of actions to push back against Chinese influence in Latin America.

Washington first targeted Panama, intervening to strip Hong Kong-based Hutchison Whampoa of its contractual rights to operate ports at both ends of the Panama Canal—a move that sparked firm opposition from China. In January of this year, the U.S. launched a surprise operation to seize Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro and bring him to the United States. Subsequently, the U.S. pushed for oil cooperation agreements between Venezuela and American companies. In late August, Trump claimed on social media that the U.S. had secured majority control over Venezuela's 65 billion barrels of oil reserves through such agreements; U.S. officials even declared that Venezuelan crude oil shipments to China would require U.S. approval.

Now, the U.S. is attempting to make a move in Peru. Peru held a presidential election this past June, won by Keiko Fujimori—a candidate of Japanese descent who is regarded as a right-wing figure. Across Latin America, the continent is currently experiencing a wave of right-wing governments coming to power. However, securing influence over Peru will not be easy for the U.S. As early as 2015, when U.S. officials learned of plans by Chinese enterprises to build the Port of Chancay in Peru, the Peruvian ambassador to Washington, Castilla, faced stern questioning from the U.S. side: Why was Peru handing over a strategic South American foothold to China? Castilla’s response was blunt: the Peruvian promoters of the port "knocked on doors across the U.S. and Europe, but no one answered; consequently, any void left behind would inevitably be filled by others."

The Port of Chancay is being developed as a joint venture between COSCO SHIPPING and a local Peruvian mining company, with COSCO holding a 60% stake. The project involves a total investment of $3.5 to $3.6 billion, with the first phase scheduled to begin commercial operations in June 2025. The port cuts the direct shipping time between Peru and China to 23 days—down from approximately 40 days via traditional routes—and has already become Peru's second-largest container port; it also serves as a transshipment hub for exports from Chile, Ecuador, and Brazil destined for Asia.

The U.S. State Department has repeatedly issued statements claiming that Chinese control over the port threatens Peru's sovereignty and even speculating that it could become a Chinese military foothold in South America; there was even a proposal to impose a steep 60% tariff on goods transshipped through the port. However, Peruvian officials have explicitly refuted these claims, noting that the Port of Chancay operates under the full supervision of the Peruvian Port Authority, customs, the Ministry of Transport, and the police, rather than functioning as an unregulated extraterritorial facility. The port also faced legal challenges in 2026: in February, a constitutional court in Lima ruled that regulators could not interfere with port operations, but on July 1, the Second Constitutional Chamber of the Lima Superior Court overturned that ruling, restoring the authority of the regulator, Ositrán, to oversee the port and sanction the operator. COSCO SHIPPING subsequently appealed to Peru's Constitutional Court, and the case is currently pending.

Although new President Keiko Fujimori belongs to the right-wing camp and has expressed a willingness to deepen security cooperation with the U.S.—including joining the U.S.-led "Shield of the Americas" alliance—she has shown absolutely no intention of excluding Chinese companies or severing economic and trade ties with China. In her inaugural address to Congress, she positioned Peru as a bridge connecting Latin America and Asia; this stance is underpinned by the economic reality that China has been Peru's largest trading partner for 12 consecutive years, purchasing approximately one-third of the country's exports. When the 2008 global financial crisis caused a collapse in demand for minerals from Europe and the United States, it was the Chinese market that absorbed Peru's exports of copper, iron, and other minerals, thereby stabilizing the Peruvian economy. Since the China-Peru Free Trade Agreement took effect, Peru has accumulated a trade surplus of $52 billion with China; in contrast, more than a decade after signing a free trade agreement with the U.S., Peru has instead incurred a cumulative trade deficit of $17.3 billion.

In contrast, U.S. engagement with Peru has largely consisted of arms procurement projects funded by Peru itself; a U.S.-backed push for Peru to purchase 24 F-16 fighter jets—at a total cost of $3.5 billion—sparked immense controversy within the country. Former Ambassador to the U.S. Castilla pointedly asked why such a massive sum was being spent on fighter jets rather than on areas affecting public welfare, such as education and healthcare. Cynthia Sanborn, a scholar at the University of the Pacific in Lima, offered a trenchant assessment of the U.S. attitude: "The U.S. comes along and says, 'Oh, you are losing your sovereignty.' It smacks of a paternalistic, 'big-daddy' mentality." Latin American economist Enrique Dussel Peters noted that Chinese enterprises have implemented over 300 infrastructure projects in Latin America, with a total investment exceeding $130 billion, yet "Washington treats Peru's trade with China as an ideological issue, ignoring the fact that it meets a fundamental economic need for Latin American nations—acting as if a single political decision could overnight erase China's vast economic presence in the Americas."

If the U.S. wishes to displace China in Latin American countries, it must match that presence with equivalent investment; otherwise, severing economic ties with China would amount to Latin America voluntarily marginalizing itself from the global economy. Latin Americans see the situation clearly: what the U.S. desires is a Western Hemisphere that is politically "clean"—free from the influence of other major powers and lying right beside the U.S. like a "backyard"—where poverty is accepted as Latin America's destiny and the sacrifice it must make for U.S. hegemony.

The U.S. might achieve temporary success in small nations like Panama, but in major Latin American economies, its policies will face natural resistance from the public. Even right-wing governments in the region have no desire to become sacrificial lambs for Trump's discriminatory policies toward Latin America. Should these nations lose Chinese investment and access to China’s vast trading market, their economies would plummet, and their incumbent governments would rapidly lose voter support and fall from power; consequently, they are compelled to weigh the choice between aligning with the U.S. and safeguarding their own national interests and political stability. Even Argentine President Milei—a natural ally of Donald Trump—has not disrupted trade cooperation with China.

Ideological slogans cannot resolve the challenges of foreign currency shortages and economic recession—a reality that all Latin American leaders must confront. https://t.co/5hzi4T45TU

text:
Got a @GoogleCloud account? You could wake up with an 87K debt tomorrow morning. And there is nothing you can do about it.

I will remember this moment forever, early August (last month). I had gone shopping with my family in Zakynthos. I logged into my bank account to see if I had to move funds to cover a payment. And there it was.

A failed attempted charge of 87K Eur.
By Google Cloud Services,

I told my wife that I had been hacked. We left the store. I left for Athens, the next morning.

Long story short. I bought a macbook in July and I was in a rush to set it up to take it with us on vacation. I searched for Claude Code, clicked on the first result (identified to be a Google paid ad during a later investigation), and it took me to Anthropic. I checked the domain, the page looked like the page I remembered, so I downloaded the file and installed. During the installaiton something felt funny and I stopped. I ran Bitdefender full scan. It found nothing.

2 weeks later, I got the bill by Google Cloud Services. I will spare you the investigation details, the forensics, other attempts of the hacker, the police, and the dozens of emails it took just to get GCC support to take this seriously and escalate.

Yesterday, GCC told me that they will do "a courtesy" and erase 65K, leaving my company with a 22K debt.

Now think about this.
@GoogleAds was paid to advertise a link with a virus
My paid @gmail account was hacked
My @googlecloud account was hacked as a result. The hacker used a seemingly PAID @gmail account.
Google has the details of the perpetrator (gmail paid account + google ads, both demand a credit card).
Google, google, google...

Now, Goole ads is NOT reasponsible if they advertise links with viruses as per tos.
Gmail and Chrome come without security guarantees, obviously.
GCC offers NO way for a user to put an absolute cap on their spending.
But I, the user, am reasponsible and wil be held liable.
 
Should I thank GCC for the "courtesy" to cut down my bill? No, I don't think so. I am gonna take this as far as it goes and won't pay a dime.

To be clear. This is not myself carelessly sharing an API key. This was a criminal compromise of my system and the Greek police is on it, but this does nothing to my debt.

My normal monthly bills with GCC are about 150 Eur. My Gemini Tier was 1 (free) or 2. So, I am a tiny fish. If this happened to me, it can happen to any fish.

To conclude. If a company like Google can 1) show ads infected with viruses with no real acountability, 2) fail to protect its users at its own auth layer, and 3) force a debt on compromised accounts as a result of 1 and 2, then, I am afraid that our world has a second problem. Not only are we not ready from an IT point of view for the cyber crime wave awaiting around the corner, but most importantly, we are not ready at a legal and institutional level.

text:
A Japanese businessman's rental car got stuck in a snowbank outside a small Minnesota town, wheels spinning uselessly at eleven at night, not another car in sight.

He'd already resigned himself to calling a tow truck and waiting out the cold.

A pickup truck pulled up behind him instead. 

Then another. Within ten minutes, five strangers in heavy coats stood around his car, discussing angles and traction like it was a shared problem, not just his.

Nobody asked where he was from, or why he was driving alone this late. 

Someone handed him a bag of sand for the tires without being asked. On a count of three, they pushed, and the car lurched free.

He tried to offer money. They laughed, waved it off, and one of them said, "Just doing it 'cause we'd want someone to do it for us."

Within minutes, the trucks were gone, taillights disappearing into the snow, and he was alone on the road again.

Except now, he could drive.

text:
On September 9, 2026, Putin and Vietnamese leadership put out a joint statement pushing back against Western asset freezes and what they called foreign interference in their internal affairs. Fine. Joint statements happen. But watch what this one is actually doing, because the direction it points matters more than the document itself.

Russia has been running this play for years across SCO communiqués, CSTO declarations, bilateral partnerships with China and Iran and now Hanoi. The formula is consistent: take the documented reality of Russian covert influence operations in Western democracies (operations that allied intelligence services, academic researchers, and platform transparency teams have catalogued extensively) and flip the frame entirely. Suddenly the interference isn't Russian active measures. The interference is Western sanctions. Western democracy funding. Western civil society support. You're not the arsonist. You're the guy complaining about the fire trucks.

What's new here isn't the rhetoric. It's the geography.

Vietnam is not Belarus. It's not a Russian client state. It's a country that has carefully avoided endorsing Russian military operations in Ukraine, that trades heavily with the United States, that has its own distinct reasons for this framing. Hanoi's government runs transnational repression operations targeting diaspora activists in Thailand and elsewhere. It's sensitive to Western human rights conditionality the way any authoritarian government is sensitive to outside scrutiny of how it treats its own people. So Vietnam didn't sign onto this framing because it loves Moscow. It signed on because the framing serves Hanoi too.

That's the development worth tracking. Russia is assembling a coalition of endorsers for its counter-interference narrative, and it's finding partners not by bribing them or coercing them but by offering a rhetorical framework that multiple governments find genuinely useful for their own reasons. China has its own version. Iran has its version. Now Vietnam has signed a version. The specific grievances differ. The core claim is identical: Western democracy support is the real interference, and sovereign states have the right to push back.

This matters for how Western counter-interference frameworks actually function, because those frameworks increasingly depend on multilateral legitimacy. Sanctions work better when allies coordinate them. Accountability narratives land harder when they're not immediately contested by a bloc of states calling the whole enterprise illegitimate. Every time Russia recruits another government to sign a statement endorsing this framing, it chips away at the diplomatic isolation Western governments are trying to maintain around Moscow, and it gives mid-tier states a precedent to cite when they want to deflect scrutiny.

Watch for a few things specifically.

The statement's language around "global and regional stability" is doing real work. That phrase directly contests the Western argument that Russian aggression in Ukraine is destabilizing behavior requiring accountability. When Vietnam, a country with credibility in Southeast Asia, attaches its name to a document describing the Russia-Vietnam partnership as contributing to stability, it hands Russian state media a quote to use. Expect that quote to show up in messaging targeting ASEAN audiences where the framing of Western interference versus sovereign pushback has real resonance.

Second, this is a template. The next iteration probably involves a country with more direct relevance to a specific accountability mechanism Russia wants to undermine. Maybe a state that sits on a UN body. Maybe a country currently under pressure over sanctions compliance. The specific partner matters less than the pattern: find a government with its own reason to resent Western conditionality, offer them the sovereignty framing, get their name on the document, add it to the pile.

Third, and this is for officials thinking about democracy support programming specifically: the framing Russia is advancing makes no distinction between covert manipulation of foreign elections and transparent funding of civil society organizations. That conflation is intentional. If you let it stand without a clear public counter-argument, you're conceding ground on the definitional question. The whole architecture of counter-interference work rests on a distinction between overt, disclosed, legitimate engagement and covert, deceptive, sovereignty-violating manipulation. Russia's messaging is designed to collapse that distinction. Vietnam's endorsement gives the collapse a little more momentum.

One more thing for voters and journalists in Western countries following this: the officials you elect and the institutions they run are going to be described, in official government-to-government communiqués, as the actual interference threat. That description will get amplified. It'll show up in domestic political arguments made by people who may not even know they're running Russian talking points. The Russia-Vietnam statement is a small document. The information ecosystem it feeds into is not small at all.

https://t.co/2NvZjdgXeR

text:
Why Osun State needs more than just e-results

OSUN State’s gubernatorial election was a “tsunami” of tenacity; it was also a warning. If Nigeria continues to allow the cost of power to rise, we risk a future in which only the highest bidder gains access to our institutions. Excellence in governance is the only way to break this cycle—because elections are temporary, but development remains. The Osun election of 15 August 2026 is now history. Governor Ademola Adeleke has secured his mandate with 511,067 votes, successfully holding off the APC’s Bola Oyebamiji, who polled 444,815. Supporters have celebrated, and political actors have moved on. However, if we treat this simply as a closed chapter, we miss the most vital diagnosis of our current democracy. Osun was a victory for procedural transparency, yet it confirmed that we remain trapped in systemic financial corruption.

Osun offered us a “transparency paradox”. On one hand, the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) achieved a remarkable technical milestone. Monitoring by the Centre for Journalism Innovation and Development (CJID) confirmed that by the morning after the election, 98.06 per cent of polling-unit results were publicly available on the IReV portal. This was not merely a performance metric; it was a systemic success that largely curtailed the traditional manipulation of result sheets at collation centres. Yiaga Africa’s independent projection confirmed that the INEC figures accurately reflected the ballots cast. Yet, this triumph of process only served to highlight the decay of practice. While we succeeded in counting the votes, we failed to prevent vote-buying. Reports of vote-trading, with sums ranging from ₦10,000 to ₦50,000, remained a pervasive reality on election day. We have perfected the digital architecture of the ballot, but the “shadow economy” of Nigerian politics—the financing that operates outside the view of any portal—continues to undermine the integrity of the voter’s choice.

The allegations of spending—with figures ranging from ₦60 billion to ₦110 billion thrown around by political camps—cannot be ignored simply because they are unverified. Whether these amounts were fully deployed is secondary to what the figures represent: the alarming commodification of the governorship stool. Consider the opportunity cost. With a state capital expenditure budget of approximately ₦402.7 billion, an alleged ₦60 billion expenditure represents a massive diversion of resources. Every naira poured into this “shadow economy” is a naira subtracted from rural roads, primary healthcare, and teacher training. We have reached a point where the cost of acquiring political power now eclipses the capacity to deliver governance. When public office is treated as a commercial investment, the electorate is no longer the beneficiary; they become shareholders in a system designed to recoup the investor’s capital.

text:
King Khatvanga was an ancient warrior known for his immense skill in battle. When the gods found themselves overwhelmed by an army of demons, they called on him for help. Khatvanga led them to victory and in gratitude, the gods offered to grant him any wish he desired. 

While others would have asked for wealth, power or immortality, Khatvanga asked something different - 

"Just tell me, how much time do I have left to live?"

The answer was shocking. He had only 48 minutes remaining. 

Khatvanga didn't panic or beg for more time. He simply dropped his weapons and walked away from his kingdom, his riches and his family. He closed his eyes and let go of every worldly distraction and went into intense dhyana of Maha Vishnu. 

By letting go of everything so quickly and directing his meditation entirely towards Maha Vishnu during his last few minutes, he attained moksha.

Bhagavata Purana, canto 2, 1.13 - 
Khatvango nama rajarshir 
Jnatveyattam ihayushah 
Muhurtat sarvam utsrijya 
Gatavan abhayam harim

"When the saintly King Khatvanga learned that his lifespan would last only one more moment (a muhurta), he immediately gave up all worldly attachments and took shelter of the fearless Lord Hari."

This story from the Bhagavata Purana serves as a reminder for any Sadhak. Time doesn't stop and the only real wealth we have is the present moment. Every small step in your sadhana is an investment in your moksha. Since most of us won't get a warning about our final 48 minutes, a steady daily sadhana i.e. a steady accumulation of our spiritual currency is profoundly important.

Jai Sri Hari 🙏

text:
Georgia Police Hunted a Man Who Kept $30 He Found on the Floor at Walmart

Officials in Georgia launched a full public manhunt over all of $30. The Albany Police Department went looking for a Walmart shopper who allegedly pocketed cash another customer dropped, even posting his shot to Facebook and calling him a suspect. All of that effort, for thirty bucks.

The alleged crime was not exactly elaborate. Per the department, one shopper dropped $30 on the store floor, and the pictured man scooped it up without turning it over to Walmart staff. That was enough to land him in an August 19 post asking the public to help put a name to the face.

The public was not remotely on board. The thread turned into a pile-on, mostly aimed at the police rather than the culprit, with the top comment reading simply "Finders keepers." Others offered to just cover the $30 so the man could be left alone, while plenty asked why loose change on the floor deserved a manhunt.

The whole saga fizzled almost as fast as it started. An update from the department confirmed the man handed the money back to its owner, who had wanted to press charges but backed off the moment they were repaid. None will be filed, so the great $30 manhunt is officially over, no harm done.

🇱🇧|Mount Ali al-Tahir: A Resistance Stronghold Erased by 1,100 Tons of Explosives, and an Election Spectacle Masked as an Earthquake

At 9:08 PM on September 10, 2026, on the Ali al-Tahir ridge in southern Lebanon, Israeli occupation forces detonated over 1,100 tons of explosives, effectively wiping the entire ridge off the map.

The shockwave from the blast reached as far as Sidon, 40 kilometers away; instruments at both the Lebanese National Center for Geophysics and the U.S. Geological Survey simultaneously recorded a magnitude 4.1 "artificial earthquake." This was not merely a military operation; it was an assault on the land itself.

Following the explosion, Israeli Defense Minister Katz announced, "We have destroyed Hezbollah's underground infrastructure." In a joint statement, Netanyahu declared that the Israeli military had achieved "operational control" over the Ali al-Tahir heights.

But what was the truth? It was a calculated political spectacle a campaign advertisement Netanyahu staged for himself using 1,100 tons of explosives, just six weeks before the Israeli general election.

💀 1,100 Tons of Explosives: A War Crime Against the Land

Located near Nabatieh, just 15 kilometers from the Israeli border and rising to an elevation of approximately 600 meters, the Ali al-Tahir ridge overlooks the entire southeastern region of Lebanon. Over the course of more than two decades, and with Iranian funding, Hezbollah had constructed an underground network spanning over two kilometers at this site. The complex housed command centers and weapons depots, and deployed dozens of Iranian-made rockets, missiles, and drones, alongside anti-tank missiles, hundreds of landmines, and other explosives. These facilities belonged to Hezbollah’s Badr Unit and served as the "nerve center" for operations north of the Litani River.

Israel chose to destroy all of this using 1,100 tons of explosives. This amounted to 550 tons of explosives per kilometer of tunnel, a scale of demolition that was militarily entirely unnecessary. There was only one true objective: to manufacture an "earthquake" that could be filmed, broadcast, and boasted about.  Lebanese geologists have issued a warning: the Ali al-Tahir ridge lies immediately adjacent to the Roum Fault one of the major active seismic zones in southern Lebanon. Detonating 1,100 tons of explosives under these geological conditions could trigger irreversible structural risks.

This is not about "destroying tunnels." It is the execution of a mountain ridge.

🗳️ A "Trophy" Six Weeks Before the Election: Netanyahu’s Lifeline

Israel’s general election is scheduled for October 27, 2026. Netanyahu is facing his most severe political crisis since October 7, 2023; the Israeli newspaper *Haaretz* revealed that the President of the UAE had warned Israel in advance about the Hamas attack a warning Netanyahu ignored.

He needs a "victory" specifically, a victory that can be captured on video and featured in campaign advertisements.

The Ali al-Tahir ridge is his lifeline. The Iranian media outlet *Mizan Online* has explicitly stated that Israel’s claims regarding the capture of the Ali al-Tahir heights represent an attempt by Netanyahu to manufacture a propaganda win ahead of the election a political maneuver following a series of failures on multiple fronts.

Netanyahu claims that Ali al-Tahir served as a "major command center targeting the settlements of Metula and Kiryat Shmona." The subtext of this statement is: "I have eliminated the threat to northern settlers so vote for me."

This is not military strategy. It is electioneering.

🏚️ A Puppet Government: A Performance of Surrender at the Negotiating Table

While Netanyahu declares "victory" on camera, the Lebanese puppet government is preparing for negotiations.

Lebanon and Israel have held seven rounds of direct negotiations under US auspices. The first five rounds took place in Washington and the last two in Rome, with the most recent round concluding on August 6, 2026. The negotiating framework was brokered by the US on June 26; its core elements include the phased withdrawal of Israeli forces from Lebanese territory, the deployment of the Lebanese Army, and the disarmament of non-state armed groups.  In a statement issued on September 10, the U.S. Embassy in Beirut declared: "Decisions regarding war and peace should rest entirely with the Lebanese state." It also expressed Washington's "appreciation" for communities in southern Lebanon that "favor Lebanese state institutions over Hezbollah's weapons."

In plain terms: the U.S. is demanding that the Lebanese puppet government disarm Hezbollah.

Israel’s use of 1,100 tons of explosives was intended to make this demand a *fait accompli* an irreversible reality replacing diplomatic rhetoric with the sound of explosions at the negotiating table.

Lebanon gained no substantive results from the Rome negotiations. Israel made it clear it had no intention of honoring its commitments, while Washington continued to preside over the talks without compelling Israel to comply. This is the true plight of a "puppet government": signing agreements at the negotiating table only to be betrayed on the battlefield.

🕯️ Buried Martyrs: The Flesh and Blood of the Resistance vs. Enemy Lies

Israel claimed to have discovered 15 bodies inside a tunnel. The pro-Hezbollah newspaper *Al-Akhbar* offered a different account: only two resistance fighters were martyred, while dozens of Israeli soldiers were killed or wounded.

*Al-Akhbar*'s report reveals a more complete picture:

"The facility beneath the mountain housed personnel, commanders, computer systems, and weaponry. At the time, the resistance was anticipating an Israeli offensive an attack that had reached the outskirts of Ali al-Tahir and threatened to extend toward the city of Nabatieh. There, the offensive was decisively repelled. Reports indicate that 'an entire enemy soldier squadron was struck during the confrontation, suffering casualties within its ranks.'"

"The confrontation did not end there; repeated infiltration attempts and clashes on the mountain followed. Throughout these engagements, intelligence suggests that enemy losses far exceeded the sacrifices made by the resistance at Ali al-Tahir."

Israel claims to have killed "dozens" of resistance fighters. The resistance maintains that only two were martyred. Who is lying?

As for the martyrs buried beneath the rubble by those 1,100 tons of explosives their remains have yet to be fully recovered.  Israel’s narrative of a "precision strike" cannot mask the fact that this was a massacre staged for political propaganda.

🇮🇷 Iran’s Silence and Warning

Before Israel launched the demolition, Iran had warned Washington via Oman that it would respond forcefully if Israel initiated a large-scale operation against the Ali al-Tahir ridge.

Three regional officials told Reuters that more than a dozen members of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) including at least two senior officers were present alongside Hezbollah fighters in the area.

Yet, when the 1,100 tons of explosives fell, Iran did not mount a military response.

Reports indicate that Iran responded negatively to Hezbollah’s appeals; Tehran informed Hezbollah that it would not intervene to protect Ali al-Tahir and could not provide financial aid at the time. Letters from Iran’s Supreme Leader Khamenei and Quds Force commander Qaani were sent, but they were not accompanied by any substantive military action.

This was not "betrayal." It was strategic calculation. Iran was weighing whether a full-scale intervention in southern Lebanon was worth the cost amidst joint US-Israeli military pressure. Regardless of Iran’s decision-making logic, however, the martyrs of Ali al-Tahir fought to the very end without support from Iranian ground forces.

text:
WODEMAN
A Romaunce in Three Actes

The Galey-Boy

Of alle prisons made by man, the galey is most honest.

A dongeoun lieth.

It hath a dore, and therfore promiseth that some daye the dore may open.

A galey maketh no swich promesse.

She hath oores.

She carrieth her prison with her.

The man hadde been chained at the fourth bank from the stern for eleven monethes.

Or twelve.

He had ceased to know.

At first he hadde counted dayes.

Then Sundayes.

Then full moones.

Then the times they were given onions.

Afterward he counted nothing.

A man may number his sorwes only so long as he believeth the sum shall ende.

No man aboard knew much of him.

He was Italian.

Of the mainland.

That was all.

Some called him Lombardo, though he was not Lombard.

Some called him Grande, for his shoulders were broad.

The overseer called him Cane.

Dog.

This was sufficiently near a name for the galey.

He had once had another.

He remembered it.

He simply saw no profit in lending it to men who owned his ankles.

His place was upon a bench six men wide.

Six men to one oore.

An old Dalmatian with one blind eye.

A Greke who coughed blood.

A murderer from Chioggia.

A farm-labourer taken for debt.

A black-haired fellow nobody understood.

And him.

Their ankles were joined by iron.

Their waists by chain when weather grew foul.

Their hands were free because hands were useful.

A slave's body is never wholly imprisoned.

Only the portions unprofitable to his owner.

Before dawn came the drum.

DOM.

No man stirred.

DOM.

The sleeping deck groaned.

DOM.

Then came the stick.

“UP, CANI!”

Men raised themselves from boards slick with old sweat.

One man did not rise.

The overseer kicked him.

Nothing.

Kicked again.

The body rolled against the bench.

Dead.

Nobody stared long.

Dead men were fortunate until it came time to remove them.

“Loose him.”

A guard unlocked the dead man's ankle.

The corpse was dragged by the heels.

His head struck each crossbeam.

Tok.

Tok.

Tok.

Then the sea took him.

No priest.

No stone.

No name.

One splash.

The man from the mainland watched the water close.

The Greke beside him spat between his feet.

“Room for another.”

He was right.

Before noon they brought the boy.

Fourteen, perhaps.

No beard.

No flesh upon him.

Brown hair hacked short as though somebody had cut it with a knife.

Bare feet.

One eye swollen.

Wrists cord-burned.

He wore a tunic too large for him and carried himself with the stiffness of a child making one last attempt to look like a man.

The guards pushed him down the ladder.

He missed the final step.

Fell upon his knees.

Nobody helped him.

One guard laughed.

“Felon.”

The boy rose.

“Sit.”

He did not understand where.

The guard struck him behind the head.

“Sit, merda.”

They chained him into the place of the dead man.

The iron ring closed around his ankle.

The boy stared at it.

Then he understood.

Not the chain.

The permanence.

His breath changed.

A little.

The mainlander heard it.

Men learned to hear such things aboard a galey.

Fear.

Fever.

Dysentery.

A broken rib.

Madness.

Each had its owne sound.

The boy touched the shackle.

“When do they take it off?”

Nobody answered.

He looked from face to face.

The murderer from Chioggia laughed.

The boy looked toward the mainlander.

“When?”

The man said:

“They do not.”

The boy went pale.

“They must.”

“No.”

“To sleep?”

“No.”

“To shit?”

“No.”

“To wash?”

At this the Greke began laughing until his cough took him.

The boy stared.

The mainlander moved his foot.

A shallow wooden bucket lay beneath the bench.

“There.”

The boy looked at it.

Then at six men chained shoulder unto shoulder.

His face reddened.

“I will not.”

“Thou wilt.”

“No.”

“Then thou wilt shit thy breeches.”

The boy swallowed.

The mainlander leaned back against the timber.

“First lesson.”

“What?”

“Keep shame where they cannot reach it.”

The boy said nothing.

“Else they shall take that also.”

At noon he learned the oore.

It was longer than three men lying head to heel.

Heavy as sin.

The boy put his hands wrongly upon it.

The mainlander corrected them.

“Not so.”

The boy pulled away.

“I know.”

“Thou knowest nothing.”

“I have rowed.”

“A fishing boate?”

The boy nodded.

“This is no boate.”

The galey-master shouted from the gangway.

“READY!”

The mainlander put both hands upon the shaft.

“Watch me.”

“I said I know.”

“Then die learned.”

The drum sounded.

DOM.

The bank leaned forward.

The boy remained upright.

The oore slammed into him.

He cried out.

The mainlander caught the shaft before it crushed the boy's ribs.

“Forward whan we forward.”

The drum.

DOM.

They leaned.

“Feet.”

DOM.

“Now back.”

They pulled.

The boy's hands slipped.

A whistle.

The overseer came.

The mainlander muttered:

“Do not look at him.”

The boy looked.

That was his second errour.

The lash came across his shoulders.

He screamed.

Not from the pain alone.

From surprise.

The first lash always surprised.

Men still half believed punishment required anger.

Upon a galey punishment required only delay.

“ROW!”

The boy seized the oore.

Blood showed where rope had already opened his wrists.

DOM.

Forward.

DOM.

Back.

DOM.

Forward.

By the twentieth pull his breathing went wrong.

By fifty his shoulders shook.

By a hundred he was crying silently.

At some number no man could reckon, the boy whispered:

“I cannot.”

The mainlander did not look at him.

“Aye.”

“I cannot.”

“Aye.”

“Then why”

“Pull.”

The whip cracked somewhere behind.

“Pull.”

“I cannot.”

The man's deep voice hardened.

“Boy.”

The child looked at him.

“Yif thou canst pull one more, pull one.”

The drum.

They pulled.

“And afterward?”

“One more.”

They pulled.

“And afterward?”

“One more.”

The boy began sobbing.

The mainlander pulled beside him.

“That is the whole secret.”

By sunset the boy's palms had broken.

Not blistered.

Broken.

The skin had lifted away in wet white folds.

Blood painted the oore.

The mainlander spat into his own palm and showed him how to wrap a strip of filthy linen around the base of the fingers.

“Not thick.”

“Why?”

“Thick cloth maketh thy grip weak.”

“It hurteth.”

“Everything hurteth.”

The boy looked at him.

The mainlander added:

“Some things matter besides.”

He gave the boy half his water.

The Dalmatian saw.

“Fool.”

The mainlander drank the remainder.

The Dalmatian shook his head.

“New ones die.”

“I know.”

“Then thou hast wasted water.”

The mainlander shrugged.

The boy heard.

That night he did not speak.

The next morn he vomited before the drum.

Nothing much came.

Yellow water.

He shook afterward.

The murderer laughed.

“Sea-sick.”

“Nay,” said the mainlander.

The boy's sickness was not in his belly.

He saw it when the child woke suddenly and did not know where he was.

When a key turned anywhere aboard and he flinched.

When men shouted and he covered his head.

When he sat staring through the oar-port at open water for so long that the mainlander finally put a hand upon his shoulder.

The boy jumped as though burned.

“Easy.”

“Do not touch me.”

The hand withdrew.

“Good.”

The boy looked confused.

“Good?”

“Tell men that.”

A pause.

“Some aboard shall listen.”

“And those who do not?”

“Bite.”

The boy laughed.

Only once.

It surprised them both.

His name was Matteo.

The mainlander learned it on the fourth day.

They sat idle because the wind favoured sail and no officer cared to spend the slaves unnecessarily.

Such hours were treasures.

Men slept.

Scratched lice.

Mended cloth.

Gambled with things they did not own.

The sea outside the oar-port shone blue-white beneath noon.

Matteo sat with his knees drawn up.

“What was thy felonie?”

The boy's mouth tightened.

The mainlander waited.

He had learned this also.

Aboard a galey, men had nowhere to go.

Silence could afford patience.

At last Matteo said:

“Bread.”

The mainlander thought he had misheard.

“What?”

“A loaf.”

The Chioggian murderer began laughing from farther down the bench.

“A terrible brigand.”

“Shut thy mouth.”

The murderer grinned.

Matteo stared at his feet.

“My mother was ill.”

“What illness?”

“I know not.”

“Fever?”

“She coughed. Then she could not stand.”

The mainlander nodded.

“There was no moneye?”

Matteo shook his head.

“My father died two winters afore. My elder brother went with soldiers and never returned. She sewed. I carried sacks. Then she grew sick.”

He swallowed.

“We owed for the room.”

The mainlander listened.

“The baker would not give more.”

“So thou tookest it.”

“One loaf.”

“One?”

Matteo looked angry.

“One.”

“What happened?”

“I was caught.”

“That doth not explain this.”

“No.”

The boy's face changed.

There was something beneath the grief.

Humiliation remembered.

“They hated me.”

“Who?”

“The men of the quarter. The serjeaunt. His clerk. The reeve.”

“Why?”

Matteo hesitated.

“I talked too much.”

The mainlander almost smiled.

“That may be felonie in many places.”

“I told them the grain scale was false.”

“Was it?”

“Aye.”

“How knewest thou?”

“I carried sacks.”

“And?”

“The weights changed when poor men sold and changed again when the lord's factor bought.”

The mainlander's smile disappeared.

Matteo continued.

“I told the others.”

“Ah.”

“They warned me.”

“And thou continued.”

The boy's chin rose.

“Aye.”

Now the mainlander understood.

The bread had not condemned him.

The bread had merely become useful.

“What did they write?”

Matteo picked at dried blood on his palm.

“Felonie. Theft. Disorder. Threauts against men of office.”

“Didst thou threaten them?”

“I told one he was a thief.”

“That is dangereux.”

“He was.”

“That maketh it more dangereux.”

Matteo looked at him.

“They said I might hang.”

The mainlander waited.

“But a man came from the arsenaul. They needed bodies.”

There it was.

Neither spoke for a while.

A galey-slave was a corpse whose labour had been scheduled before burial.

Matteo whispered:

“They said mercy.”

The mainlander looked toward the sea.

“Aye.”

“They called this mercy.”

“Aye.”

The boy's eyes filled.

“I wish they had hanged me.”

The mainlander turned sharply.

Matteo wiped his face, angry with himself.

“My mother.”

He could not finish.

The mainlander said nothing.

“If I am here..”

The boy breathed once.

Twice.

“If I am here, no man bringeth her water.”

The mainlander looked down.

“No man buyeth wood.”

Silence.

“She could scarce rise.”

The boy's voice became very small.

“No one knoweth her.”

The mainlander had heard murderers speak of men they killed.

Pirates speak of villages burned.

Soldiers speak of cities sacked.

He had heard men under the lash curse Christ Himself.

None troubled him like this.

Matteo whispered:

“She is dead.”

The mainlander said:

“Thou knowest not.”

“I do.”

“Thou knowest not.”

“There was no one.”

“Boy”

“There was no one.”

His voice broke.

He pressed both fists against his eyes.

The mainlander let him weep.

No counsel.

No proverb.

No lie concerning God's purpose.

There are griefs upon which words sit like flies.

After a while Matteo leaned sideways.

His head touched the man's shoulder.

Only because there was nowhere else aboard to fall.

The mainlander did not move.

Weeks passed.

Matteo learned.

He learned never to drink all his water at once.

He learned to tuck bread beneath his shirt when food came before labour.

He learned the drum.

The great secret rhythm.

Forward.

Set.

Pull.

Breathe.

Forward.

Set.

Pull.

Breathe.

He learned to sleep while another man shat three feet away.

He learned not to scratch sores with dirty nails.

He learned which guards beat for pleasure and which only beat from habit.

The latter were preferable.

He learned that a man collapsing upon the oore could kill his whole bank if the shaft kicked loose.

He learned to wake the Greke when blood stopped coming from his cough, because sometimes that meant he had stopped breathing altogether.

He learned the smell of storm.

The smell of shore.

The smell of a corpse hidden two benches forward until heat found it.

He learned that chains grow hot beneath summer sun.

That salt entering split hands burneth like fire.

That thirst maketh urine seem a kind of richesse.

That lice acknowledged neither free nor bond.

That every officer aboard ate better than every slave and complained more.

This is one of the great miracles of ranke.

He learned, above all, not to run.

Once, while they took water near a stony shore, Matteo watched a chained man slip from a work party.

The fellow ran perhaps forty paces.

He had been a shepherd.

Bare feet.

Fast.

For several breaths freedom seemed not merely possible but easy.

Then the crossbow struck him between the shoulders.

He fell upon his face.

The guards dragged him back alive.

That was deliberate.

All the slaves were assembled.

The runaway was tied across a beam.

The whipping continued until counting became absurd.

At first the man screamed.

Later he made noises.

Later nothing.

The mainlander turned Matteo's face toward him.

“Look.”

Matteo resisted.

“Look.”

“Why?”

“So thou rememberest.”

The whip fell.

“Yif thou runnest upon shore, they kill thee.”

Another.

“Yif thou leapest overboard chained, the iron drowneth thee.”

Another.

“Yif thou strikest a guard and failest, they kill thee slow.”

Another.

“Yif thou strikest him and prevailest, the other guards kill thee slower.”

Matteo was crying.

“So there is no escape.”

The mainlander watched the whip rise.

“I said no such thing.”

Matteo looked at him.

“What then?”

“I said do not run stupidly.”

That night the boy whispered:

“Have men escaped?”

“Aye.”

“How?”

The mainlander settled against the bench.

“I shall tell thee when thou hast lived long enough to need knowing.”

“That is not fair.”

“Nothing aboard is.”

A pause.

“Sleep.”

Matteo muttered:

“I hate thee.”

“Good.”

“Why good?”

“Hate is lively.”

The boy smiled in the dark.

The mainlander sang.

Not often.

Never when ordered.

Never for officers.

He sang when the sea was quiet and the men had been worked beyond speech.

His voice was very deep.

Deeper than Matteo expected from him.

It began one evening after rain.

The benches were wet.

Everyone smelled of salt and mould.

Two men had fever.

The Greke had lost another tooth.

No food remained save hard bread and onions.

Someone somewhere was groaning.

The mainlander looked through the oar-port.

A strip of sunset burned beneath the cloudes.

He began:

"O wynde, yif thou hast libertè,
Come lowe and breke this chaine for me;
Yif alle the see be Goddes wide,
Why rowe I bounde upon the tide?"

Nobody spoke.

The drum-master was away.

The guard at the hatch pretended not to hear.

The mainlander continued:

"The gull hath neither lord ne rent,
No seal upon his wing is pent;
He asketh neither duke ne kinge
What leave he hath to flee and singe."

Matteo looked out.

A gull followed the wake.

The boy whispered:
“Again.”
The mainlander sang it again.
This time Matteo joined the last words.

His voice was poor.

Thin.

Fourteen.

The mainlander's voice carried him.

For a few minutes the galey remained a galey,
the chain remained chain,
the sores remained sores,
the dead remained dead.

yet the men sat somewhat straighter.

Hope is a foolish victual.

It nourisheth no flesh.

Nevertheless men have crossed deserts upon it.

Matteo became better at rowing.

Too good.

The mainlander disliked this.

A man should not become skillful at his own punishment.

Yet pride came with it.

One morning they rowed against wind.

Hard.

The drum quickened.

A veteran upon another bench faltered.

Matteo did not.

Sweat ran down his nose.

Blood opened again at the thumb.

He pulled.

Pulled.

Pulled.

When rest finally came he grinned.

“I kept stroke.”

The mainlander gave him water.

“Aye.”

“Better than Goro.”

“A dead mule roweth better than Goro.”

From the other bench:

“I HEARD THAT.”

Matteo laughed.

The mainlander did also.

It was the first time the boy heard him laugh fully.

Afterward he asked:

“Hadst thou a brother?”

The man's laughter stopped.

“No.”

“A son?”

“No.”

“Wife?”

The mainlander looked at him.

“Thou askest many questions.”

“You never answer any.”

“I answer some.”

“Badly.”

“A useful skill.”

Matteo chewed his bread.

“Then what hadst thou?”

The mainlander looked through the oar-port.

“Lond.”

“What sort?”

“Enough to miss.”

“Familé?”

A pause.

“Enough to miss.”

Matteo understood the border.

He did not cross it.

After another moment he broke his bread in half.

Offered some.

The mainlander stared.

“That is thine.”

“I know.”

“Eat it.”

“Thou gavest me water.”

“That was foolish.”

“Then I have learned from thee.”

The man took the bread.

“Worst lesson yet.”

They ate.

Winter caught them at sea.

Cold aboard a galey was different from cold ashore.

There was nowhere dry.

Wind found every seam.

Men slept against one another who would have stabbed one another on land.

Hatred itself became insulation.

Matteo developed a cough.

The mainlander listened to it nightly.

Not the deep wet cough of the Greke.

Dry.

Sharp.

Still, he began giving Matteo the place nearest the inner hull.

“You are larger,” said the boy. “Thou shouldst have it.”

“Sleep.”

“I am not cold.”

“Thy teeth have been arguing otherwise for an hour.”

Matteo curled beneath a torn blanket.

After some while:

“Sing.”

“No.”

“Why?”

“Tired.”

“Softly.”

“No.”

Another silence.

“Please.”

The mainlander breathed out.

Then, so low only their bench might hear:

"No chaine is forged that knoweth me,
No oore may learn my name;
My flesh they binde unto the sea,
My soule they binde in vain."

Matteo listened.

The man's voice became softer.

"And yif I die afore the shore,
Cast not my herte with me;
But give it to the western wynde,
And bidde the fool go free."

Matteo whispered:

“That verse is sad.”

“Aye.”

“I thought songs were to make men glad.”

“Some songs make sorrow carryable.”

“Like an oore?”

The mainlander looked at him.

“Sleep.”

Matteo smiled.

“I have become poetic.”

“Thou hast become irritating.”

The boy closed his eyes.

For a little while he slept.
The year turned.
The mainlander passed the mark most men did not.
No bell rang.

No officer remarked upon it.

He simply woke one morning and understood that he had survived more than a year.

He looked at his hands.
Great callused things.
Scar upon scar.
He could scarcely remember what they had looked like free.

Matteo had been aboard near three monethes.

The boy was thinner.

Harder.

Not healthier.

No one aboard was healthier.

But alive.

His eyes had changed.

That troubled the mainlander.

Some childehoud had gone from them.

Not all.

Enough.

One afternoon Matteo saw dolphins beside the hull.

He forgot himself.

“Look!”

Men turned.

Three grey shapes broke the water.

Again.

Again.

The boy laughed.

Not the little cautious laugh he had learned aboard.

The old one.

The laugh he must have had before bread became felonie.

Before parchment made him a dead man.

Before his mother vanished behind the world.

For that minute he was fourteen again.

The mainlander watched him instead of the dolphins.

Matteo noticed.

“What?”

“Nothing.”

“You are smiling.”

“No.”

“You are.”

“Watch thy fishes.”

“Dolphins.”

“They are wet. That sufficeth.”

Matteo leaned toward the opening.

“One day I shall see them from a shore.”

The mainlander said nothing.

The boy looked at him.

“One day.”

The man nodded.

“Aye.”

It was probably a lie.

But there are lies which steal from men,

and lies which return somewhat stolen.

That one he allowed.

That evening came bread.

One loaf between four.

Matteo took his portion.

Held it a while.

The mainlander noticed.

“What?”

The boy stared at the crust.

“This.”

“Aye?”

“All this for a loaf.”

No answer.

“My mother.”

The mainlander waited.

“I dream of her less.”

He looked ashamed.

“I do not want to.”

“That is no betrayal.”

“It feeleth one.”

“Aye.”

“How can both be true?”

The mainlander tore his bread.

“Most things are.”

Matteo looked at him.

“Thinkest thou she hated me for being taken?”

“No.”

“How knowest thou?”

“I do not.”

The boy's face fell.

The mainlander continued:

“But a mother who starved beside her son and saw him steal bread for her would have many foolisher things to hate afore him.”

Matteo's eyes lowered.

After a while:

“I think she is dead.”

The man nodded.

“I know.”

“I think I know it.”

“Aye.”

“I wish I had buried her.”

The mainlander's throat tightened.

“Aye.”

“No grave.”

“No.”

“No candle.”

“No.”

“No one to say her name.”

The mainlander looked at him.

“Say it.”

Matteo hesitated.

“Lucia.”

The sea moved against the hull.

“Again.”

“Lucia.”

The man nodded.

“Then now there are two men who know.”

Matteo's mouth twisted.

“One man.”

He touched his own chest.

“One boy.”

The mainlander looked at him.

“Aye.”

“One man and one boy.”

Then, very quietly, Matteo asked:

“Will you remember?”

The mainlander answered without jest.

“Aye.”

The boy breathed.

It seemed to ease something.

Not grief.

Nothing so miraculous.

Only its weight.

That night, when the drum ceased and the chains lay quiet and black water slid beneath the hull, the mainlander began his song.

No one asked him.

"O wynde, yif thou hast libertè,
Come lowe and breke this chaine for me..."

Matteo joined him.

At first softly.

Then stronger.

Other men joined.

The blind Dalmatian.

The Greke between coughs.

Goro from the next bank.

Someone forward whom none of them knew.

The song travelled bench by bench through the dark belly of the galey.

Not loud enough for rebellion.

Not soft enough for obedience.

Above them walked armed men.

Beyond them rolled the sea.

Around their ankles lay iron.

And still they sang.

For this is the cruellest defect in slavery:

that a master may purchase the arme,

rent the backe,

number the strokes,

measure the bread,

own the sleeping-place,

and hold in his hand the key of the chaine,

yet somewhere within the condemned man there remaineth a country without lordship.

And sometimes,
upon a blacke sea.

Africa Tech-Xpo 2026 will take place on 26–27 October 2026 at the Mulungushi International Conference Centre in Lusaka, bringing together technology companies, startups, investors, policymakers, financial institutions, entrepreneurs and business leaders for two days of exhibitions, thought leadership, networking and business engagement.

Held under the theme “Innovation, Infrastructure & Africa’s Next Economy,” @AfricaTechXpo represents the evolution of Zambia Tech-Xpo into a broader continental platform, creating space for Africa’s technology ecosystem to connect, collaborate and explore new opportunities across borders.

The event comes at a time when digital infrastructure, artificial intelligence, fintech, connectivity and emerging technologies are increasingly shaping how African economies operate and grow. Africa Tech-Xpo will provide a platform for the people building these solutions to connect with those who can finance, deploy, regulate and scale them.

The programme will explore some of the key issues shaping Africa’s digital future, including artificial intelligence and emerging technologies, fintech and digital financial services, digital infrastructure and connectivity, cybersecurity, e-commerce and digital trade, agritech, climate technology, mining and energy, digital skills, investment and the growth of startups.

The event will also provide businesses with an opportunity to showcase their products and services, engage potential customers and partners, participate in industry discussions and position themselves within conversations around Africa’s next phase of economic growth.

Africa Tech-Xpo builds on the foundation established by Zambia Tech-Xpo, which over the past four years attracted more than 4,000 delegates, 120 exhibitors and over 100 speakers. The evolution into Africa Tech-Xpo expands that platform to create stronger connections between Zambia and the wider African technology and business ecosystem.

“Technology is no longer developing within national borders. The opportunities and challenges facing Africa’s digital economy are increasingly interconnected,” said Sandi Chimpala, CEO of Techtrends Zambia and organiser of Africa Tech-Xpo. “Africa Tech-Xpo is about creating a space where the people building Africa’s digital future can meet the people who can help finance, scale, regulate and deploy those solutions. The goal is to turn conversations into partnerships and ideas into opportunities.”

The event is expected to attract CEOs and senior executives, technology and ICT leaders, banks and financial institutions, fintechs, startups, SMEs, investors, government representatives and policymakers, telecom operators, development organisations, technology professionals and innovators from Zambia and across Africa.

For businesses and organisations looking to participate, Africa Tech-Xpo offers a range of opportunities including exhibition, speaking, sponsorship, partnerships, networking and technology showcases.

For registration, partnerships and exhibition opportunities: info@africatechxpo.com | +260 779 384 884

Africa Tech-Xpo 2026 Brochure: https://t.co/SxwmvrSi99

Africa Tech-Xpo 2026 Tickets: https://t.co/NfdDPFZlP9

text:
🚨 BIG American Express changes from 11 October 2026.

Amex India is upgrading its technology platform, but there are some important changes for cardholders hidden inside this update.

Here’s what you need to know 👇

1️⃣ No more pooling MR points across your Amex cards

If you hold 2 or more Basic Amex Cards, each card will now maintain its own separate Membership Rewards balance.

More importantly, MR points can NO longer be transferred between your own cards.

Redemptions will be limited to the points available on that particular card.

For people who have been pooling MR points across Gold, MRCC, Platinum Travel, Reserve etc., this is a BIG change.

2️⃣ Posting date will determine milestone eligibility

Spends will now count based on when the transaction is POSTED, not simply when you make the transaction.

Spend on 31 October but transaction posts on 1 November?

It counts towards November.

Last-day milestone chasing just became riskier. 👀

3️⃣ Milestone rewards will be credited at month-end

For monthly milestones, rewards will be awarded at the end of the calendar month once eligible transactions have posted.

For Platinum Travel, milestone MR points and vouchers will also be awarded at the end of the calendar month in which the milestone is achieved.

The milestone benefits themselves continue.

4️⃣ Overdue payments will block BOTH earning & redemption ⚠️

If your payment remains due when your NEXT statement is generated, you won’t earn MR points on transactions from that statement date.

You also won’t be able to redeem your existing MR points.

Clear the due balance and earning + redemption resume.

5️⃣ Supplementary Card applications temporarily paused

New applications will be temporarily paused from 22 September 2026.

If you need one, apply before 22 September and complete the application by 30 September.

Amex has NOT mentioned a restart date in this communication.

6️⃣ New Account Cards are going away

These are cards issued in your OWN name to help separate and track certain transactions.

Existing Account Cards can continue to be used.

But new Account Cards will no longer be available following the change.

7️⃣ Airline & hotel transfers directly inside the Amex app ✈️🏨

This is one upgrade I really like.

You’ll be able to redeem MR points directly inside the Amex app, including transferring points to airline and hotel partners.

A new Memberships tab will also bring your Card benefits and offers together.

8️⃣ Easier statement-credit redemption

Instead of selecting individual transactions, you’ll be able to apply MR points towards your outstanding Card balance in one go.

Convenience improves, but Amex has NOT announced any improvement in the actual statement-credit redemption value.

9️⃣ More card controls inside the app 📱

You’ll be able to:

• Update contact details
• Manage domestic/overseas/online transactions
• Freeze/unfreeze cards
• Request replacement cards
• Raise disputes
• Request credit balance refunds
🔟 Digital EMI gets an upgrade
Up to 10 eligible individual transactions can be converted to EMI directly from the transaction view, up from 6 currently.
Conversion will happen digitally in real time.
But SMS EMI requests and conversion of the overall outstanding balance into EMI will no longer be available.
1️⃣1️⃣ Refunds & reversals

Eligible refunds/reversals received by your payment due date will be adjusted against your Minimum Amount Due and Total Amount Due.

This includes eligible refunds received after statement generation.

1️⃣2️⃣ Late Payment Fee calculation changes

Late Payment Fee will now be calculated based on Total Amount Due instead of Minimum Amount Due.

Applicable slabs will range from ₹500 to ₹1,250.

1️⃣3️⃣ What stays unchanged? ✅

Amex says Membership Rewards earn rates and redemption options remain unchanged.

But there’s an important caveat:

Your points are now separated card-wise, so you’ll only be able to redeem using the MR balance available on that particular card.

Effective: 11 October 2026 📅

The tech upgrades are genuinely useful.

But for points enthusiasts, separate MR balances and the end of pooling between your own Amex cards is easily the BIGGEST change here. 👀

First of all I want to give credit to you for changing your mind with new information.

Second, there are some things you misunderstand with METHODIQ and Oddity the holding company.  

There a few things I’m going to mention here I think you should look into when you get the time;

METHODIQ does indeed offer ongoing care with its patients.  Their dermatology customers check in every week and perform a fresh face scan with a progress check and the option to seek further consultation.  

Oddity Tech own Voyage81.  This technology is patented and allows them to turn a standard smart phone camera into a medical grade facial scanning device.  This is why they started in dermatology because they have a major competitive edge.  

Oddity Labs does indeed develop proprietary molecules like you said, but I think you underestimate the potential power of that ability.   Look into some of their proprietary products in METHODIQ like SkinShield.  

Their none prescription products in their are seeing very strong demand, which means they are not just a private medical service offering prescription medicine.  They have the ability to solve many patient problems without needing to use prescriptions, because they have the ability to test solutions at high volume and then formulate their products accordingly.  This gives them a major edge over the likes of $HIMS who rely mainly on off the shelf products or prescription medicines.

text:
Pincher Martin (@PincherMartin8),

I invite you to compare Bill James's 12 or 13 pages on the Leo Frank case with my own examination of the case in the 2025 revised edition of my book, The Murder of Little Mary Phagan. The second revised 2025 edition contains 38 additional years of research beyond what appeared in my first edition from 1987.

I also placed my original 1987 edition in the public domain. Anyone can read or download it free, with no sign-up and no registration required, at https://t.co/J3I52F2XEP this gives true crime readers an opportunity to compare the work for themselves rather than simply accepting somebody else's opinion about which account is better.

My point is almost the opposite regarding word count. If you are going to hold up Bill James's treatment of the Mary Phagan case as “a much better account” of the case than mine, then I am entitled to look at what investigative work he did on the Leo Frank case, how much of the case he examined, what sources he used, and what kind of research he conducted.

Bill James's Popular Crime: Reflections on the Celebration of Violence was published by Scribner on Tuesday, May 3, 2011. It is a roughly 500-page book covering hundreds of years of famous crimes. The Mary Phagan material begins with “Mary Phagan Introduction” on page 106, the main “Mary Phagan Case” section begins on page 107, and the next major section begins on page 119. So James gives the Mary Phagan case about 13 pages of the entire book (James, 1) (Ingram, 2). I am not saying twelve pages are automatically wrong because they are twelve pages. I am saying twelve pages are twelve pages. They necessarily leave out an enormous amount of a four-week murder trial, the four-month investigation, the physical evidence, the testimony, the 1.5 years of appeals, and the thousands of pages of surviving primary records.

And yes, James “did a lot of reading.” Nobody disputed that either. I enjoy reading voraciously myself. James himself said he had read roughly a thousand crime books. But reading a lot of books is not the same thing as conducting original primary source research into one particular murder case. Jeff Leen made that distinction very clearly in The Washington Post on Friday, April 29, 2011, four days before Popular Crime was published. Leen wrote, “There is no original research here,” and described James as drawing heavily from secondary sources (Leen, 3).

James himself was refreshingly candid about his qualifications. Leen quotes him saying, “I'm not a real historian” and “I'm not an investigative reporter.” His own publisher describes Popular Crime as the work of a “professed amateur” examining famous crime stories (James, 1) (Leen, 3).

None of that means Bill James shouldn't be read. Read him. I have. But don't cite his approximately twelve-page summary as “a much better account” and then complain when I examine what those twelve pages actually are and realize it's a very minimal investigation into the case. If James makes a better argument, please kindly show me the argument. I'm always interested in new perspectives on the case. Please kindly show me the evidence because I'm genuinely curious. Show me which primary 1913 records he uses to establish that Jim Conley “clearly committed the murder.” Show me where he deals with the evidence presented during the trial from Monday, July 28 through Monday, August 25, 1913. Simply saying James read a lot of secondary books and your opinion is that he wrote concisely doesn't establish that his conclusion is correct.

Conciseness isn't a substitute for evidence either. A person can state a bad argument in two sentences just as easily as somebody else can state one in twenty pages. What gives an argument weight is whether the facts underneath it hold up. James concludes that Jim Conley murdered Mary Phagan. That is one interpretation of the case by Leo Frank supporters. Then let's test that conclusion against Conley's May 18, May 24, May 28 and May 29, 1913 statements, his sworn testimony on August 4, 5 and 6, 1913, the other trial witnesses, the physical evidence, the medical testimony, and the appellate record. That's how I approach the case from the primary sources, not by pro-Frank or Frank detractor work.

The same thing applies to your comment about my description of the National Pencil Company layout. It's a bit evasive to claim a “lack of judgment.” Please kindly tell me what I got wrong. I have studied the two-dimensional architectural floor plans of the factory. Which floor? Which room? Which doorway? Which staircase? Which elevator? Which location in the machine department?

It would help if you were less vague and evasive. Please kindly give me the trial witness, the page of the Brief of Evidence, the factory diagram, floor plan, or the contemporary newspaper description that contradicts me for clarity. Then we have something specific we can examine. A general unsupported opinion about my judgment doesn't correct or improve comprehension of a room or floor plan.

This is a disagreement over evidence, none of which you have presented, as far as I can tell. You offered Bill James as a superior account. I pointed out that James devoted about a dozen superficial pages of a roughly 500-page general crime book to the Mary Phagan case, that his own publisher calls him a professed amateur, that James himself said he was not a historian or investigative reporter, and that a contemporary Washington Post review specifically stated there was no original research in the book (James, 1) (Ingram, 2) (Leen, 3). Those aren't comments about word count or word volume. They tell readers what kind of source Popular Crime actually is. It's something like a tertiary, superficial interpretation of other people's secondary work, with no original research of his own.

If Bill James's argument is better, then let's put his argument beside the 1913 record and see how well it holds up. That's a lot more useful than telling me I ought to learn to write fewer words after I just spent the last number of years transcribing more than 10,000 pages of primary source records (1913 - 1915 newspapers and legal records) of the Leo Frank case and published them on my website https://t.co/MNvBytB3CS and I still have many thousands of pages still to go with expanding this library archive. 

References

James, Bill. Popular Crime: Reflections on the Celebration of Violence. Scribner, published Tuesday, May 3, 2011. Simon & Schuster official publisher page. Publisher describes the book as a “professed amateur's” examination of crime and lists the electronic edition at 496 pages.

https://t.co/Xis3Y3rzaC

Ingram. Table of contents for Bill James, Popular Crime: Reflections on the Celebration of Violence. “Mary Phagan Introduction,” p. 106; “Mary Phagan Case,” p. 107; next major section begins p. 119.

https://t.co/voK73OKjco

Leen, Jeff. “‘Popular Crime’ by Bill James, a ‘serious discussion of Trash.’” The Washington Post, Friday, April 29, 2011. Leen described the hardcover as 482 pages, stated there was “no original research” in the book, and discussed James's reliance on secondary sources and his own disclaimers about his expertise.

As for your comments on James' book, they show a similar lack of judgment as your description of the National Pencil Company layout.  Yes, James summarizes his findings based on his reading.  It takes up a small portion of his book.   So what?  He still did a lot of reading to write it, and presents his arguments cogently and concisely - something you would benefit from learning how to do."

text:
My Compact of Free Association thesis for newer followers, as a complement to @TMTLongShort's thesis QTed below:

Obviously, everything contemplated here assumes peaceful, democratic and ultimately legal constitutional change.

The starting point is that Canadian Confederation may be substantially harder to reform than to replace. Rather than endlessly attempting to decentralize an Ottawa-centred federation, Canada’s constituent nations and regions could eventually reorganize themselves into highly autonomous states linked to the United States through Compacts of Free Association.

The objective is neither annexation nor the disappearance of Canada into the United States. It is almost the opposite: trade deeper continental strategic integration for much greater political decentralization and local sovereignty.

Such an arrangement could simultaneously address American security concerns and Canadian regional aspirations. Washington gets a strategically coherent northern continent: integrated continental defence, NORAD, Arctic security, secure critical infrastructure and resources, and safeguards against hostile military or technological penetration. The associated states retain control over the overwhelming majority of their domestic affairs.

For Quebec, this offers something Canadian federalism has never been able to settle permanently: a sovereign French-speaking national homeland with control over immigration, language, education, culture, taxation and domestic policy, while remaining economically and strategically integrated with the rest of North America.

The same principle applies to Anglo-Canada. Rather than treating English Canada as merely the residual portion of a postnational federation, one or several successor states could explicitly preserve Anglo-Canadian institutions, traditions and identity as national inheritances worth perpetuating.

This produces an unusual bargain: greater integration externally can permit greater decentralization internally. The United States does not need to govern its northern neighbours if its legitimate continental-security requirements are reliably satisfied.

Compacts could also provide exceptionally deep economic integration and reciprocal mobility. Canadians could live and work throughout the associated American space, while Americans could settle in the associated Canadian states—including those attracted to the distinctive Anglo-Canadian way of life—without requiring the abolition of borders, customs controls or separate citizenship.

The resulting North America would therefore not be a unitary superstate or necessarily even an EU-style federation. It would be a network of sovereign or highly sovereign political communities sharing a continental strategic architecture while retaining radically greater control over their internal development.

This also creates common ground with American decentralists who distrust excessive federal power. The same principle can operate on both sides of the border: continental defence and economic scale where necessary; political authority pushed downward wherever possible.

The paradox is the heart of the proposal: accepting that geography makes deep American strategic alignment unavoidable does not necessarily require surrendering local sovereignty. Properly structured, it could make substantially more local sovereignty possible.

Less Ottawa, not more Washington.

Grok summary of the full Economic Blitzkrieg thesis for newer followers: 

Trump’s tariffs are framed as a blunt instrument for strategic decoupling, not a conventional trade-negotiation tool; the real objective is to isolate China and rebuild U.S. hegemony by splitting the world into two irreversible blocs of trade, security, and financial rails.

The plan targets a cluster of interlocking problems: China’s rising industrial/tech/military power, U.S. dependence on Chinese supply chains, unsustainable U.S. fiscal deficits and short-dated debt, fentanyl, European free-riding, allies’ growing economic ties to China, China’s move up the value chain (autos, semis, robotics, AI), and the political impossibility of gradual pain.

Constraints force an aggressive, time-compressed design: midterm elections, higher Chinese pain tolerance, high global debt, and the inability to simply “ask” countries to walk away from China; the strategy therefore uses game theory, binary “in or out” choices, and compressed deadlines so later administrations cannot easily reverse it.

Early joiners (Japan, South Korea, Israel, Saudi Arabia, UAE, Poland, etc.) are coerced or incentivized first with security guarantees, USD swap lines, and technology access; a second wave (India, Brazil, Mexico, etc.) is pulled in by proximity and economic leverage, after which holdouts face simultaneous shocks: NATO defunding, swap-line withdrawal, AI/GPU embargoes, and cuts from IMF/WTO.

Canada is treated as a low-risk demonstration case to show Europeans the cost of delay; the goal is not total isolation of China but a sudden, violent rupture of allied supply chains that slows China’s relative rise.

Admission to the U.S. bloc comes with extra demands on motivated partners (long-duration Treasury purchases and a persistent bid below 3 % yields) that function as outsourced yield-curve control, giving Congress political cover for large fiscal stimulus and possible income-tax cuts ahead of midterms.

Trade deficits themselves are dismissed as secondary; the reserve-currency issuer with a services-heavy economy was never going to drive them to zero.

The approach assumes China will stay relatively passive while the U.S. organizes its bloc; secrecy and vagueness in negotiations are deliberate to prevent multilateral coordination against the plan.

Even if the strategy fails, the author argues the U.S. downside is limited because it is the least trade-dependent major economy and can retreat into a North-American core plus tariffs and stealth default, while the rest of the world faces depression, security vacuums, and pressure to accommodate China or Russia.

This is how CCP influence work operates: not primarily through trolls and fakes, but through respectable institutes, sponsored panels and a frame set in the title itself. Poland has one of Europe's strongest immune systems against Russian disinformation. It has almost none against "a polite professor" from Shanghai.

text:
Today we commemorate the 25th anniversary of the September 11th terror attacks on the World Trade Center in New York City, the Pentagon in Arlington, Virginia, and the hijacked plane that crashed in Shanksville, Pennsylvania. 

As we remember and pray for the victims and survivors of those attacks, we invite you to join us in prayer. Perhaps you can offer your Rosary or say a prayer at Mass today for the families who lost a relative or a loved one.

What follows is an excerpt of a meditation about September 11th written by one of our friars.

Many first responders gave their lives on September 11th in service to others. Their sacrifice reflects Christ’s act of total self-giving. By his resurrection, Christ comforts us with his peace, reigning in our hearts as the Prince of Peace. The Risen Christ shows us that life cannot be defeated by the scourge of death.

He gives us hope, which is stronger than our despair, anger, and pain. Saint Paul reminds us of this truth when he exhorts us to “have no anxiety about anything,” for “the peace of God, which passes all understanding, will keep your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus” (Phil 4:6–7).

In addition to their respective prayer and address, both Pope Benedict and Pope Francis lit a remembrance candle for the victims of the September 11th terrorist attacks during their visits to Ground Zero. These gestures were quite fitting, for in these actions both pontiffs showed the world a tangible sign of the light of Christ, a light that never fades.

The horror of that day may still remain etched in our memories after nearly two decades. Many continue to grieve the loss of loved ones who died in the attacks. Yet Christ is victorious. His light shines brightly in the midst of darkness and despair, illuminating us with his peace and love.
—Fr. Paul Marich, O.P.
