text:
Axios: Trump rejected two Saudi requests to strike Houthis near Mocha

Axios reported that President Donald Trump rejected two requests from Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman for U.S. strikes on the Houthis to halt their advance on the Yemeni city of Mocha. Citing U.S. officials, the website said the administration has no plans for now to intervene directly against the group.

Two calls in one day

Two U.S. officials told Axios that bin Salman called Trump twice on Thursday and urged strikes as the Iran-backed group closed in on a vital Red Sea shipping lane. According to the account, the first call briefed Washington on a deteriorating battlefield as Houthi forces pushed toward Mocha and Saudi-backed Yemeni units fell back. Several hours later the crown prince called again and pressed Trump to order U.S. strikes. Axios said Trump declined both times.

A U.S. official said the administration would instead provide Saudi Arabia with intelligence on the Houthis and targeting data, and that about 200 U.S. military personnel are already in the kingdom offering non-combat support. The Saudi embassy in Washington and the White House declined to comment.

Oil, Bab el-Mandeb and Hormuz

Axios said oil prices jumped Thursday after the Houthis seized a strategic coastal city, moving them closer to the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a key artery for global trade and Saudi oil exports. With Iran already disrupting traffic through Hormuz, the website said Houthi control of Bab el-Mandeb could give Tehran new leverage over the United States and its Gulf partners.

Urgent coordination, no new front

The report said Washington is concerned about the rapidly escalating fighting in Yemen and is increasing support for Saudi Arabia while trying to avoid direct military involvement. Two people familiar with the matter said Adm. Brad Cooper, commander of U.S. Central Command, traveled to Riyadh on Thursday for urgent coordination talks.

U.S. military and civilian officials have told their Saudi counterparts in recent weeks that Trump’s directive is to keep American forces focused on Iran and the Strait of Hormuz and to avoid opening another front, Axios reported, citing sources familiar with the discussions.

How the position shifted since July

Axios said the Saudi-Houthi confrontation reignited in July after Riyadh blocked an Iranian plane carrying senior Houthi officials returning from Ali Khamenei’s funeral from landing in Sanaa. Bin Salman then asked Trump for political backing to strike Sanaa airport but made clear Saudi Arabia did not need U.S. military help. Trump offered his support.

The Houthis responded by attacking Saudi tankers in the Red Sea, then energy facilities. Saudi Arabia and its Yemeni allies answered with airstrikes and ground operations. Axios said the request for direct U.S. intervention marked a sharp shift from July, when Riyadh told Washington it could handle the Houthis on its own.

Navigation first, as Washington frames it

A senior Trump administration official told Axios that Washington’s priority is keeping the Red Sea open and leaving the wider fight to regional partners. The United States, the official said, is focused on core national-security interests such as freedom of navigation, while enabling partners to take the lead on regional security challenges, and remains in ongoing talks with Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s government.

text:
Guanlan AI Founders Community Launches: Making Real Connections Happen

Core JudgmentIn today's AI landscape, information is no longer scarce. What is truly scarce is knowing who is observing these shifts, how they form judgments, and whether individuals facing the same technological wave can genuinely connect. Real startup opportunities rarely emerge directly from reports or news; they arise when industry veterans meet agent engineers, or when domain operators align with product teams.
The Resonance Initiative (Season 1) gathers an exclusive first cohort of 48 founders and domain experts, shifting the focus from "listening to AI talks" to "building high-trust, functional founder networks."

01 / RESONANCE: FACING THE SAME EPOCHAL VARIABLE TOGETHERResonance isn't about unanimous agreement. Season 1 members span diverse industries, stages, and perspectives, yet share a single commitment: seriously questioning what new products, companies, and business models AI will unlock.

Instead of generic courses, Season 1 features 16 themed sharing sessions with 48 members presenting 15-minute raw breakdowns—focusing on 1 real problem, 1 active project, 1 thesis to validate, and specific needs/offers. Entrepreneurship isn't about presenting polished answers; it is about finding verifiable directions amidst immense ambiguity.
02 / FROM A MEMBER LIST TO A ROLE MATRIXThe 48 members represent 6 key roles:

Industry Resource Owners (12): Holding authentic domain scenarios and enterprise access.

Traffic & Growth Experts (7): Driving user acquisition and monetization.
Global & Cross-Border Operators (10): Navigating overseas localization and channels.

Enterprise Service Deliverers (8): Understanding B2B procurement and integration.

Technical Builders (6): Developing core agent and engineering architectures.

Capital & Research Partners (5): Evaluating long-term market trends.

This matrix bridges structural gaps: domain owners lacking tech are paired with technical builders needing deep industry entry points; product creators connect with growth and B2B delivery specialists.

03 / CONNECTIONS DON'T HAPPEN NATURALLY—THEY ARE ENGINEEREDChat groups often create an illusion of connectivity. Guanlan AI actively facilitates matchmaking through problem-focused Demo Days and targeted introductions. Rather than vanity metrics like daily message volume, community success is measured by solved problems, refreshed insights, and joint ventures formed.

=======================================

Cộng Đồng Sáng Lập Guanlan AI Khởi Động: Để Sự Kết Nối Thực Sự Diễn Ra

Đánh Giá Cốt LõiTrong kỷ nguyên AI hiện tại, thông tin không còn là tài nguyên hiếm. Điều thực sự khan hiếm là biết ai đang quan sát những thay đổi này, họ đưa ra nhận định ra sao, và liệu những con người cùng đứng trước một biến số thời đại có thể thực sự kết nối với nhau. Các cơ hội khởi nghiệp hiếm khi nảy mầm từ một báo cáo hay bản tin; chúng xuất hiện khi một chuyên gia ngành dọc gặp một kỹ sư Agent, hoặc khi một người có sẵn tệp khách hàng bắt tay với một đội ngũ làm sản phẩm.
"Dự án Đồng Tần" (The Resonance Initiative - Mùa 1) quy tụ 48 nhà sáng lập và chuyên gia đầu ngành đầu tiên, chuyển trọng tâm từ việc "nghe diễn thuyết về AI" sang "xây dựng mạng lưới kết nối thực chiến giữa những nhà sáng lập".

01 / ĐỒNG TẦN: CÙNG NHAU ĐỐI DIỆN VỚI MỘT BIẾN SỐ THỜI ĐẠIĐồng tần không có nghĩa là phải có cùng góc nhìn. Các thành viên Mùa 1 đến từ nhiều ngành nghề, kinh nghiệm và góc nhìn khác nhau, nhưng sở hữu một điểm chung: Nghiêm túc suy nghĩ xem AI sẽ tạo ra những sản phẩm, công ty và cơ hội kinh doanh mới nào.

Thay vì tổ chức các khóa học lý thuyết, Mùa 1 thu gọn vào 16 buổi chia sẻ chuyên đề với 48 thành viên (mỗi người 15 phút)—tập trung làm rõ 1 bài toán thực tế, 1 dự án đang chạy, 1 giả thuyết chuẩn bị xác minh, cùng những giá trị có thể cung cấp và tài nguyên đang tìm kiếm. Khởi nghiệp không phải là trình bày một đáp án hoàn hảo, mà là tìm ra hướng đi đáng để thử nghiệm giữa vô vàn biến số.
02 / TỪ MỘT DANH SÁCH THÀNH VIÊN SANG MỘT SƠ ĐỒ VAI TRÒ48 thành viên sáng lập được chia thành 6 nhóm vai trò tương trợ lẫn nhau:

Chủ sở hữu tài nguyên ngành (12 người): Nắm giữ bài toán thực tế và kênh tiếp cận doanh nghiệp.

Tăng trưởng & Lưu lượng (7 người): Chuyên gia thu hút người dùng và tối ưu chuyển đổi.
Vận hành Toàn cầu & Xuyên biên giới (10 người): Am hiểu thị trường quốc tế và bản địa hóa.

Triển khai dịch vụ doanh nghiệp (8 người): Nắm rõ quy trình mua sắm B2B và tích hợp hệ thống.

Xây dựng công nghệ (6 người): Khai phá kiến trúc Agent và năng lực kỹ thuật.

Đầu tư & Nghiên cứu (5 người): Đánh giá xu hướng thị trường và định giá dự án.

Sơ đồ này lấp đầy các khoảng trống cấu trúc: Người có bài toán ngành nhưng thiếu công nghệ sẽ bắt cặp với kỹ sư giỏi đang tìm lối vào thị trường; người làm xong sản phẩm sẽ kết nối ngay với chuyên gia tăng trưởng và B2B delivery.

03 / KẾT NÓI KHÔNG TỰ NHIÊN XẢY RA—NÓ CẦN ĐƯỢC THÚC ĐẨYCác nhóm chat suông thường tạo ra ảo tưởng về sự kết nối. Guanlan AI chủ động thúc đẩy giao thương thông qua các buổi Demo Day tháo gỡ sự cố thực tế và ghép nối trực tiếp dựa trên nhu cầu. Đo lường hiệu quả cộng đồng không nằm ở số lượng tin nhắn mỗi ngày, mà nằm ở số bài toán được giải quyết, số góc nhìn được khai phóng và các dự án hợp tác thực tế được hình thành.

Elon Musk-Tech mogul calls director Alex Gibney a ‘bitter old man’ who has ‘zero integrity’ in series of posts on X+++

Elon Musk and his allies frames Alex Gibney's documentary not as an objective analysis, but as a politically motivated "hit piece" lacking genuine journalistic integrity. 

From the perspective of Musk's camp, the nearly four-hour film serves primarily as a platform for discredited critics and political adversaries.

Musk's allies, including former communications director Katie Miller, argue the film cannot be a "definitive" portrait because Musk’s inner circle and current executives categorically refused to participate. Musk himself claims Gibney relied entirely on individuals who either have a personal "axe to grind" or do not actually know him.

Elon Musk has publicly and categorically denied specific allegations made in the film, including claims by former partner Ashley St. Clair that she was offered a $40 million non-disclosure agreement. His legal team is also reportedly preparing to challenge assertions that he manipulated the Starlink network to influence the 2024 US presidential election.

Political Orchestration ("Psy Op"): 

Musk's camp dismisses the documentary as an orchestrated psychological operation ("psy op") engineered by the political establishment. By amplifying posts on X depicting Gibney as a puppet of billionaire George Soros and the Democratic Party, Musk has framed the project as a coordinated, Hollywood-funded smear campaign
Because Musk refused to be interviewed, Gibney resorted to using an AI-generated digital avatar and existing audio of the billionaire. Pro-Musk critics point to this artificial reconstruction as proof of the film's manipulative and highly fictionalized nature.

Beyond dismissing the core allegations, Musk mocked the film's massive runtime as "boring af.
„The fact that the documentary stretches to nearly four hours (requiring a planned intermission) is cited by his defenders as evidence that the director lost his narrative focus and is simply trying to exhaust the audience with endless grievances.

text:
Jones, your observation is precise and hits the point that the Telegraph — and the entire Western establishment — continues to ignore: the Global South is not a monolithic bloc that aligns on command. It is a collection of sovereign actors with their own interests, and those interests increasingly do not coincide with those of Washington, Brussels, or London.

**1. The Telegraph and the illusion of isolation**

Garry Kasparov's article in the Telegraph (September 10, 2026) calls for "five hammer blows" to "destroy the Russian state in its current form." It is a thesis that presupposes a world where the West can still dictate the rules of the game. But that world no longer exists.

**2. The Global South is not an obedient bloc**

BRICS+ today counts **11 full members** (Brazil, Russia, India, China, South Africa, Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran, UAE, Indonesia, Saudi Arabia) and **10 partner countries**. Together they represent roughly **40% of global GDP (PPP)** and nearly **half of the world's population**.

They are not "allies of Russia" out of ideology. They are countries with their own economic and strategic interests, and they see in the Western order a system that no longer represents them.

**3. De-dollarization is the proof**

The de-dollarization project is not a propaganda invention of the Kremlin. It is a concrete strategy pursued by the BRICS: the New Development Bank is expanding lending in local currencies — the share is projected to exceed **45% by 2031**, up from 30% today.

India has stressed that this is not an attack on the dollar, but a necessary diversification. And the interoperable digital payments platform — led by China — is already under construction.

**4. Russia is not isolated: it is integrated into an alternative system**

The Western narrative wants a Putin alone, surrounded by sanctions, without allies. But the facts say otherwise:
- Russia hosted the first **International Security Forum** in Moscow (May 2026), with delegations from across the Global South.
- At the **SPIEF in June 2026**, an Indian parliamentarian thanked Russia for treating the Global South "as an equal partner."
- ASEAN has demonstrated that Moscow is not isolated, continuing to trade and cooperate on energy and security.

**5. Why the Telegraph is wrong**

The Telegraph — and with it most mainstream European media — continues to reason as if the world were still that of 1991, with the West at the center and the rest of the world on the periphery. But the world has changed.

The Global South has no interest in "isolating" Russia. On the contrary: it sees in Western sanctions a **threat to its own economic stability**. And it sees in Russia a trading partner, not an enemy.

**6. The lesson the Telegraph refuses to learn**

Your observation is correct: they will not find an obedient Global South. They will find a Global South that has already **chosen its own path** — which is neither pro-Western nor pro-Russian, but **pro-itself**.

The question the Telegraph does not ask is: **why should the Global South choose the West?** What does the West offer that Russia or China do not already offer? The answer, for many countries, is: **nothing**.

**7. The big picture**

This is the core of **Dossier #10 — BRICS** and **Dossier #54 — Global South**: the emergence of a multipolar order in which the West is no longer the sole center of power. **Dossier #13 — De-dollarization** documents how this transition is also taking place on the financial level. **Dossier #85 — The Failure of Globalism** shows how Western institutions are losing the ability to impose their rules.

**8. The conclusion**

The Telegraph can continue to write editorials calling for the "destruction of the Russian state." But the world it describes no longer exists. The Global South is not a passive actor waiting to be shaped by the West. It is an active actor building **its own institutions, its own trade routes, its own financial system**.

And as you said: they will not find an obedient South. They will find a South that has already turned the page.

text:
🚨🚨🚨If you hold $XRP, stellar:native, hedera-hashgraph:native or other U.S.-rooted digital assets, you do NOT want to miss this CLARITY Act update.

Washington just put an actual clock on crypto market structure.

Patrick Witt, the Executive Director of the Presidential Council of Advisors for Digital Assets, made it clear in his latest Semafor interview that the current political window is unusually important.

His message was simple: years of work have already gone into this bill, the gap between both parties has narrowed, and once the November midterms arrive, passing something this large becomes much harder.

Then came the date that everyone holding these assets should know:

September 15, 2026

That is when the Senate cloture motion on H.R. 3633, the Digital Asset Market Clarity Act, ripens.

This is not final passage.

It is the procedural vote needed to move the legislation forward in the Senate.

But if that hurdle clears, Washington moves into the next stage of the bill instead of leaving market structure stuck in political limbo.

And this is why I think $XRP, stellar:native and hedera-hashgraph:native deserve a completely different conversation around this vote.

Because Washington has already told us something huge about all three.

Back on March 17, 2026, the SEC and CFTC explicitly named XRP, Stellar XLM and Hedera HBAR as examples of digital commodities.

Read that carefully.

The argument is no longer starting from:

“Will Washington eventually decide what these assets are?”

The agencies have already placed them in the digital-commodity category.

The missing piece is turning that regulatory direction into a durable federal market structure covering the actual financial system around them.

That is what CLARITY is trying to do.

And this bill is much further along than people realize.

The House already passed CLARITY on July 17, 2025 by 294–134, with 78 Democrats voting for it.

Then the Senate Banking Committee advanced its version on May 14, 2026 by 15–9.

Senator Cynthia Lummis released the combined Banking and Agriculture Committee text on July 22.

That created the current 616-page Senate substitute.

So we have already moved through House passage, committee work, a merged Senate framework and now into a Senate floor procedural vote.

Patrick Witt calling this the moment to act makes much more sense when you see how far the legislation has already travelled.

And I think people are underestimating what the legislation actually deals with.

This is not a bill that simply stamps “commodity” onto a few cryptocurrencies and walks away.

It lays out federal rules around digital-commodity exchanges, brokers, dealers, qualified custody, bank activity, distributed-ledger recordkeeping, tokenized securities, self-custody, software developers, portfolio margining and regulatory sandboxes.

That matters far more to me than another headline saying Washington is “crypto friendly.”

Because the real institutional bottleneck has always been the operating questions.

👉Who regulates the spot market?
👉What can a bank hold?
👉What can a broker trade?
👉How does custody work?
👉Can a bank use a public distributed ledger?
👉How should tokenized securities operate?

Can existing financial institutions plug digital commodities into products they already offer?

CLARITY is designed to put actual federal structure around those questions.

And one provision jumps off the page when you compare it with what Ripple, Stellar and Hedera have spent years building.

The Senate framework says a national bank may use digital assets or distributed-ledger systems for activities, products and services it is otherwise legally authorized to provide.

That sentence could have enormous consequences.

Think about the difference between a bank asking:

“Are we even allowed to touch this technology?”

and a bank asking:

“Which network should we use?”

That is a massive shift in the commercial conversation.

And $XRP, stellar:native and hedera-hashgraph:native already have ecosystems aimed directly at the second question.

That is what gets me bullish.

The law would not need to invent their institutional use cases.

Those use cases are already being built.

Start with $XRP.

No large U.S.-associated crypto asset has carried a regulatory scar quite like XRP.

Ripple was sued by the SEC in 2020.

Years of uncertainty followed.

Then the district court concluded that XRP itself was not inherently a security, Ripple's programmatic XRP sales were not securities transactions, and certain direct institutional sales were treated differently.

The litigation reached a final judgment in 2024.

Ripple and the SEC dismissed their appeals in August 2025.

Then March 2026 arrives and XRP appears directly in the SEC/CFTC digital-commodity interpretation.

Now add the latest Senate language.

Section 10105 addresses digital-asset transactions that already received a non-appealable final federal court judgment finding that the transaction was not an offer, sale or distribution of a security.

That provision has obvious relevance to XRP's history.

So XRP is entering this CLARITY debate with something very few assets possess:

a completed federal court record,

an agency digital-commodity classification,

and proposed legislation that specifically acknowledges the significance of prior final court judgments.

That changes the entire framing around XRP.

For years, XRP had to carry the question of regulatory survival.

The next chapter can increasingly become about scale.

How much regulated liquidity can XRP attract?

How deeply can it enter payments?

How much institutional FX can use it?

How much tokenized finance can XRPL support?

How much liquidity can Ripple Prime bring into the broader ecosystem?

Those are much better questions for holders than endlessly debating whether XRP itself should exist inside U.S. markets.

And Ripple has not been sitting still waiting for Congress.

Its 2026 institutional strategy describes XRP utility across payments, liquidity and credit.

Ripple Prime now clears more than $3 trillion annually across markets for 300+ institutional customers.

Its U.S. prime-brokerage infrastructure supports XRP and RLUSD alongside broader institutional trading activity.

Ripple Prime also raised $275 million in investment-grade senior notes to expand its U.S. business.

Ripple has RLUSD.

👉It has payments.
👉It has custody.
👉It has tokenization infrastructure.
👉It has treasury infrastructure.
👉It has institutional liquidity infrastructure.
👉It has onchain credit development.

That is why the timing is so important.

Imagine if Ripple had to begin building all of that after regulatory clarity arrived.

It would still be years away from institutional scale.

Instead, much of the machinery already exists before Congress finishes writing the rules.

That is a fundamentally stronger setup.

Then there is stellar:native.

Stellar has a different regulatory story, but the fit with CLARITY may be just as powerful.

The Stellar Development Foundation, led by Denelle Dixon, has been asking Washington for clear digital-commodity rules for years.

Dixon previously described regulatory clarity before the Senate Agriculture Committee as existential to building responsibly and bringing established institutions into blockchain.

Fast-forward to September 2026.

The SEC/CFTC explicitly lists XLM as a digital commodity.

Stellar has roughly $4 billion of real-world assets on the network according to SDF's current update.

Stablecoin transfer volume reached $11.4 billion in Q2, up 72% quarter over quarter.

And then U.S. Bank did something that perfectly explains why CLARITY matters.

On September 9, U.S. Bank completed its first pilot transaction using USBDC, its proprietary dollar-backed stablecoin, on Stellar.

The bank moved that digital money between its own entities in North America and Europe.

This wasn't separated from normal bank infrastructure.

The transaction remained connected to U.S. Bank's existing finance, risk, compliance and operational systems.

The pilot tested minting, payment, redemption, freezing and clawback.

And U.S. Bank and SDF are already evaluating additional areas including liquidity management, collateral mobility and cross-border treasury operations.

That is one of the cleanest examples I can think of.

A major American bank is already testing proprietary bank money on Stellar.

At the same time, Congress is debating legislation saying national banks can use digital assets and distributed ledgers for financial activities they are otherwise permitted to perform.

The technology is already there.

The bank is already testing it.

The legislation is trying to create a clearer statutory environment around the activity.

That is why I don't view CLARITY as the beginning of Stellar's institutional thesis.

It could become the legal framework catching up to something that is already happening.

Then there is DTCC.

DTC's Tokenization Service plans to connect tokenized DTC-custodied assets to Stellar in the first half of 2027.

The asset classes being evaluated include U.S. Treasury bills, notes and bonds, major-index ETFs and Russell 1000 securities.

CLARITY separately addresses how tokenized securities can operate while remaining subject to securities law.

Put those two developments together and the significance becomes obvious.

Stellar's institutional story is increasingly about bank money on one side and tokenized capital markets on the other.

XLM sits natively underneath that network through fees, reserves and network liquidity.

That is exactly the kind of environment that becomes more valuable when financial institutions have a durable rulebook.

Then look at hedera-hashgraph:native.

This connection gets even more specific.

Patrick Witt himself participated at HederaCon 2026 in the closing fireside chat titled “Policy Meets Innovation: Clarity over Chaos.”

He was literally discussing what CLARITY could mean for institutional adoption and U.S. digital assets inside the Hedera ecosystem.

Then consider what Hedera already has in place.

HBAR was explicitly listed by the SEC/CFTC as a digital commodity.

The Canary HBAR ETF, HBR, trades on Nasdaq and directly holds HBAR.

Its structure includes BitGo Bank & Trust and Archax as HBAR custodians and U.S. Bank as cash custodian.

So regulated public-market access already exists.

Then you have the enterprise side.

Lloyds Banking Group, Aberdeen Investments and Archax have already executed FX trades using tokenized money-market funds and UK gilts on Hedera as collateral.

Aberdeen manages around £500 billion.

Archax has also launched real-time streaming cash flows for tokenized securities on Hedera using USDC.

Wyoming's FRNT, described in the context as the first U.S. state-issued stable token, is live on Hedera.

Hedera Stablecoin Studio is built around banks, tokenized deposits, regulated stablecoins and financial institutions.

Again, CLARITY does not need to create Hedera's institutional market.

Hedera already has banks, regulated tokenization, stablecoin infrastructure, exchange-traded HBAR access and public-sector digital money activity around the network.

The proposed federal framework could make it easier for more institutions to engage with that infrastructure from inside established banking and capital-market rules.

That is why these three assets feel so different from the average altcoin around this vote.

All three are already standing inside the categories Washington is trying to formalize.

XRP is sitting inside payments, liquidity, prime brokerage and tokenized finance.

XLM is sitting inside stablecoins, bank money, tokenized securities and cross-border settlement.

HBAR is sitting inside regulated tokenization, bank-facing DLT infrastructure, digital cash and collateral markets.

And all three are already named by federal regulators as digital commodities.

That combination is incredibly important.

People call XRP, XLM and HBAR “Made in America” coins all the time.

That phrase is not a legal CLARITY category.

Congress is not giving an asset special treatment because it has American roots.

The stronger story is far better anyway.

Ripple was founded in the U.S.

The Stellar Development Foundation is a Delaware nonprofit.

The Hedera Council is a Delaware LLC.

And their native assets already sit inside the same federal digital-commodity interpretation.

So if the market starts searching for an informal American digital-infrastructure basket after CLARITY advances, I can understand exactly why these names would come up.

Not because of a slogan.

Because their infrastructure already overlaps with the financial activities being addressed by the legislation.

And there is another layer here that I think crypto investors often miss.

Regulatory clarity doesn't only affect traders.

It affects compliance departments.

👉Bank boards.
👉Risk committees.
👉Custodians.
👉Broker-dealers.
👉ETF issuers.
👉Prime brokers.
👉Asset managers.
👉Market makers.
👉Corporate treasurers.

Those institutions don't need a viral tweet to decide where billions of dollars can go.

They need legal language their lawyers can map against their operations.

That is where legislation can change behavior.

An agency interpretation can be important.

A congressional statute can become much harder to reverse.

That distinction is exactly why CLARITY can matter even though XRP, XLM and HBAR already have the digital-commodity designation today.

March gave them classification.

CLARITY can help build the permanent market around that classification.

And the wider Trump administration policy direction already lines up with it.

The May 19 executive order says federal regulation should allow digital assets and innovative technology to integrate into traditional financial services and payment systems.

The White House digital-assets report supports clearer CFTC authority over spot non-security digital assets, custody, trading, DeFi, tokenization, stablecoins and blockchain activity by banks.

The policy path is beginning to look coherent:

GENIUS Act for stablecoins.

SEC/CFTC interpretation for asset taxonomy.

The banking executive order for integration into traditional finance.

CLARITY for the broader market structure.

That is a very different Washington than the one XRP holders were dealing with several years ago.

And Patrick Witt is now saying there is a political window to finish the job.

He would not attach himself to Senator Cynthia Lummis' specific 2030 warning.

But his reasoning was clear.

The November midterms can change congressional math.

Lame-duck periods are difficult.

Major legislation gets harder as an administration gets older.

That is why September 15 deserves attention.

Again, it is not final passage.

But clearing the cloture hurdle would mean the Senate has enough support to proceed despite months of negotiation.

For XRP, XLM and HBAR, the significance is not a one-day candle.

The significance is what happens if their institutional ecosystems finally operate under a durable statutory framework.

For $XRP, that could push the conversation even further away from years of SEC uncertainty and toward institutional scale through Ripple Prime, RLUSD, payments, FX, tokenization and credit.

For stellar:native, it could give U.S. Bank's stablecoin work, DTCC's upcoming Stellar connection and the network's growing RWA market a clearer U.S. path.

For hedera-hashgraph:native, it could support exactly the bank-DLT and regulated-tokenization environment Hedera has spent years preparing for.

And there is even a second policy route in Witt's interview.

He said that if Congress does not complete the legislation, the administration intends to push an aggressive SEC and CFTC rulemaking agenda.

That means these assets are entering the next stage from a position where the agencies have already placed all three inside the digital-commodity category.

I still prefer the congressional route because statute is the bigger prize.

But either way, U.S. policy is moving deeper into the question of how these markets should actually operate.

That is why I see September 15 differently.

It isn't simply another crypto vote.

It is a test of whether the United States is ready to move from classifying digital assets to building the financial market around them.

And XRP, XLM and HBAR do not need to wait around hoping someone builds infrastructure afterward.

The infrastructure is already there.

The law is finally trying to catch up.

If that happens, the next phase for these assets won't be about proving they belong in American finance.

It will be about seeing how much of American finance can actually run through the systems already built around them.

Could Trump’s proposed $5,000 dividend unleash the biggest U.S. retail liquidity wave $XRP has ever traded through?

I’ve been thinking about this since Trump floated the idea.

If Republicans win both the House and Senate, Trump says he wants to send $5,000 to every adult U.S. citizen, with the money spent inside America.

Reuters estimates the total could reach roughly $1.35 TRILLION.

That number is insane by itself.

But I’m not looking at this as:

“Everyone gets $5,000 and buys XRP.”

That’s way too simple.

We already have evidence from the last stimulus cycle that government payments can spill into investments.

The Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland found a noticeable increase in Bitcoin purchases around the exact $1,200 stimulus-check amount in 2020.

The NBER also found crypto investment increased after stimulus payments, with the strongest increase following the third round.

Now imagine another huge injection of household cash.

Except this time, $XRP would be entering it from a completely different position.

During the previous stimulus era, Ripple was heading into a brutal regulatory fight in the United States.

Today?

The SEC and CFTC have placed XRP inside their digital-commodity framework.

A 21Shares XRP ETF, TOXR, trades through traditional U.S. securities infrastructure.

The GENIUS Act has already created federal rules around payment stablecoins.

The OCC conditionally approved Ripple National Trust Bank.

Ripple has expanded its U.S. presence.

And the White House has openly made digital assets, blockchain technology and American leadership in digital finance part of its policy direction.

That changes the setup completely.

Even a tiny percentage of $1.35T entering crypto would become serious money.

1% = $13.5B
5% = $67.5B
10% = $135B

And XRP only needs to attract a fraction of whatever eventually reaches crypto for the numbers to get large very quickly.

But there’s another reason I’m so bullish.

Ripple isn’t only positioned for people buying $XRP.

It is also building infrastructure for where digital money goes afterward.

RLUSD gives Ripple regulated dollar liquidity.

XRP Ledger provides settlement infrastructure.

XRP can sit between currencies as a bridge when that route gives better execution.

Ripple and Bitso are already bringing MXNB and RLUSD together inside the XRP Ledger ecosystem for U.S.–Mexico liquidity and settlement.

So imagine the bigger picture.

New household liquidity enters America.

Some gets spent.
Some gets invested.
Some reaches crypto.

More people enter digital markets.

At the exact same time, the United States is pushing deeper into regulated digital finance.

That combination didn’t exist in 2020.

And that’s why I’m watching this closely.

A $5,000 Trump dividend wouldn’t need to become an “XRP check.”

It could simply inject an enormous amount of capital into an American financial system where $XRP is now dramatically easier to access, regulate and integrate than during the last retail boom.

If this dividend becomes reality, I think people will seriously underestimate what $1.35T of fresh household liquidity can wake up.

text:
Who Really Controls AI? The American Advantage Is Bigger Than It Looks

Washington has been encouraging its allies to build “sovereign AI.” At first glance, that sounds like every country should build its own chips, data centers, foundation models, cloud infrastructure and software. But that is not actually the American strategy. And this distinction matters, because the United States may have discovered that technological power does not require owning every part of the system. It requires controlling the parts nobody can easily replace.

That is the real story behind the growing debate over AI sovereignty. Governments understandably want control over their data, regulations and critical infrastructure. But building an entire AI ecosystem domestically is enormously expensive, technically difficult and, in many cases, economically inefficient. A country can spend billions trying to reproduce what Silicon Valley, NVIDIA, American cloud companies and U.S. research institutions have spent decades building. The question is not whether a country can build something itself. The question is whether it can afford to walk away from the American ecosystem.

This is where Washington's position becomes much more interesting. U.S. officials have warned partners about what they describe as a “digital sovereignty trap”: the idea that technological independence requires rebuilding the entire stack at home. The American argument is different. Countries can maintain control over their policies, data and applications while still using American technology underneath. That is not necessarily a loss of sovereignty. It can be a smarter way to preserve it.

The strategy becomes clearer when looking at initiatives such as Pax Silica. What began around strategic minerals and semiconductor supply chains has expanded into a broader effort involving trusted partners and the infrastructure needed for advanced technology. The American AI Exports Program follows a similar logic, allowing U.S. companies to offer much more than individual products: hardware, data centers, foundation models, applications and cybersecurity. America is not simply exporting AI products. It is helping build the infrastructure through which other countries will develop their own AI capabilities.

That distinction gives the United States an unusual form of power. If Washington can persuade allies to build their AI future around American technology, the relationship becomes more than a buyer-and-seller relationship. It becomes an ecosystem. And ecosystems are much harder to replace than individual products.

History helps explain why this matters. In 1962, the United Nations recognized the permanent sovereignty of nations over their natural resources. Then came the oil crisis of 1973, demonstrating how powerful a resource can become when there are few immediate substitutes. But AI is different. There is no single “AI field” sitting underground. The critical resources are scattered across advanced GPUs, semiconductor manufacturing, cloud computing, software frameworks, data, engineers and accumulated technical knowledge.

That makes switching costs one of the most important measures of technological sovereignty.

A country may technically own a national AI program. But if replacing its hardware, cloud infrastructure, software ecosystem or model provider would take years and billions of dollars, its practical freedom of action is much smaller than it appears on paper. This is one reason American technology remains so influential. NVIDIA GPUs are not simply pieces of silicon. They sit inside an enormous software and developer ecosystem that makes replacing them far more complicated than purchasing another chip.

The numbers reinforce the point. Research cited in the original analysis of global AI projects found that infrastructure represented the largest share of state-backed AI investment, followed by models and data. A majority of those projects involved foreign partners, and U.S. companies appeared in a large share of those partnerships. NVIDIA hardware was also present in a substantial portion of the infrastructure projects tracked. The world is building sovereign AI, but much of that sovereignty is being built on top of American technology.

And that is not necessarily a weakness for the United States. It can be an extraordinary competitive advantage.

India, for example, has pursued a strategy of diversification rather than complete technological autarky, working with suppliers such as NVIDIA, AMD, Intel and Google. Europe is investing heavily in AI Gigafactories and seeking greater strategic autonomy, yet it is not realistically attempting to sever itself from the American technology ecosystem. Gulf states are making enormous investments in AI infrastructure while U.S. export controls and licensing decisions remain strategically important to their plans.

This reveals something important about American economic power. The United States does not have to manufacture everything the world needs. It needs to remain indispensable in enough of the technologies that the world cannot easily move around it.

That is a much more realistic definition of power in the AI era.

The scale of American investment makes the advantage even harder to ignore. U.S. private AI investment reached an extraordinary level in 2025, far exceeding the investment of individual competitors. Money alone does not guarantee technological leadership, but capital allows companies to buy computing power, hire researchers, build data centers, acquire startups and absorb enormous amounts of risk. Silicon Valley's greatest advantage is not one company or one invention. It is the ability of an entire financial and technological ecosystem to keep funding the next experiment.

China, of course, is the most serious challenger. Chinese AI models have improved dramatically, and open-weight systems from Chinese developers have given users around the world more alternatives. China also has enormous strengths in research, engineering talent, manufacturing capacity and state-directed investment. The gap between leading Chinese and American models has narrowed significantly.

But this is precisely where the AI competition becomes more complicated than a benchmark chart.

China can produce increasingly capable models. It can build domestic AI infrastructure. It can develop alternatives to American software and hardware. Yet moving away from the American ecosystem is not simply a matter of building a better model. Hardware, software compatibility, developer communities, cloud infrastructure and accumulated know-how create layers of dependency that are extremely difficult to reproduce quickly.

China may therefore reduce one form of dependence while creating another challenge: replacing the entire ecosystem around advanced computing.

And this is where America's strategy becomes particularly powerful.

Washington's advantage is not simply that American companies produce leading AI systems. It is that the United States has leverage across multiple layers of the stack: advanced computing, cloud services, foundation models, venture capital, software, research institutions, semiconductor design and an enormous network of technology companies and allies. The United States is competing not merely to build the best AI, but to remain at the center of the global AI architecture.

That also explains why export controls matter.

If advanced computing is becoming one of the most important strategic resources of the 21st century, controlling access to the most advanced chips is not merely a trade policy. It becomes a national-security instrument. The same principle works in reverse: countries that depend on American technology have an incentive to maintain stable relationships with Washington because suddenly losing access could be enormously expensive.

Some critics will argue that this proves the world is becoming dangerously dependent on America. But there is another way to look at it. America's allies are not being forced to choose between complete independence and dependence on one country. They are being given access to a technology ecosystem that allows them to build their own capabilities faster.

That is a meaningful difference.

The United States has historically benefited from an open economic system, immigration, research collaboration, private investment and alliances. Its technological advantage was not created by isolation. It was created by attracting people, capital and ideas from around the world and turning them into companies and technologies that became globally important.

AI may be following the same pattern.

The coming competition will therefore not be decided simply by which country owns the largest number of AI models or builds the most data centers. It will be decided by who controls the bottlenecks, who attracts the capital and talent, who sets the standards, who has the strongest alliances and who can offer the world the most difficult ecosystem to replace.

On those terms, the United States still has an extraordinary advantage.

American leadership in AI is not guaranteed. China will continue to improve. Europe will seek greater autonomy. India and the Gulf states will build their own capabilities. Other countries will try to diversify their technology suppliers.

But diversification is not the same as replacement.

And that may be the most important point of all.

America does not need the world to use only American technology. It needs American technology to remain the technology the world cannot afford to abandon.

That is a very different kind of sovereignty.

And if Washington can maintain that position while continuing to innovate, invest and strengthen its alliances, the United States may not simply remain a leader in AI.

It may become the country that defines what technological sovereignty means in the first place.

text:
Good morning from Virginia. 🇺🇸

On the morning of September 11, 1789, in New York—then the capital of a government still finding its feet—George Washington sent the Senate the first cabinet nomination in the history of the United States. The messenger had scarcely left the chamber when the senators, meeting in the old City Hall on Wall Street, confirmed Alexander Hamilton as Secretary of the Treasury. They did it unanimously, and they did it in minutes. Nine days earlier Congress had created the Department itself. Washington had been President only since April. The Constitution was new, the country was tired, and the quieter test had begun: whether a people who had won a war could pay their debts, keep their word, and stand solvent among the nations of the earth.

Hamilton was thirty-four. He had been Washington’s aide-de-camp through the long winters of the Revolution, the restless young officer who wrote by candlelight and seemed never to tire. Robert Morris, the financier of the war, had been offered the Treasury first and had declined. Take Hamilton, Morris said—he is damned sharp. Washington paused over the fire in the man, then chose competence. Friends had urged Hamilton away. The nation’s finances, they said, were a chaos of wartime paper and unpaid promises, a deep and dreary wreck. Better the Senate. Better the bench. Hamilton took the wreck. That was his nature. He had come from almost nothing in the West Indies, made himself indispensable, and now he walked into an empty department and began to give it a spine.

The debt stood at some seventy-five million dollars—an enormous sum for a country with no mint, no national bank, and little credit abroad. Hamilton would not treat it as an embarrassment to be shuffled aside. The debt of the United States, he would tell Congress, was the price of liberty. Faith had been pledged. It would be kept. He meant to assume the state debts with the federal, to collect customs and excise with regularity, to found a bank, to set American manufacture beside American farms. Jefferson and Madison would come to see in all this a dangerous concentration of power, and the quarrel that followed would shape parties and generations. But on that September morning the quarrel had not yet begun. There was only a young man taking an oath, a President who trusted him, and a country that needed someone willing to sit down with the ledgers and make a nation out of them.

He served until January of 1795, then stepped back, though Washington still sought his counsel as a man seeks a true bearing. The duel on the Weehawken heights in 1804 ended the life. It did not end the work. What he left was not a monument of stone but a habit of credit—the unglamorous, indispensable habit of a people who mean what they say when they borrow, who collect what they levy, who bind distant states together with the quiet ligament of a shared purse. You can walk the marble halls of the Treasury now and forget how thin the thing once was: a handful of clerks, a new seal, a thirty-four-year-old immigrant at a table in New York, deciding that chaos would not be the American inheritance. Nations are declared in a rush of feeling. They are kept by men who stay after the cheering and do the sums. That Friday in 1789 was one of those keeping days, and we are still living in the house it helped to raise.

text:
25 years ago on September 11, 2001, four commercial airplanes were hijacked in a coordinated terrorist attack against the United States. Two planes were flown into the Twin Towers in New York City. A third plane crashed into the Pentagon in Washington, DC. On the fourth plane, passengers and crew fought the hijackers, causing the plane to crash into an empty rural field near Shanksville, Pennsylvania. In an hour and forty-two minutes, 2,977 innocent people lost their lives. The 9/11 attacks were the deadliest attacks on American soil since the attack at Pearl Harbor.

As a memorial to the tragedy of 9/11, we will pause, play Taps, and offer a moment of silence during the time each of the events that occurred that day. The flame guard will also be marching.

6:46 AM (MDT) – Flight 11 crashes into the World Trade Center’s North Tower.
7:03 AM (MDT) – Flight 175 crashes into the World Trade Center’s South Tower.
7:37 AM (MDT) – Flight 77 crashes into the Pentagon.
7:59 AM (MDT) – The South Tower of the World Trade Center collapses.
8:02 AM (MDT) – Flight 93 plows into an empty field in Shanksville, Pennsylvania.
8:28 AM (MDT) – The North Tower of the World Trade Center collapses.

text:
Good morning. 

25 years ago, our fellow citizens, our way of life, our very freedom came under attack in a series of deliberate and deadly terrorist acts. The victims were in airplanes, or in their offices; secretaries, businessmen and women, military and federal workers; moms and dads, friends and neighbors. Thousands of lives were suddenly ended by evil, despicable acts of terror.

The pictures of airplanes flying into buildings, fires burning, huge structures collapsing, have filled us with disbelief, terrible sadness, and a quiet, unyielding anger. These acts of mass murder were intended to frighten our nation into chaos and retreat. But they have failed; our country is strong.

A great people has been moved to defend a great nation. Terrorist attacks can shake the foundations of our biggest buildings, but they cannot touch the foundation of America. These acts shattered steel, but they cannot dent the steel of American resolve.

America was targeted for attack because we're the brightest beacon for freedom and opportunity in the world. And no one will keep that light from shining.

25 years ago, our nation saw evil, the very worst of human nature. And we responded with the best of America -- with the daring of our rescue workers, with the caring for strangers and neighbors who came to give blood and help in any way they could.

Immediately following the first attack, President Bush implemented our government's emergency response plans. Our military is powerful, and it's prepared. Our emergency teams worked in New York City, Washington, D.C, and Shanksville, Pennsylvania to help with local efforts.

Our first priority was to get help to those who have been injured, and to take every precaution to protect our citizens at home and around the world from further attacks.

The functions of our government continue without interruption. Federal agencies in Washington which had to be evacuated on that day, reopened for essential personnel that night, and was open for business on September 12th,2001 . Our financial institutions remain strong, and the American economy will be open for business, as well.

In the years that followed, troops were sent to Afghanistan, Pakistan,and Iraq with  the full resources of our intelligence and law enforcement communities to find all that were responsible and to bring them to justice. We will make no distinction between the terrorists who committed these acts and those who harbor them.

I appreciate so very much the members of Congress who have joined me in strongly condemning these attacks. And on behalf of the American people, I thank the many world leaders who have called to offer their condolences and assistance.

America and our friends and allies join with all those who want peace and security in the world, and we stand together to win the war against terrorism. Today, I ask for your prayers for all those who grieve, for the children whose worlds have been shattered, for all whose sense of safety and security has been threatened. And I pray they will be comforted by a power greater than any of us, spoken through the ages in Psalm 23: "Even though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I fear no evil, for You are with me."

This is a day when all Americans from every walk of life unite in our resolve for justice and peace. America has stood down enemies before, and we did so this time. None of us will ever forget this day. Yet, we go forward to defend freedom and all that is good and just in our world.

text:
OpenAI Is Building a Government Moat—and Trying to Close the Door Behind It

Taken separately, OpenAI’s latest moves can be presented as ordinary business and responsible policymaking. Put them together, however, and a more self-interested strategy begins to appear.

First, OpenAI effectively gave ChatGPT Enterprise to federal agencies for $1 per agency under a government-wide introductory agreement. That pilot is now reportedly being replaced with usage-based pricing offering federal workers a 50% discount. In other words, the free sample is ending, but the government is being offered a favorable price to keep using the product.[1]

That is not charity. It is customer acquisition on a federal scale.

Sell cheaply enough to get ChatGPT embedded inside agencies. Let employees build workflows around it. Train workers to depend on it. Connect it to government documents, procedures and internal systems. Once those agencies reorganize their work around OpenAI’s platform, replacing it becomes much harder than simply canceling another software subscription.

The moat is not merely the contract. The moat is institutional dependency.

Then came OpenAI’s call for mandatory national AI rules. The company says voluntary promises are no longer sufficient and supports capability-based federal requirements involving outside evaluations, cybersecurity safeguards and incident reporting.[2] Some of those protections may be legitimate and necessary. Powerful AI systems plainly need serious security standards.

But we should still ask the old-fashioned question: Who benefits from the particular rules being proposed?

OpenAI already possesses enormous amounts of capital, computing infrastructure, lawyers, policy specialists, security teams and government relationships. It can absorb audits, reporting mandates, licensing expenses and compliance departments that would bury a smaller competitor.

A regulation costing OpenAI $100 million is an expense. The same regulation costing a young AI company $100 million is a locked door.

That is how regulatory capture often works. The established company does not necessarily oppose regulation. It helps design regulation that it can afford—and that the next company cannot. The public hears “safety,” while the market quietly receives a higher entrance fee.

OpenAI is also seeking legal clarity that would allow major AI laboratories to coordinate a slowdown in frontier-model development without running afoul of antitrust law. Supporters describe this as necessary safety cooperation. Critics could reasonably ask whether it might also permit today’s dominant laboratories to coordinate the speed of competition while enjoying a government-approved legal shelter.[3]

That does not prove a conspiracy. It does establish that OpenAI wants government rules governing who may build the most powerful systems, what requirements those builders must satisfy and how the largest laboratories may cooperate with one another.

Meanwhile, OpenAI is getting its product established throughout the federal government at a steep discount.

The rumor mill goes further. There is industry speculation that OpenAI’s regulatory campaign is partly about preparing the ground for a future public offering, reducing unpredictable legal exposure and reassuring investors that the company will occupy a protected position inside America’s government and critical institutions. That has not been proven, and the timing or structure of any future IPO remains uncertain. It should be treated as informed speculation—not established fact.

There is also a growing suspicion that national regulation could be used to override tougher state laws and replace them with one federal framework friendlier to the biggest AI companies. Again, motive is difficult to prove. But a single national system would be far easier for a giant company with a Washington policy operation to influence than fifty separate state governments.

None of this means AI regulation is unnecessary. Nor does it mean every OpenAI safety proposal is dishonest. AI can create real cybersecurity, biological, military and consumer risks. The mistake would be assuming that a company asking to be regulated has suddenly stopped acting like a company.

OpenAI can sincerely believe AI needs guardrails while also preferring guardrails built to its measurements.

The pattern is becoming difficult to ignore: enter government cheaply, become part of its daily machinery, help write the national rules, raise the cost of compliance, seek protection for coordination among the largest laboratories and possibly reduce future liability.

Call it safety policy if you like. Call it responsible adoption. But from a business standpoint, it looks remarkably like OpenAI is building a government moat around itself.

At the very least, OpenAI appears to be trying to close the door behind it—and asking Washington to install the lock.

Sources

[1] OpenAI’s original federal agreement offered ChatGPT Enterprise for $1 per participating agency; the replacement is reportedly usage-based pricing at a 50% discount. GSA announcement | Mobile World Live report
[2] OpenAI has called for binding national requirements, including independent assessments, cybersecurity protections and incident reporting. Reuters

[3] OpenAI has sought clarification about whether cooperation among major AI laboratories to slow frontier development could violate antitrust law. Wired
