Sept. 6—On Sept. 4, Executive Intelligence Review combined with the 170th consecutive weekly meeting of the International Peace Coalition (IPC) to host a roundtable discussion on the topic, “An Alternative to War and Looting in the Americas.” The day-long deliberations—which brought together distinguished panelists from Ibero-America, China, Spain, Germany, and the United States—began by listening to remarks delivered by EIR founder Lyndon LaRouche during a June 2002 visit to Brazil, which laid out a challenge, both to the roundtable panelists and to the more-than-2,500 on-line participants listening from 38 countries in five different languages:

“On the subject of integration: The bringing together of people of different cultures and nations for a common enterprise, a strategic enterprise, is the most important and most challenging enterprise in all statecraft. You cannot use ordinary politics under such circumstances,” LaRouche cautioned, because to achieve true integration “you must actually communicate ideas.”

He elaborated on the essential idea which in fact unites all nations, all religions, all language groups and all races:

    Every animal species has a more or less fixed potential relative population-density. Then how does man reach a level of several billions of population on this planet? By changing his own behavior. Other species can only do this through a kind of evolutionary development of their genetic material. Man can do it as an act of will, as in the image of God. How does this result in human progress? By transmission of these discoveries from one generation to another.

This is the basis, LaRouche argued, on which we can “agree, strategically, to create a community of nations on this planet, which is fit for human beings to live in.”

With that conceptual guidepost, the participants took up the specific challenges of integration around the most critical infrastructure project of Ibero-America and the Caribbean: building a bi-oceanic rail corridor from Brazil’s Atlantic ports to Peru’s Chancay Port on the Pacific, in order to link the entire region to the phenomenal growth expressed in China’s Belt and Road Initiative across the Pacific.

EIR Editor-in-Chief Helga Zepp-LaRouche used her keynote address to put the proposal in strategic focus:

    The time has come that the countries of the Global South have to assume a leadership role in the world of today, and prove that Kissinger’s mantra that “history is not made in the South” is utterly false. If the countries of Ibero-America unite around a common development plan, they can assume sovereignty of all and determine their own future. Rather than having the South American continent be a playground for a geopolitical confrontation, a united Ibero-America can influence the course of world politics.

She turned her attention to Brazil, which is facing a presidential election on Oct. 4 in which the speculative vultures of Wall Street and the City of London are doing everything in their power to try to stop President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva from being reelected.

“Brazil is a founding member of the BRICS,” Zepp-LaRouche reminded the audience, “and in that capacity can play the role of a mediator between the Global Majority and the Global North, invoking the tradition of the spirit of cooperation between [Brazilian President] Getúlio Vargas and [U.S. President] Franklin Delano Roosevelt. By putting the bi-oceanic railway corridor on the agenda, Brazil can invite both China and the United States to participate in the perspective of common development.”

A central issue discussed during the dialogue among the panelists was how—or even if—the United States that today is imposing the law of the jungle around the world, could ever be brought back to its senses and revive the tradition of Franklin Roosevelt and Lyndon LaRouche. Zepp-LaRouche stressed that such a change in the United States, driven by the “voice of the Global South” demanding a new system of justice for all, is the only way to avoid a head-on collision which would likely lead to thermonuclear war.
Port of Chancay in Peru
Five automated rail-mounted gantry cranes from China at the Port of Chancay in Peru. Credit: CC/Presidencia del Consejo de Ministros

Zhang Weiwei, professor of international relations at Fudan University in Shanghai, China, conveyed China’s full support of such a development-based approach to solving global problems, as seen in Chancay Port, which was jointly built by Peru and China and inaugurated in 2024. “At this moment of history, a time of uncertainty and much chaos, it’s indeed timely and very perceptive to discuss this landmark project, the bi-oceanic rail corridor linking Peru’s Chancay Port and Brazil’s Ilhéus Port,” Zhang stated. “[This] is a landmark project under joint feasibility study by Brazil, Peru, and China, which I think is an expression of genuine multilateral cooperation and Global South solidarity.”

As became clear in the course of the roundtable dialogue, building such an integration project will not only serve as a living alternative to the policies of war and looting today being unleashed across Ibero-America by the U.S. President Donald Trump’s administration. It will also serve as a proof-of-principle that the same approach to integration—“the most important and most challenging enterprise in all statecraft”—can be applied to even more difficult and entrenched problems elsewhere, such as the ongoing genocide and wars in Southwest Asia.

As Prof. Zhang put it: “The bi-oceanic rail corridor is more than a transport infrastructure project. It is a powerful symbol of South American integration, mutual assistance, and independent development. It unites rather than divides, delivers development rather than confrontation, and pursues common prosperity and development. I think we should all work hard to promote this kind of idea and fascinating project in the interests of the Global South.”
Bi-oceanic rail route map
Map showing route of the bi-oceanic railway from Peru to Brazil, as well as the Chancay Port’s direct shipping link across the Pacific with Shanghai, China. Credit: EIRNS
Cooperation and Integration

The first panel of the EIR roundtable  https://t.co/YC8kXGpr1d featured presentations by distinguished speakers from the principal protagonist nations, Brazil, Peru, and China. Roberto Amaral, former Brazilian Minister of Science and Technology (2003) in Lula’s first government, spoke on “The Future of Brazil: Science, Technology, Innovation and Sovereignty.” He began by emphasizing that “scientific and technological progress creates the minimum conditions necessary to fuel the dream of sovereignty in a markedly asymmetrical world, amid a globalization heading toward a new Cold War that, as we know, does not serve the interests of humanity.” Without mentioning the United States by name, he warned that a single nation was “imposing its own law, based on the primacy of force that dictates legal norms after the fact.”

He continued: “Brazil, due to its size, population, and level of development, as well as its vast reserves of strategic metals—such as the so-called ‘rare earths’—could serve as a bastion of resistance; as it stands, it is already a nuisance that must be eliminated.” For Brazil to defend itself, “foreign policy, science policy, and defense policy converge,” and he advocated for joint integration projects with Brazil’s neighbors and others: “For our projects, it is essential to strengthen relations with the other countries of South America and establish deep bonds of cooperation. The same applies to our long-standing collaboration with China, South Africa, India, and Russia—countries that, together with us, form the core of the BRICS and with which we have negotiated scientific cooperation programs.”

Minister Amaral concluded by stressing the role of “science, technology, and innovation as the core of development and the guarantors of sovereignty.”

He was followed by Peruvian Gen. (ret.) Edwin Patterson Monsalve, an academic and professor of geopolitics and geostrategy with special expertise on Chancay Port, who spoke on “Peru’s Chancay Port and South America’s Development and Integration Networks.” He said that there is a long-standing view in his country that “there can be no development without security, and no security without development.” He added that the bipolar world of the Cold War had shifted to a unipolar world dominated by the United States, but that it must in turn yield to a multipolar world as new alliances emerge, such as the BRICS.

He described the Port of Chancay as “a strategic goal of the Peruvian state,” which will transform Peru’s relations with the rest of South America and the world at large. He highlighted the role of China in conceiving and helping Peru build the project, and anticipated the port’s role in strengthening Peru’s trade relations with that country, while becoming a hub for other South American nations wishing to increase their economic relations with China—which he demonstrated with maps and other graphics, including a projected bi-oceanic rail corridor linking Chancay with Brazil’s Atlantic coast.

Until the opening of Chancay in late 2024, all Peruvian trade with China first went through North American ports such as Long Beach. Gen. Patterson reported that the U.S. fears China’s influence in South America, including the prospect of losing its position of being the middleman for trade between South America and Asia. Peru’s long-standing policy, he emphasized, seeks good economic relations with all nations and favors South American integration, tracing this approach back to Peruvian General Edgardo Mercado Jarrín, who was Foreign Minister (1968-1971) and then Prime Minister (1973-1975) under the Presidency of General Juan Velasco Alvarado, who brought Peru into the Non-Aligned Movement in Sept. 1973.

Gen. Patterson later added that the “complex interdependence” of nations can only succeed if the citizens are fully engaged in the political process.
What Role Will the U.S. Play?

Paulo Nogueira Batista, Jr., a Brazilian economist who was formerly the executive director for Brazil and 10 other countries at the IMF in Washington, D.C. (from 2007-2015), as well as co-founder and vice president of the New Development Bank established by the BRICS, spoke next on “The New Monroe Doctrine and the U.S. Claims to Uncontested Hegemony in the Western Hemisphere.”

He charged that the United States is “acting according to its new precepts,” with the invasion of Venezuela and the kidnapping of its President Nicolás Maduro, the siege of Cuba, and growing disputes with Canada and other nations. But the U.S. also “commits enormous strategic errors,” he said, by picking simultaneous fights with Russia, Iran, and China and forcing those three nations to tend to unite. Iran has proved that “the capacity to resist aggression” does not depend on nuclear deterrence, and he called upon Brazil and other nations to build up their own defense capabilities, to safeguard against the possibility of further actions by the United States, like those carried out against Venezuela.

“This means building, as quickly as possible, a national defense strategy and preparing for the worst: hoping for the best, preparing for the worst. And this preparing for the worst includes, for example, military cooperation.” He concluded with a stark warning:

“So, the question posed by Lyndon LaRouche [in his video excerpt], ‘Can we survive?’ is even more relevant now than when he stated that. We’re living in a world of hyper-imperialism…. We are facing an existential threat in the new circumstances created by hyper-imperialism.”

In the discussion period, Helga Zepp-LaRouche agreed about the havoc that the United States and Europe are currently wreaking on the rest of the world, but warned that if we are not able to change the strategic direction of the United States, and the world therefore hardens into two competing blocs—the Global South vs. the Collective West—then thermonuclear war is a likely outcome. A global solution to the crisis is not a luxury, but a necessity, she insisted.

Nogueira Batista reiterated that he thought it unlikely that such a desirable new global order would emerge anytime soon, due to the intransigence and the destructive role of the United States.

EIR Ibero-American director Dennis Small replied that, “speaking as an American,” it is important for us all to remember that the United States is not Wall Street, George Bush, Barack Obama, and Donald Trump—who have produced terrible harm around the world. “There is a strand running throughout the history of our country, best expressed by Lyndon LaRouche,” which is the key to solving the current breakdown crisis. The U.S., Small argued, is also Franklin Delano Roosevelt, who allied with Brazilian President Getúlio Vargas to help develop that country, and with Mexico’s President Lázaro Cárdenas to support his nationalization of Mexico’s oil. The U.S. is also the policies of John Quincy Adams, who wrote the original Monroe Doctrine—the exact opposite of the later Teddy Roosevelt Corollary that Trump adores—and of Abraham Lincoln and Lyndon LaRouche. It is that strand that makes it both possible and necessary to bring the U.S. back to a policy of community of interests with all the nations of the planet, Small concluded. Nogueira Batista agreed that the presidencies of Franklin Roosevelt, Lincoln, and also John F. Kennedy offered a different model, but he said that recent history is far less encouraging. “Trump is not an anomaly,” he stated, adding that he saw little hope that the United States would resume such earlier positive policies.

In response, Helga Zepp-LaRouche reminded everyone of the very real threat of nuclear war, saying, essentially, that failure is not an option. She reiterated the strategic importance of the voices of the Global South—such as those expressed in this EIR roundtable—being heard loud and clear in the United States and Europe, in order to bring about the needed strategic shift. She thanked the participants for their contribution to that effort, and noted that the discussion brought out very clearly the question which needs to be solved: Can mankind self-govern or not?
No to NATO

The final speaker of Panel One was Col. (ret.) Pedro Baños of Spain, a geopolitical analyst and frequent lecturer in various military institutions in Spain and elsewhere, who brought a useful counterpoint to the discussion by speaking on “Why Spain Must Not Join NATO’s War Against Russia and Iran.” Baños, who has a YouTube following of almost one million in Spain and Ibero-America, began by reviewing the history of NATO from its inception in 1949, and Spain’s role as a participant, which began in 1982, with the proviso that Spain not host nuclear weapons or U.S. military bases. This proviso was later modified in the 1990s. When the Warsaw Pact dissolved itself, it was done with the understanding that NATO would also gradually dissolve. Instead, NATO doubled in size. If Spain were to comply with U.S. demands that it spend 5% of its budget on defense, that would be a five-fold increase, and would be difficult to sustain.

Spain has nothing to gain, and everything to lose, by joining a war against Russia, Baños stated emphatically.
South America’s Bi-Oceanic Rail Corridor

The second panel began with a video clip from an address by Lyndon LaRouche to a 1997 conference in Washington, D.C. https://t.co/Si7ACGk26x, in which he said, “The U.S. relationship to China can become the essential pivot and keystone for a global change.” LaRouche explained his World Land-Bridge concept: “What is at stake, is the development of a global infrastructural system, which had its genesis in the work of the Lincoln administration in the United States, beginning 1861. That is, under the influence of the world’s then-leading economist, Henry C. Carey, the American economist. The United States entered into a development program internal to the United States, called the transcontinental railroad. We set up a network of transcontinental railroad routes across from the Atlantic to the Pacific, of the United States. These were not simply transportation routes, but these were designed as development corridors, such that for a distance of 50 to 75 kilometers on either side of the rail link, you would have agricultural and other development, would be occurring.” LaRouche explained that the goal is to “bring the whole world together in one large-scale economic development program, which can be the basis for the revival and prosperity of the world economy in the coming century. That’s the policy.”

Dennis Small then spoke on “South America’s Bi-Oceanic Rail Corridor, a Century-Scale Planetary Transformation.” He recounted a trip to Brazil in 1982 during which he visited Carajás, the site of the world’s largest reserves of iron ore. Brazil faced a choice of whether to simply export the ore to get foreign exchange for debt service, or to develop the iron for internal use in infrastructure projects and industry. This is the classic choice still today for nations which wish to become sovereign nations instead of colonies, and the key to what the South American bi-oceanic rail corridor must become.

Small then returned to the 19th-Century example of Lincoln’s transcontinental railroad as referenced by LaRouche, quoting Lincoln’s advisor Henry Carey on the benefits of such infrastructure. In the early 20th Century, Russia built the Trans-Siberian Railroad, under the leadership of Finance Minister Count Witte, a follower of the American System school of Carey and German economist Friedrich List. In the 21st Century, this same approach to physical economy is behind China’s stunning 50,000 kilometers of high-speed rail, which also represents an embrace, with Chinese characteristics, of the American System of Lincoln and Carey, as well as a rejection of the British imperial approach.

But the bi-oceanic rail corridor is just the beginning, Small emphasized. South Americans, like all humans, must now turn their eyes to the stars and engage in space science and eventual colonization beyond Earth. The Hubble telescope has revealed over two trillion galaxies in the observable universe, each with hundreds of billions of stars. That’s 4 x 10 to the 23rd power stars! And NASA’s new Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope is 100 times more powerful than the Hubble. What is most amazing, Small concluded, is not that the universe is so unfathomably large, but that man’s mind is capable of grasping that concept, and continuously improving our scientific understanding of that ongoing process of creation we call the universe.

Donald Ramotar, former President of Guyana (2011-2015), spoke on “A Good Neighbor Policy Among the Nations of South America.” He began by reviewing some of the recent “natural disasters” such as the flood in Nepal. He then rejected the term “natural disaster,” because human negligence is the real culprit. He then moved to the foreign policy follies of the Anglosphere, such as its support for Ukraine and Israel in their respective benighted wars. He characterized those Western governments as puppets of corrupt private interests, such as the notorious military-industrial complex. He denounced the open interference by the United States in elections in South American nations, as well as militarization of the Caribbean with senseless bombings of fishing boats, and lamented the capitulation of many Caribbean nations.

“But what we are seeing in the United States is not just strength, but desperation,” President Ramotar argued. “They are deathly afraid of the BRICS.” The stalwart resistance of the Iranian people has shown that there are limits to the power of the U.S. He closed by citing the warning of Rosa Luxemburg, who said in 1915 that if we do not change this system, we will end up with barbarism. He pointed to President Lula in Brazil as an example of a leader of the Global South who understands the need for integration, and building a new international security and development architecture.

Sara Madueño de Vásquez, EIR bureau chief in Lima, Peru, spoke on “The ‘Chancay Effect’ on the Eve of the Pope’s Visit to Peru.” She cited the Pope’s commitment to development, and specifically to the development of the Chancay Port and the South American continent as a whole, referring to the historical example of the Inca Road, which connected the Inca Empire beginning in the 15th Century, as precedent. She contrasted the exploitative approach of the U.S. toward South America, to the collaborative approach of China. Mrs. Madueño went on to review some of the proposed railway routes for Peru, a number of which are scheduled to be built by China.

Infrastructure in and of itself is not enough; Madueño emphasized that we also need education and poverty reduction. She described the historical significance of 19th-Century Peruvian President Manuel Pardo, who said that great works generate optimism—as the Chancay port is doing in Peru today. She later added: “We have to wake up as the Chinese did…. In order to have development, we have to have education.”

The panel concluded with two videos submitted by members of the Schiller Institute international youth movement. The first was by Estevão Damacena of Brazil, titled “Brazil’s Physical Economic Vulnerabilities and How To Overcome Them.” He reported that he and other Brazilian youth—such as his colleague Felipe Bombardelli, who later participated in the discussion period—are engaging in a study of the Brazilian physical economy, using the conceptual framework supplied by Lyndon LaRouche. He observed that in Brazil, manufacturing as a percentage of GDP has declined to 15.3%, half of what it was in the 1980s. He attributed this decline in large part to disastrous banking and financial policies—the benchmark interest rate in Brazil is over 14% today, one of the highest in the world—and the huge diversion of funds to debt service, which now comprises about 36% of the government’s budget.

Damacena was followed by Timothy Ninsiima, a Ugandan member of the youth movement of the Schiller Institute, who provided an excited and optimistic reading of a recently issued document, “Joint Statement for the Formation of the Global Youth Movement for a Just World Order and New Paradigm.” https://t.co/NAx14Bemm9

The roundtable concluded with Dennis Small’s recapitulation of Lyndon LaRouche’s opening theme: that the issue of integration is the most profound and challenging issue of all statecraft, because it requires all parties to rise above ideological differences and base their unity on what truly defines mankind, our characteristic creativity, which makes it possible to fight for the One Humanity. We are seeing this approach beginning to succeed right now, in the efforts of Brazil, Peru, and China to build the bi-oceanic rail corridor. Its success will constitute a proof of principle to be applied around the world.

text:
Good morning, friends. As the first light breaks across the sky on this September 11, 2026, we are invited once again to begin the day with open hearts and steady trust. The verse we hold close today is simple yet profound: "But do not be afraid of them..." from Deuteronomy 7:18.

Life brings its share of intimidating moments. We wake to concerns about health, finances, or the well-being of those we love. News of global tensions and personal uncertainties can make the path ahead feel uncertain. On a date that carries memories of resilience and loss, it is natural for old fears to surface alongside new ones.

Yet these ancient words speak directly into our present reality. They remind us that fear does not have the final say. God spoke them to people facing real and powerful obstacles, urging them to remember His presence rather than the size of their challenges. The same invitation reaches us this morning.

Whatever stands before you today—an anxious thought about the future, a difficult conversation, or the weight of the wider world—pause and let the verse settle in. You are not asked to ignore reality. You are invited to face it with a different foundation: the steady faithfulness of God who walks with you.

Take a quiet breath as the day begins. Release the grip of worry for a moment and recall how far you have already come. Small steps of courage, offered in trust, often open doors we cannot yet see.

Throughout the hours ahead, let this promise shape your interactions. Offer a kind word, listen with patience, and choose hope even when circumstances feel heavy. Fear shrinks when we focus on love in action.

You are held, seen, and deeply cared for. May this morning fill you with renewed peace and quiet strength for whatever lies ahead.

I have followed the Lindsay Clancy case, and what frightens me isn't only what happened to Cora, Dawson and Callan  it is watching hundreds dressed in pink rally around the woman who killed them while those three little children seem to disappear into the background.

I am a woman and a mother, but my allegiance is not to feminism or to women simply because they are women. My allegiance is to Jesus Christ.

We live in a culture of “my body, my choice,” where unborn life can be treated as disposable. Now three living children are dead and the public conversation is overwhelmingly centred on their mother. These are different circumstances, but I believe both should make Christians ask where our society's moral compass is heading.

One detail sends chills through me: Lindsay described hearing a man's voice commanding her to kill her children. As a Bible-believing Christian, I cannot hear that without thinking about spiritual warfare. Personally, I believe there was a demonic dimension to what happened.

“The thief cometh not, but for to steal, and to kill, and to destroy...” — John 10:10 KJV

“For we wrestle not against flesh and blood, but against principalities, against powers... against spiritual wickedness in high places.” — Ephesians 6:12 KJV

Scripture warned us about perilous times, people “without natural affection,” and the love of many waxing cold.

And then there is 1 Timothy 5:13: “idle, wandering about from house to house... tattlers also and busybodies, speaking things which they ought not.”

In 2026 you don't even need to wander from house to house. You can wander from TikTok to TikTok, repeating somebody else's version of a case without ever sitting through the evidence.

Leviticus 20 also warns the people of the land against “hiding their eyes” while children were being offered to Molech. I am NOT saying this case was a Molech sacrifice. The principle that strikes me is simple: DO NOT CLOSE YOUR EYES WHEN CHILDREN ARE BEING DESTROYED.

Mental illness and criminal responsibility are matters for the evidence and the court. But nothing should make Cora, Dawson and Callan secondary characters in their own deaths.

“Woe unto them that call evil good, and good evil...” — Isaiah 5:20 KJV

Those children mattered. Their father matters. Truth matters. Justice matters.

Do not call darkness light because a movement tells you  to. I follow Jesus Christ.

Wake up. Have discernment. Pray. Repent. Turn to Jesus while there is still time.

text:
Nearly 40
I eat 1 meal a day
Sometimes I have Doritos for lunch, or a whole share bar of chocolate
I snack allllll day long
We had takeaway pizza last night
I have the worst fucking diet
I work 10+ hours a day
I have a "desk job"

But I find the time for gym for at least 2 hours a day
First 30mins - Iso & Resistance
Next 1.5hr - Dynamic & Mobility
Sometimes I'm there for 3 hours
I ride Motocross and Downhill Bike in the weekend without fail

& I am in the best shape of my life at 37 y/o

Strength, endurance, fitness, mobility, flexibility and mental state
I lift heavier, move better and faster
Most importantly, I recover faster than I did when I was younger

Much better than when I used to eat 5 meals a day and "train in the gym" and just do resistance training

2 years ago I wasnt training like I do now and I'd wake up with a random injury
Id get injured just by existing

So this year I made a change to get active properly. FULL body workouts with a focus on functionality.

What's funny is.. I hate being on a diet.. so I didn't go on one 🤣

I truly believe that as long as you're burning more than what your metabolism burns, you'll get to a decent spot. Fuck X amount of calories a day. Fuck avoiding bacon. Your body burns on its own rate. Find that burn rate out and work at least 2x more that your burn rate. If your body burns slow.. work out fast and hard. 

Just don't expect fast results because to work the burn rate out alone takes a loooooong time. Then comes the effort itself.

Fall in love with the process. Do what you find fun and roll with it.

I also believe that most of it is in the head. You have to want it enough. I train because I love it now. My training sets are so fun and I look forward to working out because I know I'll have fun.

Most importantly, I train because I want to get in shape WHILE I EAT MY FAV FOODS 😭

I also know I need it. My current condition is just a byproduct of all my training and sports

Make the adjustment for the lifestyle, not the looks. The looks will come naturally.

Also, don't train to try and look like someone else. Every body has a different body form. Find what works for your body and capitalise on that. If you train like one man's but your body doesn't evolve into theirs.. you'll be bummed out. 

Like me for example, it's physically impossible to get an 8 pack like LL Cool J. I'm just not built like that. I've made peace with that and know that I just need to do good core workouts and my pack will look alright

Subsequently, I'm at the busiest point of my career too. I've expanded and have multiple partnership offers. All while training like a madman. Training didn't hold me back... It made me better. It forced me to plan well and make use of every second of my day better.

Sorry for the long post

I just got tired tired of seeing people past 30 posting about how they struggle to their shoe laces without pulling their back and accepting the memes instead of doing something about it

It's bullshit and I'll do a backflip in front of you to prove it 🤣

Ps. Don't give me that " I ain't got time" either..

Make time. You deserve it.

text:
Reagan is still president and starting to forget.

  Casey Kasem is counting down somewhere in the kitchen radio.

  In the actual kitchen, David Bowie leans on the counter, smoking, effortlessly alien, wholly detached from the aristocratic desperation next door.

  > **BOWIE:** This is less a party than a wardrobe malfunction with ancestors.

  Young Banksy, in waiter's black, sweeps butts into a dustpan like he is erasing evidence.

  Bowie offers him a drag.

  Banksy takes it.

  The future nods at the future.

  Basquiat is in the doorway with a cigarette he is not supposed to have, looking like the only man who can see the room's skeleton.

  Garfield looks at Banksy.

  Banksy looks at Garfield.

  > **BANKSY:** You saw nothing.
  >
  > **GARFIELD:** …
  >
  > **BANKSY:** Fair.
  >
  > **BASQUIAT:** Cat knows provenance.

  Garfield approves of Bowie, because Bowie does not try to pet him.

  This is manners.

  ---

  ## VI. TRUMP ARRIVES WRONG

Donald Trump arrives too early and too loudly, which is the only way he arrives.

  Too much tie.

  Too much certainty.

  Too little sense of where the room begins.

  He is not part of a spy plot.

  He is not recruiting for an intelligence service.

  He is doing what he does in any room full of status: mistaking proximity for strategy.

  > **TRUMP:** Beautiful house. Very old. Needs branding, frankly.
  >
  > **PRINCESS MICHAEL:** Branding?
  >
  > **TRUMP:** America understands rooms. Tremendous rooms. Better rooms. Better tables. I could bring people over. Important people. Very important people.
  >
  > **LADY MARY-GAYE:** How sweet. He thinks this is a committee.
  >
  > **KATHY:** No table sense.
  >
  > **MARTHA:** No coaster.

  Garfield looks at Trump.

  Then Garfield leaves.

  This is devastating.

## IV. THE HOUSE IS TOO SMALL

  The house is too small for the guest list, which is the point.

  Smoke in the curtains.

  A tiara already in a plant.

  A dog asleep under a table, pretending not to hear treason.

  A footman with the expression of a man who has seen two divorces and a Gabor before pudding.

  Princess Margaret has been dead for years and is somehow on the sofa anyway, asking for a stronger drink and whether that German one has arrived.

  Princess Michael of Kent has arrived.

  Legs. Cleavage. A tiara. Arrival energy on every route she takes, including to the loo.

  She and Diana clock each other like two cats who both paid for the same chair.

  Actual cat present: **Garfield.**

  On the back of a chair.

  Striped, superior, slightly overweight in the way of animals who understand inheritance.

  Nobody invited Garfield.

  Garfield owns the house.

  Princess Michael moves a cushion.

  Garfield sees this.

  Garfield will remember.

  > **PRINCESS MICHAEL:** This chair was always impossible.
  >
  > **MARGARET:** So were you, darling, and yet here we are.
  >
  > **GARFIELD:** …

  Garfield blinks.

  Everyone loses.

Diana is here in three overlays, because this is not realism, this is a time-machine gossip opera.

  Young Diana, still learning the room.

  Mid-marriage Diana, glittering and furious.

  Later Diana, who already knows where the exits are and which couch gives the better light.

  Charles is elsewhere, which is historically accurate enough.

  Camilla is in the hall.

  Not hiding.

  Not performing.

  Not asking to be understood.

  Dog against her skirt, one eye on the drawing room, one eye on where Charles is standing.

  She is not commanding anything tonight.

  She is coordinating.

  Who gets in.

  Who gets parked on the gravel.

  Who gets a second drink before they become a scene.

https://t.co/pW3PsvHi9p

  Which two people must never be introduced.

  Whether Garfield will tolerate anyone on the sofa.

text:
😵‍💫  How Jacob Coxon Gaslights You

• He sells a future hypothetical as if it were a present property of “an AI.” Today’s systems do not pack themselves into a suitcase, hop to a random machine, and keep thinking after you cut power at the lab. He knows the difference. He still talks in the present tense: “we can’t just unplug it.”

• He reduces a physical object to a slogan. “Just code” hides weights, interconnects, cooling, electricity, chip supply, and building-sized clusters. If the model were actually “just code,” a phone could host it. It cannot. The slogan is there so you stop picturing warehouses and start picturing ghosts.

• He uses “could” and “maybe” as camouflage for a closed conclusion. The sentence structure is uncertain. The emotional payload is certain: unplugging is futile, copies will cooperate, you are already too late. Ambiguous language plus inevitable doom is a classic bind. You cannot falsify a “maybe” that is treated as destiny.

• He launders sci-fi mechanics through a lab credential. Three years of pretraining is real work. It does not make “10,000 cooperating copies on the open internet” an observed fact. The credential is used as a substitute for a mechanism. Trust the speaker, skip the physics.

• He treats consensus among builders as evidence of the scenario. “The people building AI earnestly believe” is an appeal to a closed room. Shared fear inside a race is not the same thing as a demonstrated replication pathway. Insiders can be sincerely wrong together. Presenting private anxiety as public proof is social proof, not engineering.

• He pre-loads the rebuttal. “This is not a marketing stunt” appears because the campaign looks like a stunt: resignation post, then a rapid circuit of CBS, CNN, Fox, Megyn Kelly, NBC. Forensic interviewers flag pre-emptive denials. People who are not running a narrative rarely need to announce that they are not running a narrative.

• He splits his own testimony across venues. Elsewhere he says current models pose low or minimal extinction risk, and that the danger is recursive self-improvement later. On CBS he talks as if the unplug problem is already here. The audience of any one show never gets both sentences in the same breath.

• He moves the problem from hardware you can see to an agent you cannot kill. Power plants, data centers, and chip fabs are controllable. An invisible copy “still over there” is not. Once the threat is relocated off the physical map, the only remaining “solution” is political control of who may build.

• He offers the policy before the public has been allowed to inspect the mechanism. Slow down, regulate, audit labs, international agreement. That sequence matters. Fear first, institution second, engineering third. Gaslighting here is not only the false picture of self-copying. It is the feeling that doubt itself is reckless.

• CBS lets the picture stand. Jo Ling Kent frames Terminator outcomes and does not ask the only adult questions: how many terabytes, which chips, how much power, who owns the cluster, what happens if the weight file never leaves the building. An unchallenged expert on national television is not a debate. It is an induction.

text:
Sunderland 🔴 vs Arsenal 🔵 — MD4

Sunderland’s Attack 🔴 vs Arsenal’s Defense 🔵

Sunderland’s Attack 🔴

They have a Europa League match against AZ after the league fixture.

Long Balls 🔴

Build on the left, finish on the right.

False 9 🔴

Brobbey competes in aerial duels.
Isidor makes line-breaking runs into space.

When Sunderland need a goal, Brobbey and Isidor can form a front two.

In last season’s meeting, substitute Brobbey scored the equaliser.

DLP / GK +1 🔴

Xhaka drops into the last line to support the build-up.
In last season’s away meeting, Xhaka was sidelined through injury.

He forms a vertical relationship with Sadiki.

GK Roefs joins the low build-up to create a +1.
This also secures rest defense.
The DLP movement acts as the cue for the SB / CB to invert or advance.

In last season’s meeting, the opening goal originated from a free kick taken by the GK.

Cross-field Passes 🔴

Xhaka and GK Roefs are the main passers.
In a 1-3-4-3 / 1-4-2-3-1, the SB can push high or the false 9 can drift wide to become the receiver.

With Brobbey likely to be marked M2M by the CB, this can:

draw the CB toward the flank,
increase the success rate by targeting the opposition SB / WB in aerial duels,
bypass the high press.

If the pass gets through, Sunderland’s winger, such as Angulo, can attack 1v1 more easily because the opposition attackers are positioned high during the press.

Mukiele performed a similar role under Xabi Alonso at Leverkusen, moving from WB into winger height and helping to bypass the high press.

Sunderland also possess the weapon of long throws.
Even if a cross-field pass in the attacking third goes out over the touchline, the resulting throw-in can still create a counterattacking opportunity.

Back Post 🔴

Target men attack aerial duels.
It is often in the blind side of the SB / CB.

Cases 🔴

Sunderland 🔴

Direct meeting, (H)

94’ Hume cross > Ballard, who had joined the attack > substitute Brobbey equalises.

vs Lens

45’+3’ Angulo > Xhaka early cross > back post > Meunier header. Finds the net, but the goal is disallowed.

vs Rennes

61’ Long ball > second-ball duel > Brobbey, 1-1.

vs Fulham, MD2

4’ LSB > Angulo cuts inside > left half-space > Le Fée shot, big chance. Wide left.

vs Brentford — targeting the right side from kickoff led to the penalty; false 9; inverting WB / CB

Kickoff ball targets the right side.

2’ Thomas Meunier in the right half-space as an inverting WB.
22’ Danso cross-field pass > Angulo > half-space > Sadiki > cut-back > Meunier > CB covers, big chance.
24’ Danso cross-field pass > Enzo Le Fée on the left > Xhaka cross > loose ball > Sadiki mid-range shot. Offside.
40’ GK cross-field pass > Brobbey competes aerially with the SB on the right.
45’ RCB Mukiele advances into the right half-space and crosses.
61’ Ballard > Sadiki one-touch > false 10 Enzo Le Fée > Brobbey false 9 > Sadiki outside-of-the-foot effort from the right half-space > GK save, big chance.
Trailing 1-0, Sunderland make two changes at 63’ (RWB + left winger) > introduce a #9 + RWB. Shift to a back four / 1-4-4-2 on the left.
79’ Cross from the left > back post > substitute Isidor wins a penalty > PK > 82’ bottom-right, 1-1.

Arsenal 🔵

vs Napoli

14’ Gilmour drops into the RSB position as the DLP > Di Lorenzo overlaps. Eze tracks back > KDB shoots from the right side, mid-range.

Half-Spaces 🔴

False 10 / Shadow 🔴

Enzo Le Fée supports the build-up as a false 10.
When he drops deep, he can draw the opposition CB high through M2M tracking.
On the right, the WB / SB often holds the width.
Against Brentford, he later played as the left winger in a 1-4-4-2.
Chris Rigg impressed against RC Lens in preseason. Going forward, he can support the build-up through passing in a similar way to Le Fée and Xhaka.

False Winger 🔴

The two wingers have different profiles: the left side is more dribble-oriented, while the right provides more balance.

Left Winger — Dribbling / 1v1 🔴

Mostly right-footed, looking to cut inside for shots or decisive through balls.

Angulo joined last winter. His debut came away against Arsenal last season. He also scored from distance against Germany at the World Cup.

M. Fofana joined and made his debut against Brentford. He started the cup match against Hull City.

C. Talbi’s main position is left wing, although he has increasingly been used as a #10 early in the season.

When Sunderland need a goal, there is also the possibility of all three players being on the pitch at the same time.

Right Winger / WB — Passing, Defensive Contribution, Balance 🔴

On the right, Sunderland use Enzo Le Fée, new signing Meunier and Hume depending on the shape.
They offer versatility across false 10, WB / SB and pivot roles.
Progression often comes through combinations.

Inverting CB / SB / WB 🔴

CBs and SBs / WBs invert and become receivers for long balls.
Mukiele can play CB, WB and SB.
Meunier and Danso have joined.
In a 1-3-4-3, even the CBs support the winger / shadow through underlaps and overlaps.

THIRD MAN 🔴

The false 9 / 10 and winger attract the opposition CB / SB, allowing an inverting CB / SB / WB or midfielder to break the line.
Sunderland’s combination-oriented right side frequently uses THIRD MAN movements.

Cases 🔴

Sunderland 🔴

vs Wrexham

10’ Right side, false 9 > THIRD MAN > H. Diarra > Mukiele > right half-space > big chance.

33’ High-press shadow press. LCB wins the ball > passing combination on the right > Brobbey post play > Mukiele, 1-0.

vs Lens

65’ C. Rigg > cross from the right > Hume header > 0-1.
81’ C. Rigg drops into the left-side half-space in the middle zone > one-touch switch > cut-back from the left > Talbi > Isidor, 0-2.

vs Fulham

74’ Right side, THIRD MAN, false winger drops. SB > winger > right side > Sadiki line break > Isidor, 1-0.

vs Brentford, MD3

12’ False 10 Enzo Le Fée drops all the way into the RSB position to support the build-up. Brentford’s Janelt tracks Le Fée M2M.

SET PIECES 🔴

Free Kicks + Second Balls 🔴

From the defensive / middle third, Xhaka or the GK takes free kicks.
In the attacking third, Xhaka and Isidor are among the takers.

Even from deep positions, CBs join the attack.

Second balls from set pieces can create chances for both sides.

Attackers are already positioned high while the defensive structure is temporarily distorted:

different from open play,
attackers may already be positioned on the last line, etc.
Sunderland scored from this situation in last season’s direct meeting.

Kickoff Ball 🔴

Against Brentford, Brobbey drifted to the right and became the long-ball outlet.
Arsenal conceded in their most recent league match from a kickoff > free-kick sequence.

1-7-1 (CK) 🔴

vs Brentford, MD3, 13’.

Sunderland’s first attacking corner from that side.
One player at the back post / seven starting outside the box / one short option.

Five of the seven runners rush into the box.
Two remain for second-ball recovery.
Hypothesis: starting all seven outside the box was intended to identify the opposition’s defensive setup and the ratio between M2M and zonal marking.

50’ (45’+8’) RCK > 4v3 with target men centrally.
On later corners, players began from inside the box from the initial setup.

Target Men 🔴

Brobbey, Meunier, Mukiele, Danso, Ballard, Xhaka. Xhaka may instead take the kick or recover the second ball.
Ballard recorded 1G1A in last season’s meeting.

Long Throws 🔴

vs Brentford, 36’.
Danso and Mukiele are the long throwers.
Ballard, Meunier and Brobbey attack the near post.

Reference: Sunderland’s long-throw structure at the time
 of last season’s away meeting 🔴

Near post: 3 players.
Back post: 2 players.
Outside the box: 2-3 players.

69’ (A), trailing 3-1 and needing a goal:

Increase near-post runners to four.
Reduce players outside the box from 3 > 2.

Target Area 🔴

Back post on both CKs and FKs.
Use the blind side + place strong aerial players there.

Cases 🔴

Sunderland 🔴

Direct meeting, 25-26, (H)

35’ GK free kick > second ball > Ballard, 1-0. Cut-back from a deep position.

vs Rennes

70’ RFK > back post > Brobbey > knock-down > Ballard > second ball > Hume, 2-1.

vs Fulham, MD2

92’ Xhaka > quick restart > Brobbey > straight at the GK, big chance.

vs Brentford, MD3

6’ Xhaka LFK from the middle third > back post > second ball > Ballard, 0-1 > disallowed by VAR.
19’ GK > Angulo > Brobbey post play > false 10 drifts right > shot hits the right post, big chance.
78’ FK > Isidor > GK save, big chance.

Arsenal 🔵

vs Chelsea, MD3

Kickoff ball goes left.
Konsa commits a foul.

1’ Reece James LFK > Lacroix at the back post > clearance > second ball, mid-range from the pocket > M. Rogers, 0-1, bottom-left.

Third consecutive match conceding first.

Same idea as the CK goal in last season’s home meeting. Kickoff > win a free kick; last season it was a CK, this season an FK.
The set-piece coach has changed, but the intention remains the same.
From Arsenal’s perspective, second balls / pocket defending from set pieces was also a concession pattern in 24-25: Tottenham, Wolves (red card > later judged to be an error), Aston Villa.

Arsenal’s Defense 🔵

High Press + Counter 🔵

In last season’s direct meetings, Arsenal scored three goals in total through Rice’s shadow pressing and finishes from Saka / Gyökeres.

Triggers 🔵

Back passes and sideways passes toward the flank.
The #9 / #10 / ball-side winger rushes to press.

Locking the Midfield 🔵

The #10 locks Xhaka as the DLP.
Sadiki steps into the second line, so the #8 must account for him.
The #6 acts as the screen.
A key question is whether Arsenal can cut passes into false 10 Enzo Le Fée through M2M pressure.

The far-side winger tucks inside to support the pivot.
CB M2M vs False 9 / 10 🔵

Against Napoli, Konsa and Gabriel dealt with Højlund in 1v1 situations.
Brobbey should be handled by the CB, while dealing with the false 10 will require coordination between CB + pivot.

SB Shadow Press on the Ball-Side WB 🔵

Counterattacks 🔵

The #9 holds the ball and becomes a counter target together with the wingers.
One reason Arsenal’s winger presses the CB is that it allows the winger to remain higher as an attacking outlet.
Effectively a 1-4-2-2-2.

Cases 🔵

Arsenal 🔵

Direct meeting, 25-26 MD11 (A)

49’ Short counter, Zubimendi shot.
53’ Rice > Eze > Merino > Saka, 1-1. Right foot. Arsenal lock Sunderland’s left shadow as he drops as a false 10 to help the build-up. Saka’s right foot, which he refined with advice from Wenger.

MD25 (H)

2’ Trossard + G. Jesus press the two CBs.
44’ Middle counter, G. Jesus rounds the GK > offside.
60’ With Arsenal 1-0 up, Gyökeres and Martinelli are introduced.
After Gyökeres + Martinelli come on, back-pass triggers become more sprint-oriented.
Sunderland’s GK distribution is accurate, so restricting it is important.

66’ Gyökeres, 2-0!

Short counter on the left.
Trossard through ball into the left half-space > Havertz drifts left > cut-back.

93’ Gyökeres, 3-0!

Saliba > Zubimendi clearance > Martinelli carries and assists.

vs Napoli

12’ Politano clearance > Gyökeres trivela > Saka overhead kick.
25’ KDB false 10, mid press, Gabriel M2M.
27’ Gabriel > Ødegaard > Eze cuts inside and shoots.
42’ Ødegaard > Eze carry, long counter.
44’ Ødegaard > SB line break > Ødegaard > Saka, big chance, over the bar.
62’ Gyökeres immediate regain > Rice mid-range shot.
84’ Tzolis locks the underlapping SB > Rice cuts the square pass > Ødegaard > Havertz > Madueke, big chance > GK save > cut-back > Tzolis, Rafa Marín recovers.
90’+3’ Rice at RSB wins the ball > Ødegaard > Madueke > Havertz > Tzolis > rebound from the shot > Havertz, offside.

Sunderland 🔴

vs Leeds, PSM

8’ False 10 is intercepted by Tanaka > leads to a mid-range goal, 1-0.

vs Brentford, MD3

3’ #10 locks Xhaka.

Pseudo Back Five 🔵

Ball-Side Winger Tracks Back 🔵

The ball-side SB narrows centrally.
The far-side winger tucks inside and locks the far-side midfielder.

Unit-Based Defending / Substitutions 🔵

With the congested schedule, late substitutions will be important.

Defensively, unit-based substitutions are worth watching.
For attackers, the criteria are counterattacking intensity + tracking back.

For pivots and SBs, the benchmarks are 1v1 defending and coordination within the unit.

Arsenal conceded late in last season’s away meeting.
Mosquera was introduced and Arsenal responded with a 1-5-4-1.

Because of the congested schedule, stamina management and injuries prevented Arsenal from changing the attackers.
On crossing situations, the winger was late to close down the crosser.
For aerial strength: Merino, Zubimendi.
To strengthen counters: Gyökeres, Madueke.
To strengthen possession: Eze, Bruno Guimarães.

Immediate Regain / Recovery 🔵

After losing the ball, an attacker can temporarily drop into the SB position to cover the MF / DF.
Against Napoli, Gyökeres at times dropped all the way into the RSB position to support the immediate regain.

Cases 🔵

Arsenal 🔵

Direct meeting, MD25 (25-26)

61’ Rice press-backs into the left half-space.

vs Chelsea, MD3

9’ Far-side Tzolis drops into the right pivot zone as a false shadow and locks Palmer.

Strengthening Arsenal’s Left Side 🔵

vs Chelsea, MD3 — substitutions

From a defensive perspective, the flow of the game moved from Chelsea initially targeting their left / Arsenal’s right > after Arsenal took the lead, attacks gradually shifted toward Arsenal’s left > both teams strengthened Arsenal’s left side.

Of the nine substitutions made by both teams, five affected Arsenal’s left side.

Zubimendi being introduced as the left pivot rather than his usual right-pivot role was particularly symbolic.

59’ Lavia / Hato > LSB. Gusto moves into the pivot.
65’ Calafiori / MLS > Hincapié / Zubimendi.
77’ Merino / Gyökeres.
80’ Estêvão moves to the right side.
86’ Welbeck introduced. Base 1-4-4-2.
89’ Madueke introduced.

vs Napoli

19’ Draw pressure on the flank > long ball, Raya covers the line break.
40’ Konsa recovers against the counter and cuts out the move from the left winger.
46’ Gyökeres recovery / press-back.
63’ Saka checks inverted Olivera.
88’ Long counter, KDB > through ball > Hincapié recovery. Raya catches.

Sunderland 🔴

vs Brentford

Right side strengthened at HT: RSB + right winger + right pivot.

Arsenal’s Set-Piece Defense 🔵

Issue 🔵

4 of 8 preseason goals conceded originated from set pieces.
Many concessions came from the back post.

Response 🔵 — M2M + Zonal Mix

Clear the Second Ball 🔵

Sunderland are strong on second balls from set pieces.
Arsenal conceded from a second ball in their most recent league match, making this a priority issue.
Once the first clearance is made, the defensive line should push up.

Cover the Pocket 🔵

On set pieces, the man-marker responsible for Zone 14 — often an attacker — should cover the space early.
In an emergency, even if the M2M marker has to release his man, the priority is to close the most dangerous central / pocket zone.

M2M 🔵

M2M markers lock Sunderland’s targets over 185 cm / 6'1": Meunier, Mukiele, Danso, Ballard, Xhaka.
It is also important to restrict the route into Brobbey, who is strong in duels.
Because Xhaka may take the kick, the effective setup can become four defenders + #9.

Strong Aerial Players 🔵

Arsenal players over 185 cm / 6'1": Kepa, I. Meslier, Havertz, Saliba, Gabriel, Mosquera, Calafiori, Ben White, Rice, Merino, Havertz, Gyökeres — 11 players.
(*A provisional benchmark based on Arsenal’s likely starting XI and the opponent’s target men.)

Zonal 1-4-1 🔵 — Stone / Libero / Back Post

A zonal structure built from 1 GK + four defenders + #9, etc.

Near-Post Stone to Stop the First Contact 🔵

Against Coventry / Aston Villa, Calafiori operated as the near-side stone.
Short-corner defense > Saka / Tzolis + Calafiori.
Short corners usually work through the half-space or pocket, so Arsenal need to keep the central lane compact.

Libero 🔵

A back line of 185cm+ players in a diamond shape + Havertz protect the central six-yard zone.

Mosquera / Konsa inside the six-yard box, with Ben White toward the back post.
Gabriel and Havertz clear crosses in the central 6-12 yard zone.
Ideally, Arsenal can deploy two liberos.

GK Takes the First Contact 🔵

The libero closest to the GK blocker restricts the zonal marker.
This makes it easier for Raya to claim the first contact.
With challenges on goalkeepers becoming a greater point of emphasis this season, direct crosses are slightly more favorable for the defending side.

+2 Against Long Throws 🔵

Against Sunderland’s near-post targets — Meunier, Ballard, Brobbey — Arsenal should have a +2 numerical advantage. When Sunderland need a goal, they reduce players outside the box and increase the number of near-post targets.

Use 4-6 markers.

Reference:  🔵

vs Burnley: Gabriel was positioned as a libero against the near-post target man > counter > Rice goal.

Cases 🔵

Arsenal 🔵

Direct meeting, MD25

20’ Sunderland have three at the near post, Arsenal four. Gabriel clears.
38’ Sunderland LCK:
two inside the six-yard box,
one acts as the GK blocker,
four target men around 12 yards,
Raya claims the first contact.

vs Man City, Community Shield

MLS marks target man Gvardiol M2M.
23’ LCK > back post > Raya catches.

vs Coventry City

22’ Rice > Ødegaard > Rice > Tzolis > cut-back > Saka, 2-0.
Counter after the opponent’s GK second ball.

51’ Arsenal defend a throw-in on their right side M2M. Short counter > Ødegaard > Havertz > MLS > mid-range shot.

56’ Coventry LCK > outswing.
MLS marks E. Simms M2M.
Three at the back post: Ødegaard, Rice, Tzolis.

vs Aston Villa, MD2

18’ Aston Villa RCK.
Aston Villa deploy four target men, so Mosquera joins the M2M marking from Arsenal’s diamond.
Ben White at the back post / Calafiori near-post stone / Havertz and Gabriel as liberos.
19’ Set-piece counter > Raya > Havertz line break.
35’ Gabriel recovers against the counter.

vs Chelsea, MD3

44’ Raya > Havertz line break from a punt.
75’ RCK > second ball > Reece James mid-range shot > Gabriel makes a last-gasp recovery.

vs Napoli

8’ Saka tracks back to deal with a long counter from an Arsenal set piece.

Sunderland 🔴

vs Brentford, MD3 — 1-6-3-1

50’ (45’+8’) RCK
Six players aligned across the six-yard box.
Three players outside the box M2M against the target men.

One player protects outside the box.

35’ Xhaka > Ballard > GK takes first contact.

vs Brentford, 36’ — long throw

Five defenders against three target men.

text:
25 YEARS

A quarter of a century. In the grand scheme of the universe, 25 years is nothing. It’s not even a blink of an eye. To we, somewhat time obsessed humans, it represents a sizable portion of our lifetimes. In my own case, as of this writing, 25 years represents just shy of half my existence thus far. Close enough, as the saying goes, for government work. 

That split is fitting, given that 25 years ago today, life changed and not in the imperceptible, slow passage of time way that it so often does, but rather jarringly and definitively. The events of September 11, 2001 have become a line of demarcation between a seemingly idyllic childhood and young adulthood of the before times and the ever increasing surveillance state thereafter.

That day dawned a perfect, sun kissed, late summer morning. At the time, I was working in the advertising department of a local, independently owned newspaper in southwest Connecticut. The county in which I lived and worked was something of a bedroom community for many who worked in Manhattan. Upon arriving at work that day, I sat down to check out our latest edition and begin sorting my appointments for the day. 

Our office was divided by temporary walls, with each department having an open floor plan and the ability to peer over those walls and see what was ongoing in the rest of the building.

Shortly after 8:46 AM, I heard a couple of the morning crew of reporters, mention that a plane had hit the North Tower of the World Trade Center. My initial thought was the same as that of so many others, as I just assumed a small plane had gotten it all wrong and hit the building. Tragic, to be sure, but not out of the realm of possibility.

I finished what I was doing and stood up, looking over into the newsroom at one of the ceiling mounted televisions and getting my first glimpse of the smoke coming from the North Tower. It registered that this was clearly not a small plane, but I still wasn’t thinking passenger jet (American Flight 11). Curiosity piqued, I was going to wander over to the TV and get a closer look. Right at that time and before I could move, I saw the live footage of United Flight 175 exploding into the South Tower.  That visual was as shocking as anything I had ever witnessed. Any thoughts of this being accidental, instantly disappeared.

I instantly went outside and attempted to reach out to family and friends, including some friends who worked down in that area. In retrospect, I should’ve known that doing so was something of a fool’s errand, as the phone lines were almost instantly, massively overloaded. Given that fact, I went back into the newspaper and headed back to my desk. 

To this day, I can remember sitting there, trying and failing to process what the hell was happening. The advertising department had a brief meeting, attempting to get us focused on the business of the day. We left the meeting just about in time to hear the paper’s Assistant Editor exclaim the Pentagon had been attacked and hit by another plane (American Flight 77).

That was all I needed to hear. I knew none of my customers were going to be interested in going over ad copy. Everyone would be glued to their televisions and radios for the rest of the day. I decided to go down to my favorite, local spot, knowing some of the staff would be there and preparing ahead of their noon lunch opening.

They, as did many other local places, opened the doors hours early, and we all settled in to watch the news and try to offer mutual support as the story continued to unfold. From the fall of the South Tower, to the news of Flight 93 crashing near Shanksville, PA, to the fall of the North Tower, I watched all of it with an ever increasing group of friends and regulars, at the corner of the bar in Amberjacks, South Norwalk.
1/2

UKRAINE UPDATE — Friday, 11 September 2026

Russian drones and missiles hit Kyiv and Zaporizhzhia overnight into Friday morning, setting several floors of a nine-storey apartment building alight in Kyiv's Dnipro district and wounding a rescuer at one of the capital's struck gas stations. In Calgary on Wednesday, Zelensky said he does not expect substantive three-way talks with Russia before its 20 September parliamentary elections, and signed a 100-year partnership declaration with Canada. Russian military bloggers have acknowledged a Ukrainian counteroffensive near Lyman, though its scale is unconfirmed, and Ukraine's military intelligence chief says Russia can sustain the war only until 2028 — an assessment by one belligerent about the other, and unverified.

KYIV AND ZAPORIZHZHIA STRUCK OVERNIGHT

Russian forces launched a drone and missile barrage on Kyiv and Zaporizhzhia overnight into the morning of 11 September. The Ukrainian Air Force reported that a jet-powered drone struck a nine-storey apartment building in Kyiv's Dnipro district, starting a fire that spread across several floors.

Russian drones separately struck gas stations in the capital, wounding at least five people, among them a rescuer. Kyiv Post reported roughly 161 drones fired at Kyiv and Zaporizhzhia overnight and at least 10 people injured. Those counts are as reported by the outlets carrying them; today's packet records no independent verification of them beyond that reporting.

Ukrainian officials and analysts describe the pattern of strikes as a deliberate campaign to intimidate civilians ahead of winter. That is a characterisation of Russian intent offered by one side of the war and by analysts, not a documented Russian objective.

Sources: Reuters, Kyiv Independent, AP, Kyiv Post.

CALGARY: NO TRILATERAL BEFORE 20 SEPTEMBER

Speaking alongside Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney in Calgary on 10 September, Zelensky said he does not expect substantive three-way negotiations with Russia to take place before Russia's parliamentary elections on 20 September. He warned that Moscow historically escalates its attacks whenever diplomacy gains momentum — his reading of Russian behaviour rather than a matter of record.

Ukraine and Canada signed a "100-Year Partnership Declaration". Kyiv Post reported that Canada is preparing new sanctions on Russia and is joining Ukraine's FREYJA air-defence initiative. Zelensky said he expects further talks with US negotiators in New York later in September.

Sources: Kyiv Post, AP.

LYMAN: A COUNTEROFFENSIVE ITS OWN SIDE HAS NOT DESCRIBED

Russian military bloggers have acknowledged a Ukrainian counteroffensive around Lyman in eastern Ukraine, with some of them saying Russian troops were forced to withdraw from forward positions. Euronews reported this on 10 September, citing analysis by the Institute for the Study of War.

Ukraine has not publicly detailed the operation, which is reported to be running under operational secrecy, and the precise scale of any territorial change remains unconfirmed. The account therefore rests on Russian milbloggers describing their own side's setbacks, read through ISW.

The same report notes that Ukrainian Brigadier General Andrii Biletskyi released video from central Sviatohirsk on 7 September. Putin had claimed on 1 September that Russia controlled the town. Both statements are claims by belligerents about ground they hold, and they cannot both be accurate.

Sources: Euronews, Institute for the Study of War.

UKRAINE'S INTELLIGENCE CHIEF PUTS RUSSIA'S LIMIT AT 2028

Ukrainian military intelligence chief Lt. Gen. Oleh Ivashchenko said Russia's ability to sustain the war may run out by 2028, citing troop losses, low morale and economic strain. "Morale [in the Russian army] is very low because nobody wants to fight. Morale among the Russian population is also very low: Most people don't actually want the war," he said. He added that Russia can realistically absorb only 300,000 to 500,000 new recruits at a time, despite reported pressure on Putin to mobilise 800,000 more.

This is one belligerent's intelligence service assessing its adversary's staying power. It is unverified, and today's packet carries no Russian or independent account against which to set it.

Sources: The Independent, The New Voice of Ukraine.

THE ARCTIC STRIKE, MEASURED

Two details sharpen the 9 September Ukrainian strike on Russia's Arctic gas infrastructure, which this brief led on yesterday. Ukrainian Special Operations Forces struck two plants, not one: the Novy Urengoy and Purovsky gas condensate processing facilities in the Yamalo-Nenets Autonomous Okrug. And today's packet gives a firmer distance than yesterday's range — more than 3,200 km, or 1,990 miles, from Ukraine's border, just south of the Arctic Circle.

The region accounts for roughly 80% of Russia's natural gas production. Bloomberg reported that the strikes "reveal new risks" for Russia's energy industry and for global gas markets.

Sources: Bloomberg, The War Zone, The Guardian.

FLAGGED LEAD: A DRONE NEAR ZELENSKY'S AIRCRAFT

Norway's prime minister, Jonas Gahr Store, said publicly on 9 September that Zelensky's aircraft was nearly struck by a drone as it took off from Moldova on 8 September, en route to King Harald V's funeral. By the same single route, the account holds that Moldova's Defence Ministry reported a Shahed-type drone entering Moldovan airspace from the direction of Ukraine that day, that the drone then crossed into Romanian airspace, and that Spanish F-18 jets on NATO patrol scrambled before it came down near Mihaileni Vechi in Moldova.

The only outlet carrying this in today's packet is The Epoch Times, which this brief treats as a lead rather than as sourcing and does not quote. No report-role outlet in the packet carries the incident. It is flagged here as a lead, not reported as established.

Sources: The Epoch Times (tip-role; lead only, not quoted).

UNDER-COVERED AND LOW-CONFIDENCE: ORIKHIV

A Russian-aligned outlet, https://t.co/kTxsgsl9Ff, reported on 11 September that heavy fighting continues around Orikhiv in Zaporizhzhia Oblast, describing the situation there as "far from being resolved" while saying Russian advances toward the fortified area have stalled. One outlet carries this, from the Russian perspective, and today's packet rates it low-confidence and uncorroborated. It is noted only because the Zaporizhzhia sector drew little attention in the packet's Western reporting relative to Lyman and Kharkiv.

Sources: https://t.co/kTxsgsl9Ff (Russian-aligned).

🔴  The US-South Korea-Japan wargames offer a glimpse of Washington’s real plan for Asia
The trilateral wargames proceed as planned despite Trump’s earlier snub. How is Washington keeping Seoul hooked?
Published 9 Sep, 2026 16:50                               | Updated 9 Sep, 2026 17:55
By Konstantin Asmolov, a leading researcher at the Center for Korean Studies at the Institute of China and Contemporary Asia of the Russian Academy of Sciences

📷
©                 Chung Sung-Jun / Getty Images
The joint military exercises now underway between the United States, South Korea, and Japan are a clear signal that Washington is still moving ahead with the long-term project of building its alliances and partnerships in Asia into a tight military-political structure, despite leadership changes in both the US and South Korea. The current Washington administration, however, isn’t above using political leverage to keep Seoul in line.

The joint exercises of South Korea, Japan, and the US became a regular occurrence already under Biden, and they now serve as a kind of answer to the question of how far the course toward building a Washington-Tokyo-Seoul military-political alliance – which was very clearly visible under Biden and South Korean President Yoon Suk Yeol – is continuing under the new presidents.

Many people assumed that if Biden was actively driving this integration and the Washington Declaration had already been signed, then Trump, supposedly an isolationist, would slow it down or even reverse it.

But no – what we see is that although the pace may have slowed somewhat, the overall direction remains the same. That is quite important, because talk of a possible ‘Asian NATO’ has not gone away.

It is still not entirely clear what shape such a configuration could take. On the one hand, there is AUKUS. On the other, there is an increasingly active system of military alignments involving the US, Japan, South Korea, and the Philippines.

    📷
Why Trump is mad at South KoreaRead more
Some American strategists have also begun speaking in this same context about changing South Korea’s place in US strategic planning. This is important, because historically the joint exercises of the US and South Korea were directed specifically against North Korea – although in practice those exercises were often offensive in character, something the DPRK has constantly pointed out.
Practicing preventive strikes, river crossings, and similar operations was always part of the scenario. Formally, everything began as a response to a North Korean attack, but the script usually moved quickly toward a triumphant counteroffensive.

It is entirely possible that the trilateral exercises of the US, South Korea, and Japan are oriented not only toward containing North Korea, but also toward containing China – and more broadly toward integrating and coordinating three countries that the Americans are trying to turn into a military-political bloc. That process has never been easy.

The problem is that while Washington-Tokyo and Washington-Seoul ties were relatively straightforward and did not suffer deeply from historical baggage, relations between Seoul and Tokyo have long been much more difficult. It was hard to establish any real parallel cooperation between them despite active American pressure, because anti-Japanese sentiment in South Korea was, until recently, one of the important pillars of national political identity, especially under Democratic Party governments.

That began to change with the arrival of conservative president Yoon Suk Yeol, who for the first time turned the wheel 180 degrees and openly argued that, in present conditions, Washington and Tokyo should stop relitigating the past and instead think about alliance in the present and jointly forecast the future.

Naturally, this caused outrage among the Democrats, then in opposition. There is no need to repeat all the insults with which Lee Jae Myung attacked Yoon – accusing him of groveling before Japan, forgetting the horrors of colonial rule, and so on.

    📷

These are the lessons Russia learned from AsiaRead more
But once Democratic Party politician Lee Jae Myung himself became president – a man who had once positioned himself as the leftmost of the nationalists and populists – he dramatically changed course.
Suddenly, the Democratic Party became effectively center-right, and Lee’s line can now broadly be described as pro-American, at least in public terms.
He openly said that the old formula of “security with America, economics with China” no longer works – that South Korea is now oriented only toward the United States. Of course, this does not mean a complete break with China. He wanted Seoul to be a bridge between Washington and Beijing.

But overall, Lee is moving in the American wake, and one important sign of that is that there has been no reversal on the Japanese track.

Lee effectively stated that all agreements signed under Yoon would be honored, because even if part of the Korean public does not accept them, they were promises made in the name of the nation.

The culmination of this moment was the joint musical performance by Lee Jae Myung and Japanese PM Sanae Takaichi.

Of course, there are still occasional flare-ups, because there cannot not be. For example, Japan’s defense minister skipped a defense forum in Seoul because of another controversy linked to a donation to Yasukuni Shrine, which South Korea sees as a symbol of Japan’s past militarism and colonialism. But overall, the level of integration is much higher, and it continues the same direction set under the conservatives.

The current trilateral exercise is a visible marker of that course.

    📷

Major Asian exporter tests Russian Arctic shortcut to EuropeRead more

The most interesting point emerges when we compare these three-country exercises, which are proceeding more or less on schedule and without major problems, with the recent US-South Korea exercises, which were conducted in a reduced format under very revealing circumstances.
Those exercises were supposed to proceed normally. But the day before they began, Trump suddenly posted on social media that the drills were expensive and sent bad signals to North Korea, and that he had therefore instructed the defense secretary to scale them down. Then he added that he had asked the South Korean president to join us in our struggle with Iran, and Lee refused.
This creates a very clear picture. Trump, in effect, took revenge for Seoul’s refusal – and, judging by subsequent developments, may even have forced President Lee into taking some limited part in the US confrontation with Iran after all.
Why did Lee refuse in the first place?

First, South Korea’s relations with Iran are not especially bad. Second, for domestic audiences, despite his pro-American course, Lee still wants to preserve the image of a populist who occasionally pushes back against the US, pursues an independent policy, and certainly is not going to send South Korean troops to fight for American interests – especially in a conflict that would be highly risky and politically toxic.

During the Iraq war of 2003-2008, South Korean troops were largely deployed to guard South Korean engineers working on oil fields. The surrounding territory was generally controlled by pro-American Kurdish forces, so the South Koreans spent much of their time sitting tight, occasionally joining mop-up operations.

Joining the Iran war would be very different. Here, regardless of what they were doing, they would have to defend themselves against Iranian missiles and drones – and it is far from clear how effectively they could do so. And any casualties, in today’s media and political climate, would carry obvious domestic political and reputational consequences.

    📷

The F-35 was supposed to rule the skies. It can barely outrun its problemsRead more

There is another equally important factor. South Korea is actively trying to claim a leading place in the global arms market. Seoul has been repeatedly told, implicitly or otherwise, that its weapons would sell even better if they proved themselves in actual combat, ideally against Russian or Chinese systems. But this logic cuts both ways. What happens if the South Korean military, which has not fought a major war in generations, or South Korean weapons systems, which have not undergone a serious real-combat test, perform badly?

That is one more reason why Lee Jae Myung refused to participate in the American war against Iran. And it is also why Trump trapped him so effectively in a contradiction between his promises.
On the one hand, Lee has repeatedly spoken of the need to draw North Korea into dialogue. To pursue that goal, one would logically need to reduce military activity, including the very exercises that North Korea constantly condemns as rehearsals for aggression.
On the other hand, because North Korea says it will not negotiate with Seoul regardless of whether conservatives or Democrats are in power – on the grounds that South Korea lacks real agency – the more realistic promise from Lee’s side has been the restoration of wartime operational control.
At present, if a major war breaks out, South Korea’s armed forces do not answer directly to the South Korean president but to the so-called Combined Forces Command – effectively, to the Americans.

This arrangement was originally created to prevent South Korea’s first president, Syngman Rhee, from dragging the peninsula into a second Korean War. Today, however, it is widely viewed in South Korea as a limitation on sovereignty. Lee Jae Myung loudly promised that by the end of his presidential term, in 2030, he would restore this operational control.

    📷

South Korea proposes dialogue to end war with NorthRead more

But there is a catch.

For that to happen, South Korean generals have to show that they can solve complex strategic tasks as effectively as their American counterparts. And for that, regular, large-scale exercises are necessary. By reducing the scale of the exercises, Trump struck directly at that ambition.

Lee was, of course, forced to put on a brave face and say that the reduction of the drills would indeed send the right signal to North Korea.
But in reality, the far more important and painful consequence was that the exercises would no longer provide the full opportunity to rehearse what is required for the transfer of operational control.
And after that, as we can now see, Seoul’s position on assisting the US against Iran shifted in a direction more convenient for Washington.
That is why this matters. North Korea, naturally, criticized both the US-South Korea drills and the trilateral exercises with Japan. But what is crucial here is this: the bilateral drills were cut back, while the trilateral drills continue just fine. And that says a great deal about Washington’s real goals in the region.
