text:
Nobody warned the lions that the herd would come back for blood. In the golden haze of an African dawn, dust rising like smoke from a battlefield, a pride of lions believed they had already won. They had not. What unfolds in the seconds that follow is one of the rarest, most electrifying confrontations in the entire animal kingdom, a moment so violent and so loaded with raw emotion that even seasoned safari guides who have watched thousands of hunts say their hearts stopped. This is the story of the African Cape buffalo, an animal so underestimated, so quietly powerful, that it has earned a nickname whispered with genuine fear across the bushveld: the Black Death.

Most people picture Africa's dangerous animals as lions, leopards, or crocodiles. Almost nobody thinks of the buffalo first. Yet ask any professional hunter, any ranger, any tracker who has spent a lifetime in the wild which animal they fear most, and an overwhelming number will say the same thing without hesitation. Not the lion. Not the elephant. The buffalo. Because a wounded, cornered, or enraged Cape buffalo does not run. It hunts you back. It circles behind bushes, waits in ambush, and charges with a memory for grudges that borders on unsettling. This is not folklore. It is documented, repeated, and respected by everyone who has ever faced one down.

What you are witnessing here is nature refusing to follow the script we think we know. A pride of lions, working together with the discipline of a small army, has done what lions do best: identify a target, isolate it from the safety of numbers, and bring it down using pure coordinated force. For a few moments, it looks like the ending we have all seen a hundred times in documentaries, the lone buffalo overwhelmed, the pride closing in, the dust rising as claws and teeth do their brutal work. But then something extraordinary happens, something that separates buffalo from almost every other prey species on the continent. The herd does not scatter. The herd does not run. The herd turns around.

This single decision, made collectively and almost instantly by dozens of animals with no leader shouting orders, is one of the most astonishing displays of coordinated defense in the natural world. Cape buffalo, scientifically known as Syncerus caffer, live in herds that can range from a handful of individuals to staggering aggregations of several hundred, sometimes even more than a thousand animals moving together across the savanna like a single dark, breathing organism. Within that herd exists an unspoken code, a survival instinct passed down through countless generations, and it is deceptively simple: when one of us is taken, we come back for them.

This behavior, known among researchers and guides as mobbing, is not just heroic to watch, it is scientifically fascinating. Unlike wildebeest, zebra, or impala, which almost universally sacrifice the individual for the safety of the group and flee the moment a predator strikes, buffalo herds have been recorded doing the opposite in a meaningful percentage of documented lion attacks. They wheel back toward the danger. They lower their heads, weaponized with some of the most formidable horns in the animal kingdom, and they charge directly into the very predators that were seconds away from a successful kill. Lions, apex predators that fear almost nothing, have been documented abandoning fresh kills, sometimes even losing pride members, when a buffalo herd commits to a full counterattack.

Look closely at the anatomy that makes this possible. A mature bull buffalo can weigh well over eight hundred kilograms, sometimes close to a ton, built like a living tank of muscle and bone. Its horns fuse together across the top of the skull into a structure called a boss, a helmet of solid keratin and bone so dense that it can shatter a car windshield and has been known to withstand direct blows that would kill almost any other animal outright. Beneath that boss, the horns sweep outward and curve upward into sharpened points capable of piercing hide, muscle, and bone with a single committed thrust. This is not a passive grazer. This is an animal engineered by millions of years of evolution to survive exactly the kind of ambush you are watching unfold right now.

And yet, for all that raw power, buffalo are not naturally aggressive animals. They spend the overwhelming majority of their lives in a state of calm, communal grazing, moving slowly across grasslands, wallowing in mud to cool their massive bodies and rid themselves of parasites, and maintaining a complex social structure built on cooperation rather than conflict. Dominant bulls establish hierarchy through ritualized displays rather than constant bloodshed. Mothers and calves stay tucked safely within the protective core of the herd, surrounded on all sides by adults who instinctively understand their role as a living wall. It is only when threatened, when one of their own is in mortal danger, that the switch flips, and gentle giants transform into something the lions themselves seem to fear.

Lions know this. It is written into every strategic decision a pride makes before committing to an attack. This is precisely why prides spend so much time studying a herd before striking, watching for the old, the sick, the very young, or an individual that has strayed dangerously far from the protective mass of bodies. A pride will patiently stalk for hours, sometimes days, reading the herd's movement patterns, waiting for the split second of vulnerability. Even then, taking down a healthy adult buffalo typically requires the combined effort of multiple lionesses working in perfect synchronization, one gripping the nose to cut off breathing, others hanging from the flanks and hindquarters to drag the animal down under sheer accumulated weight, while still others block escape routes. It is teamwork at its most brutal and most impressive, honed by evolutionary pressure because buffalo have made solo hunting attempts a costly, sometimes fatal mistake for careless lions.

That is what makes this particular scene so remarkable. In the chaos of dust and roaring and thundering hooves, you are watching the exact moment where the hunters become uncertain of their own victory. The herd's return is not a random panic response, it is closer to an emergent, collective decision, a wave of urgency passing from animal to animal until dozens of buffalo, acting almost as one mind, wheel around and drive straight back toward the pride. Ears pinned, heads low, horns forward, hooves throwing up choking clouds of ochre dust that swallow the entire scene in a haze of gold and amber, lit from behind by the low angle of the rising or setting African sun. It is cinematic without a single camera trick, raw nature producing a spectacle no filmmaker could ever fully choreograph.

For the lions, this counter-charge changes everything in an instant. A single, well-placed strike from a buffalo's horn can cause catastrophic internal injuries, break bones, or kill a lion outright. There are documented cases across the continent of lions dying not during the initial takedown but afterward, gored fatally by herd members returning to defend, or even, in some recorded instances, by the supposedly dying buffalo itself finding one last surge of strength before the herd arrives. Nature does not care about the narrative we expect. It cares only about survival, and in this moment, survival for the herd means risking individual lives for the safety of the group, a form of altruism seen in remarkably few other species on Earth outside of elephants and a handful of primates.

This is also where the myth of the fearless lion, unshaken and unchallenged, quietly falls apart. Lions are ambush predators, evolved to strike with overwhelming initial force and then disengage the moment the risk outweighs the reward. When faced with a genuinely committed, coordinated charge from an enraged herd, even the largest, most experienced males will often abandon a fresh kill entirely rather than risk serious injury, injuries that in the wild frequently prove fatal simply because there is no veterinarian, no antibiotic, no safety net. A broken leg or a punctured lung in the wild is very often a slow death sentence. Lions know this instinctively, and it shapes every single decision they make in these high-stakes moments, weighing calories gained against the very real risk of death.

Zoom out from this single dramatic encounter and you begin to understand the broader ecological role that Cape buffalo play across the African continent. They are considered a keystone species in many ecosystems, meaning their presence and behavior ripple outward to shape the entire landscape around them. Their grazing patterns keep grasslands healthy, preventing overgrowth and encouraging the kind of biodiversity that supports countless other species. Their wallowing behavior creates temporary water pools used by smaller animals. Their sheer numbers and size make them one of the primary prey sources sustaining lion populations across much of sub-Saharan Africa, meaning the fate of the buffalo and the fate of the lion are locked together in an ancient, ongoing balance that has played out for millions of years, long before any human ever witnessed it.

Buffalo herds also display a level of social intelligence that continues to surprise researchers studying them closely. Studies using GPS collars and long-term observation have shown that herds appear to make quasi-democratic decisions about which direction to travel, with individual buffalo essentially voting with their body orientation while resting, and the herd eventually moving in the direction favored by the majority. This might sound almost unbelievable for an animal often dismissed as a slow-witted grazer, but the evidence keeps accumulating that buffalo possess a far more sophisticated social cognition than their reputation suggests. Combine that decision-making capacity with the mobbing defense you are watching here, and a much richer picture emerges of an animal that is calculating, cooperative, and fiercely loyal to its own.

There is also the matter of memory. Anecdotal reports from rangers across South Africa, Zimbabwe, and Tanzania describe wounded buffalo that have survived lion attacks going on to display heightened aggression toward lions specifically for extended periods afterward, as though carrying forward a grudge that shapes future encounters. While this remains an area that is difficult to study with strict scientific rigor, the sheer volume and consistency of these firsthand accounts from experienced observers suggests there may be more emotional and cognitive depth to these animals than we have historically given them credit for. An animal that remembers, that holds onto experience and lets it shape future behavior, is an animal operating on a level far beyond simple instinct.

Watch the dust again. Watch how it billows and swirls, catching the low sunlight in streaks of amber and gold, transforming the entire scene into something that looks almost mythological, ancient gods of the savanna clashing in slow, thunderous motion. This is not staged. This is not exaggerated for effect. This is simply what happens when two of Africa's most formidable forces collide in real time, unscripted, unpredictable, and utterly indifferent to whether anyone is watching. The lions came for an easy meal. The buffalo came back for their family. Somewhere in between those two competing instincts lies one of the most gripping, primal spectacles the natural world has to offer.

It is worth remembering, too, just how ancient this dynamic truly is. Fossil evidence places buffalo-like bovids and big cats in overlapping African habitats for millions of years, meaning this exact standoff, in some form or another, has likely been repeating itself since long before modern humans ever walked upright across these same plains. Every generation of lion learns anew, through trial, injury, and sometimes death, exactly how dangerous a determined buffalo herd can be. Every generation of buffalo calf grows up witnessing, and eventually participating in, the same defensive charges that may one day save its own life or the life of its mother. This is not a single dramatic event. It is a living tradition, written into the behavior of two species locked in an evolutionary conversation that never truly ends.

There is also something deeply humbling in watching an animal so consistently underestimated rise to a moment like this. The buffalo will never have the cultural mythology of the lion, will never star in the same children's films or wear the crown of king of the jungle in popular imagination. It simply grazes, wanders, wallows, and lives its quiet communal existence across the grasslands, until the day it does not, until the day it becomes something else entirely, an unstoppable wall of muscle, horn, and collective fury bearing down on the very predators that dared to test it. That transformation, from placid grazer to something the most feared apex predator on the continent will actively choose to avoid, is one of the great, underappreciated stories of the African wilderness.

To truly understand the weight of what unfolds in these frantic seconds, you have to understand the two societies colliding against each other in the dust. A lion pride is not a random gathering of predators. It is a tightly bonded, matriarchal society, usually built around a core of related lionesses, sisters, mothers, daughters, and cousins who have hunted together their entire lives, joined by a smaller number of resident males whose primary role is defense of territory and cubs rather than daily hunting. Lionesses coordinate with a precision that borders on choreography, assigning themselves roles almost intuitively before a hunt even begins. Some circle wide to flank a target from the side, cutting off escape routes long before the herd even notices danger is near. Others crouch low in the grass, patient as stone, waiting for the signal to explode forward. Communication happens through subtle body language, flattened ears, a lowered head, the faintest flick of a tail, an entire silent vocabulary built over years of shared hunts and shared survival.

Buffalo society, by contrast, runs on an entirely different but equally sophisticated logic. Herds are typically led, in terms of movement, by older, experienced cows who seem to hold institutional memory of water sources, migration routes, and dangerous terrain. Bulls drift between bachelor groups and the main herd depending on the season, competing for breeding rights through impressive but rarely lethal displays of strength, clashing horns, pushing, bellowing low guttural warnings that can carry for surprising distances across open grassland. Calves are born within the relative safety of the herd's center, protected on every side by a living perimeter of adult bodies, and they begin building the herd's collective muscle memory of danger almost from the moment they can stand, watching, learning, absorbing the instinctual code that one day they too will be expected to answer without hesitation.

What you witness in a moment like this is the sudden, violent intersection of both systems, one built for controlled aggression and calculated risk, the other built for collective defense and generational loyalty. Neither society yields easily. Lions do not walk away from potential food without cause, hunger among wild predators is a constant, gnawing pressure, and a failed hunt can mean days without a meal for cubs who cannot yet fend for themselves. Buffalo, in turn, cannot afford to lose members of their herd without consequence either, every individual represents genetic investment, social structure, and, in the case of a cow, potentially a calf whose survival depends entirely on her. Both sides are fighting not just for the moment, but for the future of their bloodlines, and that is precisely what injects this kind of scene with such unbearable tension.

Consider, too, the sensory chaos unfolding for every animal involved. Dust this thick muffles scent trails that lions rely on to track movement, and it disorients buffalo relying on herd cohesion through sound and smell as much as sight. The air fills with low bellows, sharp warning grunts, the coughing roars of lions mid-struggle, and the thunderous rhythm of dozens of hooves striking dry earth at once. Every sense is overwhelmed simultaneously, which is exactly why moments like this so often produce outcomes nobody could have fully predicted.

There is a reason wildlife guides across the Kruger, the Serengeti, the Okavango, and beyond speak about buffalo encounters with a caution reserved for very few other animals. Elephants can be unpredictable when startled, but rarely hunt down a perceived threat with intent. Hippos are dangerous but tend toward avoidance rather than sustained pursuit. Buffalo occupy a different category entirely, capable of calculated, coordinated retaliation, willing to abandon the safety of numbers to punish a predator that dared to test the herd. This is precisely why old bulls pushed out of the main herd, sometimes called dagga boys, are considered among the most dangerous encounters possible in the African bush, carrying decades of wariness and grievance with nothing left to lose.

The scene you are watching also offers a rare window into something ecologists call the landscape of fear, an invisible map that shapes how prey species move, graze, and behave based purely on the perceived risk of predation in any given area. Buffalo herds that have experienced repeated lion pressure in a particular stretch of territory will often alter their grazing patterns entirely, avoiding dense bush where ambushes are easier, favoring open ground where they can see danger approaching from a distance and mount an organized response in time. Lions, in turn, adapt their own strategies constantly, probing for weaknesses, testing herd cohesion, learning through repeated interaction exactly how far they can push before the cost becomes too high. This is evolution playing out in real time, not across millennia, but within single seasons, single years, single encounters exactly like this one.

It is tempting, watching footage like this, to assign simple labels, hero and villain, victim and aggressor, but nature resists that kind of framing at every turn. The lions are not cruel, they are hungry, driven by an evolutionary imperative as old as the species itself, and a successful hunt here could mean the difference between survival and starvation for cubs waiting hidden in the long grass, cubs who cannot hunt for themselves and depend entirely on their mothers succeeding. The buffalo are not righteous avengers either, they are simply answering an ancient call written into their genetic code across countless generations of ancestors who survived precisely because they learned that turning back sometimes saves more lives than running away. Both species are doing exactly what millions of years of evolutionary pressure built them to do, and there is a strange, humbling beauty in watching that raw, unfiltered truth play out with absolutely no human interference.

Scientists who study predator-prey dynamics across Africa have long noted that buffalo represent one of the clearest examples of what is sometimes called effective mobbing behavior in large mammals, a strategy also observed, though in very different forms, in some primate troops and elephant family groups. The core principle remains consistent across species, individual risk accepted collectively in order to protect the group as a whole, a kind of biological insurance policy against predation that only works because enough individuals commit to the response simultaneously. A single buffalo charging alone accomplishes very little against a coordinated pride. Dozens charging together, however, create a wall of horn and muscle that even the most confident lion will think twice about testing, and that collective courage, replicated across thousands of similar encounters over millions of years, is precisely why the species has not just survived alongside Africa's apex predators but has actively shaped how those predators are forced to hunt.

This dynamic extends far beyond the immediate drama unfolding in the dust. It shapes population numbers, territorial boundaries, and the very evolutionary pressures pushing lions toward larger pride sizes and more sophisticated cooperative hunting strategies where buffalo are the dominant prey species. Where herds are smaller or fragmented by habitat loss, lion hunting success on buffalo tends to rise, while large, cohesive herds often push prides toward more vulnerable prey instead, a subtle ripple effect conservationists track when assessing an ecosystem's health.

There is also a deeply practical reason buffalo have earned such enduring respect throughout African wildlife culture, one that goes beyond mere statistics and observed behavior. Local communities living alongside these animals for generations have developed detailed oral traditions and practical survival knowledge specifically around buffalo behavior, teaching children from a young age to recognize warning signs, to understand herd movement patterns, and above all to never underestimate an animal that appears calm one moment and lethal the next. This inherited wisdom, passed down long before modern wildlife biology ever formalized these observations into scientific literature, speaks to just how consistently, across countless generations and countless individual encounters, the buffalo has proven itself worthy of genuine caution and genuine respect.

As the dust begins to settle in scenes like this one, and the outcome hangs in that impossibly tense balance between predator and prey, it becomes almost impossible not to feel something profound stirring beneath the surface of pure adrenaline. This isn't entertainment. This is survival, raw and immediate, playing out exactly as it has for millions of years across these golden grasslands, indifferent to any distant human eye watching from a place of safety. The lions will either walk away with a meal that sustains their pride for days, or they will retreat, hungry, having learned once again the hard lesson that buffalo teach any predator willing to test them. The herd will either lose one of its own to the inevitable cycle of predation that keeps ecosystems balanced, or it will reclaim what was nearly taken, hooves and horns proving louder than claws and teeth in this particular round of an ancient, ongoing negotiation between two of Africa's most formidable species.

So the next time someone asks which animal truly rules the African bush, remember what you just watched. Remember the dust, the thunder of hooves, the pride caught in that split second between triumph and retreat, and the herd that refused to simply walk away. Power is not always about who strikes first. Sometimes it is about who comes back. And on this stretch of ochre earth, beneath a sky turned gold by dust and light, the buffalo reminded every lion watching exactly why they call it the Black Death, and why respect for this animal is earned the hard way, one charge at a time.

@RScottClark is perfectly correct 🎯
History & Dorothy L. Sayers remind us How & Why → “The choice is not between creed and no creed, but between creed and chaos.” 
→ 
On the absolute necessity of dogma:
“If we do not know what is right, we shall do what is wrong; if we do not know what is true, we shall believe what is false; if we do not know what is good, we shall choose what is evil. The choice is not between creed and no creed, but between creed and chaos.”

“If we really want a Christian society, we must teach Christianity, and that is absolutely impossible to teach without teaching Christian dogma.”

On why the churches are discredited:
“And however unpopular I may make myself I shall and will affirm that the reason why the churches are discredited today is not that they are too bigoted about theology, but that they have run away from theology.”

On why watered-down teaching fails:
“We are constantly assured that the churches are empty because preachers insist too much upon doctrine—‘dull dogma,’ as people call it. The fact is the precise opposite. It is the neglect of dogma that makes for dullness.”

Close cousin of same complaint but different wording:
“We are constantly assured that the churches are empty because they’re full of machinery and dogma… The precise opposite is the truth. The Church of England washed out its machinery and its dogma and it has left its churches empty.”

On the intellectual demand of faith:
“It is a grave mistake to think that the Christian faith is an emotional or sentimental affair. It is an intellectual challenge, demanding the strenuous application of the mind to the deepest problems of existence.”

“It is worse than useless for Christians to talk about the importance of Christian morality, unless they are prepared to take their stand upon the fundamentals of Christian theology. It is a lie to say that dogma does not matter; it matters enormously. It is fatal to let people suppose that Christianity is only a mode of feeling; it is vitally necessary to insist that it is first and foremost a rational explanation of the universe. It is hopeless to offer Christianity as a vaguely idealistic aspiration of a simple and consoling kind; it is, on the contrary, a hard, tough, exacting and complex doctrine, steeped in a drastic and uncompromising realism.”

On how theology defines reality:
“Christianity is a religion for adults, not for children… It is a complete and satisfying philosophy of life, which fits the facts as we know them.”

“But if Christian dogma is irrelevant to life, to what, in Heaven’s name, is it relevant?—since religious dogma is in fact nothing but a statement of doctrines concerning the nature of life and the universe. If Christian ministers really believe it is an intellectual game for theologians and has no bearing upon human life, it is no wonder that their congregations are ignorant, bored, and bewildered.”

On why doctrine is inherently practical:
“Teachers of religion have been too prone to represent Christian dogma as something arbitrary, or as something which must be believed for the good of the soul, rather than as a statement of fact about the nature of the universe.”
“There is the essential doctrine, of which the whole elaborate structure of Christian faith and morals is only the logical consequence.”

On the drama of core beliefs:
“The Christian faith is the most exciting drama that ever staggered the imagination of man—and the dogma is the drama.”

“It is the dogma that is the drama—not beautiful phrases, nor comforting sentiments, nor vague aspirations to loving-kindness and uplift, nor the promise of something nice after death—but the terrifying assertion that the same God who made the world lived in the world and passed through the grave and gate of death.”

On the connection between work and faith:
“Work is not, primarily, a thing one does to live, but the thing one lives to do. It is, or it should be, the full expression of the worker’s faculties, the thing in which he finds spiritual, mental, and bodily satisfaction, and the medium in which he offers himself to God.”

Close cousin with the same argument applied to a trade:
“The Church’s approach to an intelligent carpenter is usually confined to exhorting him not to be drunk and disorderly in his leisure hours, and to come to church on Sundays. What the Church should be telling him is this: that the very first demand that his religion makes upon him is that he should make good tables. … No crooked table legs or ill-fitting drawers ever came out of the carpenter’s shop at Nazareth.”

“It is the business of the Church to recognize that the secular vocation, as such, is sacred. … In nothing has the Church lost Her hold on reality as in Her failure to understand and respect the secular vocation. She has allowed work and religion to become separate departments.”

On the inevitable result of abandoning truth:
“Theologically, this country is at present in a state of utter chaos, established in the name of religious toleration, and rapidly degenerating into the flight from reason and the death of hope.”

& Again & Again:
“If we do not know what is right, we shall do what is wrong; if we do not know what is true, we shall believe what is false; if we do not know what is good, we shall choose what is evil. The choice is not between creed and no creed, but between creed and chaos.”

Dorothy L. Sayers

text:
As a Christian, I don't believe I can support it. I don’t want people to suffer. I also find it hard to believe that ending your own life is ever the good option.

On the practical side: some people are suicidal for a season. With time and help they come through it, or they have days and weeks of wanting to die that later pass.

If, in one of those seasons, the system had offered to help them die instead of helping them live, some of them would be gone — people who later wanted to stay.

I don’t believe suicide is a good answer. A state-backed assisted dying law still risks steering desperate people toward death when they needed care.

text:
I suppose it is fitting, in the light of current events, that the RNLI's profile page on X offers a lie. The RNLI hasn't been saving lives since 1824. It wasn't established until 1854.

For sure there was a precursor organisation, the Royal National Institution for the Preservation of Life from Shipwreck (RNIPLS), which did start in 1824. But that wasn't the RNLI.

In fact, the original RNIPLS was not a success. By 1850 it was effectively in a state of terminal collapse. It had become broke, bureaucratic, and top-heavy. Its fleet was deteriorating, and local communities were actively withdrawing their support because the London-based management had lost touch with the coast (where have we heard this before?).

It took a total institutional reformulation - driven by the fourth Duke of Northumberland in 1851, who launched a national competition to completely redesign the lifeboat from scratch - to strip away the accumulated rot and rebuild the service. 

From that emerged the centralised RNLI in 1854, a new organisation which took on the responsibilities of the RNIPLS and expanded on them.

That doesn't change the fact that the RNLI has been an honourable institution, saving many lives, but there is no need for it to reinvent its history.

text:
Remembering and honoring the lives of people lost twenty five years ago on 9/11 and the unbelievably, extraordinary bravery of rescuers and aid in NYC! ❤️

I also have to remember and honor the unbelievable kindness, generosity, warmth and love in a time of just unknown horror, fear and darkness … of a little place in Canada - Gander, New Foundland.

I was on a flight on Sept 11th 2001, flying from Manchester, England intended for Orlando, Florida. About 5/6 hours into the flight, when the aircraft was kind of over that north eastern part of Canada, the pilot announced there had been an event in NYC. It was not described or expressed to us passengers what precisely had happened, only that all aircraft were being grounded and US airspace was closing. 
We were directed to land at Gander Int Airport. We landed sometime around 10am ish, by the time we were on the ground; the third of what would ultimately be about 38 wide bodied airplanes to land. Of a population of about 10k people, the planes landed almost doubled the amount of people in Gander. 7000 people across those aircraft stranded.
With being the third aircraft to land, somehow our plane was able (and was the last of the supply) to be refueled in anticipation we would be turning immediately back around across the Atlantic. 
That would not be the case. Not for almost 40 hours (much sooner for my flight than many who became the “plane people” of Gander and were stranded for many days). All air space internationally was closed. After about 12/13 hours on the plane on the tarmac, Canada granted refugee status immigration so we could disembark the aircraft. We were given cards around our neck, and transported on school buses to a nearby Salvation Army sponsored summer camp (I believe it was called Twin Ponds if I remember right). We spent almost two days there among the most generous, kind, warm and supporting New Foundlanders, who let us go to their home to shower, make phone calls to loved ones. We were beyond safe and in no way facing anything like what was happening in NYC. Still the NF’ers took all 7,000 of these peole as their own. Offered beds when space in the town ran out. Fed every mouth. Brought toys for children. A community wrapped its arms around complete strangers as their own … an act and a message I will never forget or carey deeply in me. 

The story of Gander’s sheer humanity continues to live on in books, movies and also a broadway musical! Thank you Gander!!

My heart to everyone today and 25 years later. In the darkest and most awful of time, there was resilience, bravery and courage … and most importantly LOVE! Today we remember! ❤️❤️❤️

text:
The largest known great white shark in the Atlantic was just spotted near North Carolina — and it’s over 1,700 pounds.

A satellite tag attached to 'Contender,' a nearly 14-foot-long mature male great white shark, transmitted a brief signal near North Carolina’s Outer Banks this week, confirming he is migrating up the U.S. East Coast.

First tagged off the Florida-Georgia coast in January 2025 by the marine research organization OCEARCH, Contender has since logged more than 7,000 miles.

Because satellite tags only transmit when a shark's dorsal fin breaks the surface, Contender's brief 'ping' offers crucial, rare data on the movements of the largest male great white ever tagged in the western North Atlantic.

These long-distance migrations are seasonal patterns that have occurred for thousands of years, with sharks heading north toward cooler, prey-rich waters around Cape Cod and Atlantic Canada for the summer.

While shark sightings near popular beaches often spark public anxiety, marine scientists emphasize that attacks remain exceptionally rare. Instead, tracking Contender's multi-year journey helps researchers understand how these apex predators navigate the ocean, providing vital insights necessary to protect marine ecosystems and maintain ocean balance.

Source: WVEC. (2026). Largest tagged male great white shark in Atlantic spotted near Outer Banks.

-Ancient History & Mysteries World

A dark-universe telescope rides Falcon Heavy’s 27 Merlin engines skyward — opening a five-year hunt across billions of galaxies.

NASA’s Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope lifted off at 3:26 p.m. GST on 30 August 2026 aboard a SpaceX Falcon Heavy from Launch Complex 39A at Kennedy Space Center in Florida. The rocket’s 27 Merlin engines generate more than five million pounds of thrust as they push rapidly through the atmosphere. The first stage is a centre core plus two side boosters; the second stage, mounted atop the centre core, carries the Roman observatory.

Roman’s wide field of view and rapid survey capabilities will help scientists map billions of galaxies, uncover planets beyond our solar system, study black holes, and provide vast volumes of daily data for astronomers to analyse. The five-year flagship mission samples such a large volume of the cosmos that it offers practically limitless opportunities for additional science — from dark matter and dark energy to exoplanets and galaxies at the edge of the observable universe.

text:
Russia’s Catastrophic Syrian Defeat

By kicking Putin out of Syria, Sharaa deprives Russia of a 70-year investment in its most important forward base, and cripples its ability to project power across the Mediterranean and North Africa.

Last month, wheat and cement began arriving at a berth in Tartus that had served Russia’s military for decades. In sight of the pier, Russian personnel were packing up equipment to move out of their building.

Ahmed al-Sharaa is finishing what he started. Syria has been a stalwart Soviet and later Russian client since the mid-1950s. In more recent years, the country cozied up to Iran as well, joining the mullahs’ “Ring of Fire.” 

The sudden December 2024 defeat of longtime dictator Bashar al-Assad and Sharaa’s victory in the Syrian Civil War ended all that, and broke Russian and Iranian power over Syria. Even worse for Putin, Sharaa announced Russia’s eviction from its most important overseas bases.

Russia wasn’t wrong (other than morally) to bet on Assad: they’d been betting on both him and his father since the elder Assad helped lead the 1963 coup and then seized power for himself in 1970. The Baathists (same party as Saddam Hussein’s) were gleeful participants in the spread of Soviet power and terror proxies, to a degree that even their pro-Soviet predecessors had not been.

But Russia’s power isn’t what it used to be, and wasn’t enough to prevent Assad’s collapse and subsequent flight into exile in Moscow. Seventy years of Russian investment have come to this: bargaining with the men Moscow bombed for permission to keep a foothold in a country it once dominated.

The August 9 agreement finalizes the return of facilities at Hmeimim Airport and the port of Tartus. The military installations are to become joint training centers, with a three-month transition. To allow Putin to save face, a small number of Russian personnel will be allowed to remain. But gone forever are the forward bases from which first the Communists and then Putin supported operations across the Eastern Mediterranean, North Africa, and the Sahel.

The Kremlin described the August agreement as an improvement in bilateral cooperation. Which was a bit like Iran claiming it had sunk the USS Abraham Lincoln three times.

A Very Long Way From Home

Russia is by far the largest country on Earth, and by some measures one of its most powerful. It certainly was during the Cold War.

But good luck getting a Russian warship into the Mediterranean. From the Black Sea, it must pass through the Bosporus and Dardanelles, both controlled by NATO ally Turkey. From the Baltic, it must sail past Finland, Sweden, Norway, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, Poland, Germany, and Denmark — NATO countries all — just to enter a North Sea also surrounded by NATO allies.

Murmansk is better, but it’s north of the Arctic Circle. Getting from there to Syria means sailing around Norway, past Britain and Iceland (or Greenland), through the British and U.S. controlled Strait of Gibraltar, and then past more NATO allies all the way across the Mediterranean. Few Russian ships have the range for that trip without a port call. 

Then once there, the Russians have to keep it supplied somehow, thousands of miles from home. Putin can’t intimidate anyone off the Syrian coast with a warship that has to go back to the Arctic for repairs.

Tartus (and Latakia before it) spared the Russians that trip, and in the process, greatly extended their reach. Syria provided naval and air bases sufficient to refuel and replenish their ships, make repairs, and threaten the Suez Canal and NATO’s southern flank. Without it, Russia’s ability to project power beyond its own “near abroad” dries up.

In Pat Frank’s legendary Alas, Babylon, published in 1959, the incident that sets off the nuclear war takes place off a Soviet submarine base at Latakia. The Russians have depended on these forward bases for a very, very long time.

Putin added Hmeimim when he intervened in the civil war in 2015, giving Russia a new forward air base to complement and protect his naval foothold. In 2017, he renewed Russia’s agreement for Tartus with a 49-year lease. Moscow expected to stay forever, long after all its other Soviet-era bases, from Lourdes, Cuba to Cam Ranh Bay, had been lost. And it built its strategy accordingly.

The African Empire Syria Enabled

Few in the United States have paid as close attention to the African situation as have the French.

For decades, France stealthily maintained its African empire by other means, through economic rights, a Paris-dominated common currency (the CFA Franc), basing privileges, a legal right to militarily intervene, and countless other ways. France didn’t leave Africa. It pretended to leave Africa. Colonies became de facto protectorates, but nothing real changed.

By the mid-2020s, though, the Russians were rolling up the old French Empire in West and Central Africa, mostly through coups spearheaded and then reinforced by its officially private Wagner Group. Syria made that possible.

Most Americans know Wagner as the mercenary army that fought in Ukraine and then briefly turned on Putin in 2023. But its African business was an important part of the operation, and it survived the mutiny. Russia’s Defense Ministry has since taken over much of that business through its Africa Corps.

The Wagner Group offered rulers a fairly straightforward deal: we’ll help keep you in power, and you’ll make it worth our while. Gold, uranium, lithium, diamonds, oil, and many other minerals supplied much of the payment. The Russians made money, expanded influence, and pushed out the French, all on the cheap compared to Ukraine.

But even mercenaries need ammunition. And replacements. And spare parts. And a way to get home. Hmeimim gave Russia a base from which to move men and cargo into Africa, with Libya serving as a further stop on the way south. Tartus supported the naval side. Assad’s dependence on Moscow allowed the Russians to operate this far-off system without much concern for what the Syrians thought of it.

This arrangement also let Moscow attack European interests without attacking Europe directly, a pretty useful tactic while those same Europeans opposed them in Ukraine. Paris lost access and influence in countries it had dominated for generations. The people who like to describe Russia as a victim of Western imperialism might want to have a look at what their favorite victim was doing in Africa (ditto for China).

You may have wondered why the Russians got involved in the Syrian civil war in the first place. That’s an awful lot of why. It’s also why all that Russian blood and treasure is so ruefully lost now.

Without Syria, the Russians are scrambling to salvage what they can. They’ve expanded facilities at Libyan air bases, and flight tracking through July shows that they’ve been able to continue supplying their African deployments…barely.

But Libya doesn’t give Putin another Assad. No facility in Libya can replace Tartus, nor can Russia’s strained budget easily build a new one, especially in a country at least as unstable as Syria became. A Libyan airfield can help airlift cargo into the Sahel. It can’t repair a warship, much less support a fleet (if Russia still had one worthy of the name).

Moscow spent decades building the Syrian position because it needed the whole enchilada, including a government whose survival depended on Moscow. That’s gone. Putin will have to pay for losing Syria long after the last handover. Up to a point, he can pay with money, with concessions, and by accepting a smaller role in places where he once expected to dominate. But this is no new beginning: it’s the death rattle.

The Long Goodbye

Sharaa could overthrow Assad faster than he could get rid of Moscow. The Russians built much of the military he inherited. Their troops pulled back to the coast, but they still had equipment to remove and facilities from which to decamp. Sharaa also needed to keep a shattered country functioning while he found other sources of support.

Perhaps above all else, Syria needs money for reconstruction, and Sharaa needs his independence. Erdoğan doesn’t just want to replace Russian domination: he wants to rebuild the Ottoman Empire, of which Syria was always a key province. 

Multiple patrons seem to be Sharaa’s answer. This puts him in bed with the Saudis, perhaps the Israelis, but certainly the United States. For the former terrorist’s own private reasons, he is rapidly locking himself in as a Western ally, or at least in opposition to the status quo ante bellum.

Trump gave him the room he needed. By lifting U.S. sanctions, the President opened the way for Syria to attract investment from America and the Gulf, and to trade its way out of its wreckage. Already, U.S. companies are flowing in, even to the extent that Chevron is reconstructing the damaged oil pipeline from Iraq to Baniyas on the Syrian coast.

The Saudis pitched in: despite their “friends close, enemies closer” defense pact with Ankara, they have no desire to see Turkish power restored. And as he always does, Trump conditioned much of what’s to come on Syria joining the Abraham Accords, a prospect no doubt distasteful to a new strongman with origins in the Golan Heights, but likely necessary if he wants to end the Israeli security zone in his south.

All of this adds up to a new order.

Meanwhile, every ruler buying Russian protection can see what happened to Assad. Moscow had a longer relationship with Damascus, and a greater stake in keeping it, than it has with any of its new African “friends.” Those men hired Russian troops to guarantee their power vis-a-vis Paris. A dacha beside Assad’s near Moscow would be a poor substitute.

When Putin rescued Assad with direct Russian intervention in 2015, he meant to cement Russia’s return as a great power. Instead, Russia spent nine years defending a regime that collapsed anyway, and lost the bases it went to war to preserve.

For all his talk of restoring Russian greatness, Putin has managed to lose what even poor Boris Yeltsin was able to keep.

[If you appreciate geopolitical analysis like this, subscribe on my site -- link in bio -- to get it daily, better formatted, with more illustrations and links.]

text:
India Converted Half of Asia Without an Army.

One of the largest cultural expansions in history was carried out almost entirely by merchants waiting for the monsoon wind to change.

Over roughly a thousand years India gave much of Asia its religions, its epics, its scripts and its ideas of kingship, using convoys timed to the monsoon's twice-yearly reversal rather than armies. Buddhism set aside caste and the food laws that made travel among strangers difficult, and it moved east in the holds of merchant ships until, by one count, China had thirty thousand monasteries and close to two million monks. The courts of Southeast Asia adopted Sanskrit, Indian law and Indian statecraft by choice, judging it the best system on offer to a king who wanted to look legitimate at home and abroad. The former Thai capital Ayutthaya took its name from Ayodhya, the city of Rama. Angkor Wat, the largest religious monument on earth, is a working diagram of the Indian cosmos, its moat standing for the ocean that surrounds Mount Meru.

The era's other great power took a different route. China's Confucian order required a foreign ruler to acknowledge the emperor as his superior before exchange could happen, tribute, not trade. The ports of the region answered to Chinese demand while its temples, script and kingship were Indian-influenced.

It wasn't wholly peaceful. The Indianised kingdoms fought each other readily enough. What the pattern lacked, for the better part of a thousand years, was an Indian conqueror.

I've written up the full story, with sources and further reading. Link to essay in the comments below.

text:
25 years ago this morning I had my hands inside a 1970 Monte Carlo. 

Cary's Service Center, Opelika, Alabama.  $5/hr, under the table, pulling an alternator.  I was 19.  Enrolled in ROTC at Auburn and doing considerably more drinking than studying, if we're being honest about it.

I walked into the break room just in time to watch the south tower get hit.

Took us a minute to understand it was real and not some 2001 version of War of the Worlds.  When the gravity landed, I wiped my hands, clocked out, and walked across the street to talk to an Army recruiter named SFC Coffin.

Took the ASVAB, got offered a $20k signing bonus to go 97b, counterintelligence, but ended up going 11b at MEPS for a zero dollar bonus 🤣.  Cause dad was infantry so I wanted to be.  

Lied at MEPS about an ACL injury which definitely ended up biting me in the ass - barely had time to put a uniform on before being chaptered out.

I didn't enlist to defend anybody.  I enlisted to go to Afghanistan and kill people so I could be “a hero” instead of a drunk failure.  A 19 year old with a drinking problem and a head full of anger.

I never got there.

Never made it to Afghanistan - in fact never made it out of Ft Benning and the attempt at service never fixed whatever was broke in me either, which is what I'd actually been counting on it for.

The next two decades did what they did.  Walked into an ER with a .46 and spent nine days in the ICU.  Heart attack at 35.  Another at 36.  Stabbed.  Homeless on the dope track in South Memphis.

There’s another story here that needs to be told.

Two weeks after the morning I decided I wanted to burn Afghanistan to the ground, a baby girl was born in it.

She survived the war.  Survived the Taliban.  Survived things I'm not going to type on this post.  She came out of one of our safe houses in Mazar-e Sharif and made it all the way to Memphis, Tennessee.

This spring, Jess and I adopted her.

On Father's Day I drove in from Georgia and got to my oldest daughter's house late, not expecting a thing.  

Came down the stairs to cake, candles, sparklers, balloons.  My first thought was oh “shit, whose birthday did I forget.”

Then it hit me that Arezo had done all of it.  For me.  I am not an emotional guy.  She got a couple tears out of me anyway.

She's at Rhodes now.  Studying for the MCAT, shadowing a surgeon, volunteering at a clinic, working full time.

I say all that to say this.

Anger is the cheapest fuel there is.  It burns hot, it burns fast, and then you're sitting on the side of the road with nothing.  I know because I ran on it for years and it left me exactly there.

The kid at the service center wanted to take a country apart.

He got a daughter out of it instead.

Today we remember the 2,977.  We remember the ones who went UP the stairs.  We remember the twenty years of caskets that came after, and the brothers we're still burying who made it home and never actually got home.

Then tomorrow we get up and do something with it.

I love y'all.

text:
Tommy Robinson’s Peasant Act

A 2015 sting that was real, a 2026 finance film that wasn’t the answer, and the “peasants” line that only works if you don’t look at the paperwork.

In the same week of September 2026, two films appeared bearing Robinson’s signature method: take a real scandal, build a defence or an accusation on top of it that the real facts can’t support, and let the kernel of truth carry the weight of everything stacked above it.

The first, “Tommy Robinson exposes a Jihadi spy working inside parliament,” retells the story of Afzal Amin, the Conservative candidate whose 2015 campaign collapsed when Robinson secretly filmed him plotting a fake EDL march. It was posted by something called SpyNews UK, a separate channel from Urban Scoop, though the material and method are Robinson’s. 

The second, “The Dispatches Deception: The Hit Job That Collapsed Under the Evidence,” is credited directly to Urban Scoop and is Robinson’s rebuttal to Channel 4’s “Tommy Robinson: Where’s the Money Gone?”, the @C4Dispatches investigation into his finances that aired the same night, 9 September 2026.

The part of the Amin story that’s true

Amin was the Conservative prospective parliamentary candidate for Dudley North in 2015, a marginal seat. He met with EDL figures, including Robinson, and was recorded discussing a plan for the EDL to announce a demonstration against a proposed mosque, which would then be “cancelled” days before the election so Amin could present himself as the man who brought peace to the town. He told Robinson he’d be an “unshakeable ally” in Parliament.

Robinson leaked the tapes to the Mail on Sunday, and Amin resigned as candidate on 23 March 2015. He had also served eleven years in the Army and trained at Sandhurst. None of this is in dispute.

The pamphlet, inflated

A week after the sting, the Mail on Sunday reported that Amin had briefly belonged, at 18, to the Birmingham wing of the Murabitun, a small Sufi-derived sect founded by the Scottish convert Ian Dallas. The group is generally described as Holocaust-questioning and antisemitic rather than as an organiser of violence.

A text credited to Amin two years later, when he was 19 or 20, does use the language of “mujahidun” and describes building separate Muslim “villages” in European cities. Amin disputes writing most of it, saying a former member of the group doctored an account he’d sent him and fabricated the closing paragraphs, and calls the document defamatory. That dispute has never been resolved.

Robinson’s video collapses all of this into leaflets describing how the Mujahideen would set up in cities across Britain and then explode and take over certain areas, which isn’t what the text says, and places it three years before Sandhurst. He was commissioned in April 2003; the disputed text dates to 1994, roughly eight to nine years earlier.

A genuinely troubling, disputed document from Amin’s teenage years becomes, in the retelling, a confirmed terror plot MI5 somehow missed.

The claims that don’t check out

1. The cabinet seat.

Amin was an unelected candidate who had not yet won a seat in Parliament, let alone a place in government. No source supports the claim that Cameron offered him one, and it would be constitutionally extraordinary if true.

2. Shabana Mahmood’s cousin.

Robinson claims in the film that the “money man” at the meeting identified himself as Mahmood’s first cousin. No outlet from 2015 or since identifies him or connects him to Mahmood. She also didn’t become Home Secretary until September 2025, a decade after the events described, which undercuts the claim that she was signing off on anything related to it.

3. The Prince Harry and William connection. This one is real as a claim, just not as a fact. Amin’s own campaign material described him as having served as education officer to both princes during his Army career. It was reported in 2015 as his own account, never independently confirmed.

4. What the Amin video gets right - by accident

A £45,000 payment does check out, and Robinson’s own rebuttal film removes the need to infer the connection: he confirms on camera, in “The Dispatches Deception,” that this is the same payment Dispatches found and the same story the “Jihadi spy” video retells.

The film Dispatches provoked

“Where’s the Money Gone?” was the product of a year-long investigation by reporter @Matt_A_Shea into Robinson’s fundraising, company filings, court records, and cryptocurrency transactions. It raises two distinct allegations.

The first is fraud: shown a case in which a survivor, referred to in press coverage of the programme as “Kate,” said she never received money publicly raised in her name, plus, in the programme, a further example involving funds promised for a headstone that never materialised, Sir Max Hill KC, the former Director of Public Prosecutions, told Dispatches it was “likely to be fraud” to tell a victim you’re raising money for them and tell the public the same, when the victim neither knows about it nor receives a penny.

The second is perjury: material uncovered by the programme, including a 2018 legal agreement Robinson signed on behalf of Lennon Consultancy, a company he told the High Court in 2022 was not his, which Hill said could justify a separate criminal investigation. 

Dispatches also found an active Metro Bank account registered to “Mr S C Lennon” capable of receiving funds, despite Robinson’s repeated claims to supporters that he had been “debanked by every single bank possible.”

Robinson responded that the account was personal and unused for donations, and told Dispatches he believed money had reached the families in question. No charges have been brought and no court has made a finding against him; Hill’s comments are an assessment offered to a broadcaster, not a verdict.

“The Dispatches Deception” is Urban Scoop’s answer, released the same night. It bills itself as “a forensic dismantling,” promising recordings, messages, bank transfers and witnesses the public “deserves to see,” and on the specifics it does engage.

On the £45,000, Robinson says on camera the payment was the Mail on Sunday’s fee for the Amin story, paid to Jenna Lennon rather than to him because he needed money to relocate and protect his family while the story broke.

On the fraud allegation, he brings on three other survivors to say they did receive money, plays a recorded call with one confirming ongoing support, and turns the film’s fire on the credibility of the one survivor whose account anchors Hill’s assessment, using recordings of her that predate the investigation.

What the film doesn’t do is address the specific evidence each allegation actually rests on.

The perjury question turns on a signed 2018 legal agreement and emails showing Robinson managing Lennon Consultancy’s affairs, not on whether the £45,000 had an innocent origin, and neither is mentioned.

The fraud question turns on why this survivor’s account differs from the other four, and Robinson’s answer is that she is lying and colluding with the reporter, which challenges her credibility rather than the substance of what changed in her story.

The house style

Neither Robinson film is a one-off. Urban Scoop’s catalogue runs “SILENCED,” “The Rape of Britain,” and “Lawfare: A Totalitarian State,” all following the same structure: aggrieved-insider narrative, archive-footage montage, direct-to-camera monologue, released at a moment of external pressure.

“The Dispatches Deception” itself carries an on-screen production credit for a pseudonymous handle, 187LASCD, confirmed by its own title cards; the same handle is credited as director on “Lawfare,” alongside a separately credited writer, Chris Agoston, on that title’s on-screen credits.

No filed officer or public identity attaches to the 187LASCD handle. That anonymity sits oddly against an operation that markets itself on transparency: a named, self-branded presenter in front of the camera, an unidentified production credit behind it.

Urban Scoop presents itself as “independent, autonomous journalism,” “genuine, unbiased, and corporate-free.”

Hope Not Hate’s June 2022 investigation, “Lennon’s Filthy Lucre,” disputed that framing: it found donations to Urban Scoop and a second company, SquareFT, were both channelled into an account labelled “Donate TR,” and concluded, as its own investigative characterisation rather than a court finding, that Robinson was in practice a “silent director” controlling both while undischarged from bankruptcy, which the report said would have been illegal at the time.

Who’s actually on the paperwork

Companies House confirms the shape of that arrangement, even where Robinson’s name is absent from it.

Freestyle Freelance Ltd (company no. 13789284), the entity reported as trading as Urban Scoop, was incorporated in December 2021 with its sole director and person of significant control listed as Adam Geary, the associate Hope Not Hate identified as Robinson’s “number two,” known as “Nem.”

The company entered creditors’ voluntary liquidation in December 2023 and remains in liquidation.

Hope & Pride Ltd (company no. 11871782), used to process donations and merchandise sales, was incorporated in March 2019 with Jenna Lennon, Robinson’s ex-wife, as sole director. It entered liquidation in September 2023.

The UK Insolvency Service confirmed in an official notice that the company owed an estimated £319,000 in unpaid corporation tax, that no accounts were ever filed at Companies House, and that Lennon was disqualified as a company director for seven years for failing to preserve or hand over accounting records to the liquidator.

Court reporting put the company’s unexplained revenue at £1.18 million, with no paperwork showing where it went.

Neither Robinson nor his production alias appears as a listed director of any of these companies. Urban Scoop, SpyNews UK and 187LASCD exist as brands and handles, not as registered entities in their own right.

None of this is new in kind. In June 2022, before either liquidation, Robinson told the High Court, in the same hearing where the Lennon Consultancy question arose, that he had spent around £100,000 gambling in casinos and online over the preceding two years, on top of money spent on “drink, alcohol, partying,” while receiving £1,000 to £4,000 a month from supporter donations.

That is his own sworn evidence, not an allegation. It establishes, four years before Dispatches and from Robinson’s own mouth, the pattern the later investigation would spend a year trying to trace at scale: money raised for a cause, and no clean account of where it went.

The peasant and the platform

One line from “The Dispatches Deception,” visible in its own captions (see screenshot below), is worth pausing on for what it reveals rather than what it claims. 

Robinson, earnestly addressing the camera, escalates through a list of clichéd right-wing/Elite-Populist adversaries: the “world media”; the “globalist elite”; the “establishment”; “the best funded ideology this world’s ever seen,” and lands on; “we’re on the front line like peasants.”

It’s a textbook piece of populist inversion: cast the target of an investigation as the powerless commoner, and the professional broadcaster asking questions about his finances as the distant elite.

The rhetorical move has a long lineage on the populist right, positioning a media figure or movement as underdogs standing against a shadowy, over-resourced establishment, even where the actual resource asymmetry runs the other way.

It only works if the audience doesn’t look too closely at who is actually amplifying the operation making the claim. What’s documented is platform power and a headline stage appearance, not a published donation ledger: Elon Musk, the world’s richest man, reinstated Robinson’s @X account in 2023 and addressed the “Unite the Kingdom” rally Robinson organised, by video link, on 13 September 2025, telling the crowd of more than 100,000 that “violence is coming” and they should “fight back or die.”

No genuine peasantry in history has had its platform reinstated, its message amplified, and its rally addressed, all by the wealthiest man alive.

The framing depends on the audience not noticing that its author is, by any reasonable measure, one of the better-amplified figures in the story he is telling.

Why it matters

A real, well-documented scandal supplies the credibility for both films. On top of the Amin story, one already-disputed document from his youth is stretched into a confirmed terror plot, an unelected candidate’s imagined cabinet seat appears from nowhere, and a future Home Secretary is linked to the 2015 meeting through a relative nobody has independently identified. 

On top of the Dispatches investigation, Robinson contests both allegations at length, without ever addressing the specific evidence either one is actually built on: the signed 2018 agreement behind the perjury claim, or the change in one survivor’s account behind the fraud claim.

Underneath both sits the same structure: an operation that brands itself independent and unbiased while its own paperwork, where it exists at all, names an ex-wife and an associate rather than its public face; that took in over a million pounds through a company that filed no accounts and can produce no record of where it went; and that responds to scrutiny of that record with a film calling itself the answer, while positioning its own presenter, amplified by the world’s richest man, as a ‘peasant’ on the ‘front line’.

Both films end on the same framing: Robinson’s legal jeopardy as punishment for a ‘service’ he once did the country.

Seven years, the figure he repeats for what Dispatches is supposedly trying to “lock him up” for, is the real statutory maximum for perjury under the Perjury Act 1911, not an invented number. But no perjury charge has been brought against him, let alone a conviction. 

Treating the ceiling sentence for a charge that doesn’t yet exist as an imminent punishment is its own kind of inflation, the same move as the Amin pamphlet, just run on a legal statute instead of a teenage document. That is the pattern that matters: not outright fabrication, but a fluent answer to everything except the specific evidence each charge actually turns on.

text:
The traditional practice of raising the eldest son of a Punjabi (or Sindhi/Balochi) Hindu family as a Sikh is known as Gurdino. 
•The Tradition: For generations, many extended families—particularly among trading castes like Khatris, Aroras, and certain sehajdhari lineages—dedicated their first-born son to the Sikh faith by having him grow his hair and adopt Sikh traditions, while the younger siblings remained free to practice Hindu or mixed traditions. 
•Historical Context (Mughal Era): Culturally and historically, some families viewed Sikhs as defenders or the "sword arm" of the community against outside oppression, leading families to offer a son to the Khalsa. 
•Colonial Motivations (British Era): After 1857, British military recruitment policies heavily favored distinct "martial races," giving preferential hiring and economic benefits in the army to baptized (Keshadhari) Sikhs. Many non-agricultural or trading Hindu families used this practice to secure military employment and economic stability for their eldest son.
•Modern Reality: While some families maintained this joint Hindu-Sikh identity well into the 20th century, communal polarizations later caused the informal tradition to largely fade away. You can read a deeper historical overview on the Wikipedia Gurdino Page.

text:
As a teenager, I would mow my neighbors' yards in Charlotte for $20 (It was the late 90s). A group of men lived in a house a few doors down from us. They rarely cut their grass. They also kept to themselves. 

One day, I knocked on the door and offered to take care of their yard every other week. My neighbor took me up on the offer but said, “I’ll pay you $20 to cut the front yard. Don’t worry about the backyard.” 

I didn’t ask any questions. Full price, half the work. I cut their yard as often as needed. 

A few years later, in July of 2020. I was awakened at 6:00 am, looked out the window, and saw a lot of commotion around my neighbor’s house. I sat on our front steps and watched the FBI, ATF, and local police raid the house. They took all the men into custody. They also confiscated guns, ammunition, and other types of evidence. 

I found out later that my neighbors, for whom I mowed the grass, were a sleeper cell for an international terrorist group. I had no idea. 

The FBI has been monitoring them from a rental house across the street. I’ve always wondered if there is an FBI file somewhere with pictures of me talking with the cell group leader on the front porch. 

Either way, I tell this story today (9/11) to express thankfulness to the intelligence agencies, military, and first responders who monitor these activities for the purpose of keeping our country safe. Most of the time, we don't even know these things are happening. #neverforget

Note: You can learn about this operation by looking up “Operation Smokescreen.” CNN’s documentary “Declassified” has an episode on this operation titled “The Terrorists Next Door” (Season 3, Episode 3).

text:
THE ‘TROUBLESOME’ MAU MAU LAWYER
Some men fall back on comfortable choices. C.M.G. Argwings-Kodhek fell on the difficult ones.
Born in 1923 in Malanga, Gem, Clement Michael George Argwings-Kodhek was a bright young man whose journey took him from St. Mary's Yala to St. Mary's College, Kisubi, in Uganda, where he sat for his Cambridge School Certificate. He graduated from Makerere College in 1940 with a teaching diploma, proceeding to teach at Kapsabet Boys High School. Here, he would cross paths with a young Daniel arap Moi. But teaching was not where his ambitions ended.
A scholarship took him to England to study teaching. Instead, he set his sights on law, a discipline the colonial authorities did not allow Africans to pursue on their scholarships. His scholarship was terminated after a year, forcing his father to sell cattle to keep his son in school. Argwings-Kodhek persevered, qualified as a barrister and was called to the Bar at Lincoln’s Inn, the first East African to do so.
He could have stayed in England, practised law and lived comfortably. He chose Kenya.
Back home, the colonial government offered him a position as a legal assistant. He soon walked away from it and into a much more dangerous calling: defending Africans detained and prosecuted during the Mau Mau Emergency, often for little or no pay. To the colonial authorities, he became the troublesome Mau Mau lawyer. To many Africans, he became something else: proof that the colonial order could be challenged not only in the forests and detention camps, but also in the courtroom.
And Kodhek was not content merely to defend individuals. He entered politics, founded the Nairobi District African Congress and later became one of the legal minds helping Kenya's delegation navigate the difficult negotiations at Lancaster House. When the colonial administration tried to restrict African politics to district-based parties, he pushed against the walls being built around the country's emerging nationalism.
Then came Hola. When 11 detainees were killed at Hola detention camp in 1959 and the colonial authorities attempted to conceal what had happened, Kodhek used his connections with friends in Britain to help expose the truth. The story travelled from a remote detention camp in Kenya to the corridors of power in London. The resulting inquiry badly damaged the credibility of the colonial administration.
At Independence, the lawyer became a statesman. Jomo Kenyatta appointed him Assistant Minister for Defence in 1963. He later headed Natural Resources and, in 1967, became Minister for Foreign Affairs. He was also the first Member of Parliament for Gem, serving from Independence until 1969.
But the man who could be diplomatic was never afraid to be blunt.
In Parliament, Kodhek could dismiss noisy opponents as ‘sounding like old crows’, while arguing for one united Kenya. His nationalism was not merely rhetoric. In a 1965 Budget debate, he appealed to his fellow legislators to put Kenya above all and leave the country better than they found it.
He warned against tribalism, called for peace between communities and cautioned that liberty could be lost when divisions and secret political groupings were allowed to fester.
In 1969, after two years as Foreign Minister, Argwings-Kodhek died in a mysterious road accident in Kilimani, Nairobi; just months before his former political rival, Tom Mboya, would meet a similarly violent fate.
Today, the road where he died bears his name.
Perhaps that is one small way a country remembers a man who spent his life insisting that Kenya could, and should, become something greater.

text:
From Karl Streed -

I BET YOU DIDN'Y KNOW ABOUT THIS: AFTER FLIGHT 77 HIT THE PENTAGON ON 9/11, THE FOLLOWING HAPPENED.

A daycare facility inside the Pentagon had many children, including infants who were in heavy cribs. The daycare supervisor, looking at all the children they needed to evacuate, was in a panic over what they could do.

There were many children, mostly toddlers, as well as the infants who would need to be taken out with the cribs. There was no time to try to bundle them into carriers and strollers.

Just then a young Marine came running into the center and asked what they needed. After hearing what the center director was trying to do, he ran back out into the hallway and disappeared. The director thought, "Well, here we are, on our own."

About 2 minutes later, that Marine returned with 40 other Marines in tow.

Each of them grabbed a crib with a child, and the rest started gathering up toddlers.

The director and her staff then helped them take all the children out of the center and down toward the park near the Potomac .

Once they got about 3/4 of a mile outside the building, the Marines stopped in the park, and then did a fabulous thing - they formed a circle with the cribs, which were quite sturdy and heavy, like the covered wagons in the Old West.

Inside this circle of cribs, they put the toddlers, to keep them from wandering off. 

Outside this circle were the 40 Marines, forming a perimeter around the children and waiting for instructions. There they remained until the parents could be notified and come get their children.

The chaplain then said, "I don't think any of us saw nor heard of this on any of the news stories of the day. It was an incredible story of our men there.” There wasn't a dry eye in the room.

The thought of those Marines and what they did and how fast they reacted; could we expect any less from them? It was one of the most touching stories from the Pentagon.

It's the military, not the politicians that ensures our right to life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness. 

It's the military who salutes the flag, who serves beneath the flag, and whose coffin is draped by the flag.

If you care to offer the smallest token of recognition and appreciation for the military, please pass this on and pray for our men and women, who have served and are currently serving our country, and honor the memory of those who have given the ultimate sacrifice!

God Bless The USA!

Never forget!!!

text:
For many of us, myself included, #September11 is a day of remembrance, a day to honour fellowship, courage, sacrifice and the very best of humanity. 

But today is also a day to remember and never forget the very worst of which humanity is capable, the forms in which that evil and darkness can manifest, and how readily –whether through insidious erosion or sudden violence–the things we can take for granted, including freedom, sovereignty, security and liberty, can be attacked, diminished or lost. 

Today, I choose to remember the heroes like Welles Crowther, a young man who repeatedly returned to the South Tower to lead others to safety –many in NYC will remember him as "the Man in the Red Bandana".

Rick Rescorla, who helped evacuate thousands before going back for more. FDNY Battalion Chief Orio Palmer, who climbed to the South Tower’s impact zone. 

And Todd Beamer, the passengers and crew of Flight 93, who fearlessly fought  their attackers back before losing their lives.

And the thousands and thousands of firefighters, police officers, first responders and ordinary people whose names we don't know. 

And then there were those who were far from Ground Zero, but not beyond the reach of what happened that day. 

In Gander and communities across Canada, people opened their schools, churches, community centres and homes to tens of thousands of stranded strangers whose flights had been diverted. They offered food, shelter, comfort and fellowship.

That is what I choose to carry forward, and what I'll never forget.

text:
Zac Brown did not buy 400 acres of Georgia farmland to build a private retreat. Instead, he turned it into a camp that serves children in summer and veterans for the rest of the year. The idea had been with him since childhood.

In 2011, Brown purchased the land in Fayetteville, about 30 miles south of Atlanta, and began building Camp Southern Ground. Its summer sessions bring together children ages 7 to 17, including kids with autism spectrum disorder, learning differences, military families, underserved youth, and typically developing campers.

When summer ends, the property shifts toward military service. Warrior Week supports veterans after military service, while Warrior PATHH focuses on post-traumatic growth among combat veterans. The organization says its veteran programs are offered at no cost to participants. One piece of farmland now supports two different groups through a shared mission of connection.

text:
Her attorney arrived twenty minutes later carrying copies for every adult standing in the driveway.

“The trust will pursue repayment for documented misuse of Ruth’s accounts,” he said. “Discretionary family access is revoked permanently.”

Blake swore.

Aunt Patricia cried.

Mom kept repeating, “This is not what Christmas is about.”

I looked at the vans packed for a holiday inside a house they had never even asked to enter.

“You’re right,” I said. “Christmas was never supposed to be about taking.”

Dad finally looked at me.

“Nora, please. We have nowhere to go.”

That sentence almost broke me.

Then I remembered fifteen years of empty chairs I had never been offered.

“There are hotels in town,” I said.

They left before sunset.

No dramatic shouting.

No grand collapse.

Just twenty-three people loading suitcases back into vans while the ocean wind did what shame could not.

That night, I lit Grandma’s fireplace and placed one slice of pie on her blue plate.

I cried, but not because I was lonely.

Because the house was finally peaceful.

Over the following months, the estate recovered enough money to fund Grandma’s favorite coastal library program.

I kept the beach house open for people who had loved her quietly: her nurse, her neighbor, her book club, and the young cashier she used to tip every Friday.

My family sent cards the following Christmas.

I did not open most of them.

For fifteen years, they forgot to invite me and called it an accident.

Grandma remembered everything.

And when they finally showed up at my door, I gave them the only gift they had earned.

The truth, wrapped in legal paper.

text:
Dear Mike,

I came across Road Runner: A Noir Mystery  and was especially drawn to the way you combine a missing daughter, a  fanatical cult, criminal violence, and a relentless rescue mission into a  high-stakes noir mystery.

Detective Heinz Calloway’s desperate  search for his seventeen-year-old daughter, Josh Pratt’s pursuit of the  God’s Breath cult, and the unlikely alliance with rapper, hacker, and  tech genius Ninja Preston create a powerful visual and emotional  framework for a cinematic trailer. I can envision a story that moves  through the dangerous trail of terrified former members, the Colorado  Rockies, the hidden compound beneath the Continental Divide, and Josh  being forced into a brutal fight for survival as enemies close in from  every direction.

With Road Runner: A Noir Mystery ahead, I  think a cinematic trailer could offer noir mystery readers,  crime-thriller fans, and readers drawn to fast-paced biker fiction, cult  conspiracies, and high-stakes rescue stories a compelling introduction  to the heart of the book.
